#9046. Lighting design a "strategic economic investment" says Signify's Sameer Sodhi

According to business leader of entertainment and Color Kinetics at lighting brand Signify, Sameer Sodhi, lit-up architecture and public installations can encourage interaction, strengthen local identity and support overall wellbeing.

Sodhi explained that for decades, the value of a building has been measured by appearance, energy performance, return on investment and construction costs. A building’s lighting design is one of the most influential factors but is often overlooked and seen as a “finishing touch”.

He added that well-designed lighting can shape the experience of places, support local economies and strengthen communities.

“The question is no longer whether lighting matters,” Sodhi said. “But whether we can accurately measure the (overlooked) value it creates.”

Sodhi points to a recent study by lighting brand Color Kinetics that examined four illuminated spaces across the United States and found that lighting generated social, economic, and cultural benefits “well beyond the initial investment”.

“The report assesses lighting through a broader framework that includes community engagement, tourism, economic development, media visibility, partnerships, sustainability and health and wellbeing,” Sodhi explained.

“Rather than viewing lighting as an isolated building system, it recognised it as infrastructure capable of influencing how cities function and how communities connect,” he added.

Sodhi cites the lighting of Daniel Hoan Memorial Bridge in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, as an example, which has transformed the infrastructure into a “dynamic visual icon” that reflects the city’s identity and connects residents and visitors to the waterfront.

“The bridge now hosts community and civic events, causes and initiatives and annual festivals, while serving as a canvas for civic celebrations throughout the year,” he said.

According to Sodhi, architectural lighting also creates economic value. For example, the thoughtful lighting design of West Sacramento’s Barns in California has supported the area’s placemaking.

Although the venue was originally conceived as an event and dining venue, the strategic lighting design has helped establish it as the focal point for the surrounding mixed-use district, which includes spaces for hosting concerts, festivals, community activities and sporting events.

Sodhi explained that, because of the building’s lit-up impact, approximately ten residential developments have since been built or are under construction nearby, highlighting the role “quality public spaces” can play in wider regeneration.

“Importantly, the value created extends beyond construction economics,” added Sodhi. “Visitors stay longer, businesses benefit from increased footfall, and the location develops an identity that encourages repeat visits and investment.”

According to Sodhi, lighting can also serve as a form of public communication. For example, Philadelphia City Hall’s lighting is programmed to respond to national celebrations, charitable campaigns and civic events, “transforming a historic landmark into a dynamic expression of the city’s identity”.

“Whether celebrating sporting victories or marking important social causes, the building becomes an active participant in public life rather than simply a backdrop,” added Sodhi.

This also applies to Nashville’s illuminated installation, Loqui, Sodhi explained. The artwork includes words and stories from more than 400 local residents and demonstrates how illuminated public art can amplify local voices and bring a community together.

“Rather than lighting serving the artwork, the lighting becomes integral to the experience itself,” he added.

“These projects suggest that good lighting is no longer simply about visibility. It is about participation.”

Sodhi added that buildings are also assessed by how efficiently they operate, but also how effectively they create meaningful experiences.

“Architectural lighting is uniquely positioned to support that ambition,” he explained. “It can extend the usability of spaces after dark, strengthen local identity, encourage social interaction and help transform ordinary infrastructure into memorable landmarks.”

“When thoughtfully integrated from the earliest stages of design, lighting becomes a strategic investment rather than an aesthetic upgrade,” he added. “Perhaps this is the real measure of good design.”

To learn more about Signify, visit its website. To learn more about Color Kinetics, click here.

#9045. Mummy in Glasgow may be repatriated to Egypt following removal from display

The Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum in Glasgow previously had mummified human remains on display in its ancient Egypt gallery

A mummy removed from display last month at Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum could be returned to Egypt. According to the Scottish newspaper The Sunday Post, Egyptian authorities have asked for the ­mummified remains of the priest Nekht to be repatriated.

Glasgow Life, the charitable organisation which operates the museum, confirmed to The Art Newspaper that it had received a request to send remains of Nekht back to Egypt. The organisation has not confirmed the origin of the request.

Last month, officials at the museum removed the coffin and mummified corpse of the ancient Egyptian priest from public view. A spokesperson for Glasgow Life said: “Glasgow Life Museums’ draft Human Remains Policy proposes human remains should only be displayed where there is documented and informed consent from the deceased individual or, in appropriate circumstances, their descendants. In the absence of such consent, we believe removing ancient Egyptian human remains from display is more respectful to the deceased individuals.”

The move comes after the International Council of Museums (Icom) revised its code of ethics in June, recommending the “inherent dignity” of human remains be upheld; Icom does not state however that all remains should be removed from display.

Meanwhile the Hunterian gallery in Glasgow confirmed to Museums Journal that it had covered an open sarcophagus containing the mummified remains of Lady Shep-En-Hor following an internal ethical review, although the sarcophagus itself remains on display.

The removal of the mummified remains at Kelvingrove and other museums feeds into current debate in the UK museums and heritage sector over the care and display of human remains. In response to the museum's policy on the lack of consent by the deceased, Stuart Robertson, the former director of the Charles Rennie Mackintosh Society in Glasgow, wrote on LinkedIn that “applying modern, 21st-century bureaucratic consent standards retrospectively to ancient history is an absurd and impossible standard. It completely undermines the educational mission of public museums”.

Last year, officials at the Manchester Museum asked visitors if the mummified remains of an Egyptian woman should remain on display. The mummy, known as Asru, was subsequently taken off public view.

“Asru now lies in the museum’s stores within her outer coffin, which will remain closed, but this is not intended to be her permanent resting place. We are thinking about how we better care for ancestors, in line with the wishes of the dead and of living communities,” says the museum's website.

#9044. Cinga Samson "Ukuphuthelwa" @ White Cube Gallery, NYC

South African artist Cinga Samson’s exhibition of new paintings is titled ‘Ukuphuthelwa’, an isiXhosa word in the artist’s native language that translates as ‘unable to sleep’. Unlike the English word ‘insomnia’, the isiXhosa term carries no negative connotation and accordingly, for Samson, sleeplessness is not a condition to be cured but a state of spiritual alertness, a sensitivity that deepens in the dark. Rendered in the artist’s signature occluded palette of near-blacks, carbon and deep Prussian blues, Samson’s scenes depict men-like figures, dogs in overgrown fields and portraits of plant life native to South Africa. Encouraging slow, contemplative looking, a sense of existential gravity pervades Samson’s new series of oil paintings, attempting to depict a vast reality that is continuously in motion. As the artist has it, his quandary pertains to the existential question of how to create a ‘true and honest painting'. The exhibition will be on view through April 18, 2026.

With ‘Ukuphuthelwa’, Samson considers his role as an artist in relation to his inability to represent the whole truth of reality, and the fact that he can merely make symbols. Between the static, painted sign and the fluid experience it gestures towards, he contends that there exists a gulf that no image can close. Though the technical mastery and convincing realism of these paintings appear to invite interpretation, the artist asserts that his work confronts the very dilemma of representation: that the image can only ever be a relative symbol of what it reflects, never its equivalent. Acknowledging the open-ended nature of symbols and their subjective interpretation, Samson takes the figure of the dog as an example. The viewer may, for instance, look at Intsingiselo II (2026) and perceive the loyalty conventionally associated with dogs, while an amaXhosa understanding might highlight the dog as signifying the guiding, protective principles of ancestors. Comprising painstaking detail and deft brushwork, Samson’s paintings do not disguise the limits of representation but, rather, aspire to harness his skills towards that which exceeds the representable. Above all, the artist’s work seeks out the authority of the unnameable and the territory of the sublime, one in which the divine is not found elsewhere but present in the vernacular of all things.

Samson’s larger compositions carry a palpable sense of reverence and ceremony. In Umlindo (Watcher) (2026), figures are gathered in a forest clearing with wildflower bouquets and lengths of fabric, a scene that carries the visual grammar of ritual without specifying its addressee or terms. For Samson however, ‘the ritual itself is not the important thing – it’s an opening to what exists beyond’, and the paintings use the aesthetics of ritual to speak to a collective need for orientation, as well as the capacity of ritual to mediate an encounter with a vast unknown. That the works are titled with enigmatic words and phrases in isiXhosa, such as Imfihlo (Secret) and Intsingiselo (Meaning) (both 2026), infer the same problem the paintings contend with – the instability of interpretation as it pertains to the knowable and unknowable. Each word carries a weight in isiXhosa that its English translation approaches but can never fully reach; here, just as between the painted sign and living referent, meaning slips between the interstice of two languages.

The objects, people and settings that recur in these paintings and across Samson’s oeuvre are identifiable and quotidian, yet Samson corrals in each an unexplained mystery. In Tshee (2026), a vast field stretches out, the silhouetted trees meeting a murky sky, though the void of the night is interrupted by a moonwashed cloud, its brilliant white destabilising the eerie, cold atmosphere suffused with majesty. ‘The sky can be so friendly, but sometimes so heavy, dark, so scary. It’s the same energy, but it exists in different forms’, Samson notes, conjuring an oscillation between the approachable and the overwhelming that recalls the affective register of the sublime. Sithini ngelilitye (2026), distils the same sensation: a rocky crag emerges from arid undergrowth, its surface rendered in forensic detail against a sky of barely-there wash, charging the scene with the same quality of mute enormity.

Marshalling light ‘like a magic trick’, Samson imparts a unique kind of rhythm to his paintings – a flickering that emerges and disperses across the picture plane, granting varying degrees of visibility to the dark, nighttime scenes. Producing an unsteadiness that is at once optical and psychical, the artist leaves large sections of the painting’s under-drawing visible to lend moments of transparency to the work. In Isiganeko (2026), for example, thin layers of glaze are applied and wiped back in his typical style, a means of building colour that lends the figures a brooding chromatic density, whilst elsewhere, in the undergrowth and the bird caught mid-flight, the under-drawing is left entirely exposed. In all Samson’s figures, the pupils of the eyes are left unpainted and allow ‘light’ to further circulate, a decision that renders them porous, so they are ‘completely one with the whole painting’. Without pupils, these figures are not personified identities, but ‘human’ forms enmeshed with the painting’s landscape and atmosphere, no element ever possessing full mastery over the other. In places where the ‘trick’ of painting reveals itself, it is as if Samson’s works were stepping back from the pretence or promise of representation. What ‘Ukuphuthelwa’ reaches towards is not individual transcendence in subordination, but rather the mystery that can be unearthed in ordinary forms, whose immanent magic is available to those who are sensitive to it. This is the condition that ‘Ukuphuthelwa’ ultimately describes: not an absence or deficit, but a hypersensitivity that affords everything in existence the same potential for eliciting wonder or fear. Samson’s pupilless figures do not ‘look’ outward because the figures’ knowing comes from within the world they inhabit, a shared knowledge that exists between the bowing foliage, the vigilant dog, the bird in flight and the foreboding of the night sky enshrouding them all. In Samson’s hands, each optical device and representational motif prises apart what it cannot contain, in service of painting ‘a thing that links us to God – by God, I mean everything’.

#9043. Al-Jawad Pike refreshes Aesop store with terracotta-tiled counter evoking ancient Persia

Local studio Al-Jawad Pike has given skincare brand Aesop’s shop in London department store Harrods a revamp, centred on a terracotta-clad counter designed to have “the qualities of a miniature building”.

Aesop has had a counter in Harrods for over a decade. For this revamp, Al-Jawad Pike, which is a long-term collaborator of Aesop’s, aimed to take the design further than a regular beauty-brand counter.

“We were interested in giving the counter the qualities of a miniature building, with suggestions of apertures, openings and floor levels: something designed with the architectural ambition of a building but the care of a cabinet,” Al-Jawad Pike co-founder Jessam Al-Jawad told Dezeen.

“Through carved alcoves we also wanted to recall the architecture of ancient Persia – the highly literate civilisation that developed liquid perfumery.”

The studio drew on Harrods’ easily recognisable red brick facade when designing the central counter, which is clad in terracotta tiles from Italy that were chosen for their ability to hold scents.

“We chose glazed terracotta early on in the process because of its connection to traditional fragrance production, but also because of its strong association with Harrods’ iconic facade,” Al-Jawad explained.

The counter is decorated with an alchemist-style design piece, described by Aesop as an “olfactory sculpture.”

Glass vessels filled with fragrances hang from a copper stand, with copper cones that let visitors experience the different scents.

“The olfactory sculpture is something that Aesop has been independently developing in different forms across a number of their projects,” Al-Jawad Pike explained.

“Our take on this was to create a delicate but organised structure of copper piping and blown glass, through which fragrance-infused air is pushed to scent funnels for customers to interact with.”

The colour palette of the Aesop store complements the monolithic terracotta counter, with brushed copper brought in as a tactile contrast.

“The colour palette was chosen in collaboration with the team at Aesop for its intensity and richness, which we felt resonated with the olfactory experience of fragrance,” Al-Jawad said.

“We paired this with matte, brushed copper because of its connection to fragrance creation and distillation.”

Earlier this year, Aesop launched its first lighting collection at Milan design week. Previous Aesop stores featured on Dezeen include a Barcelona shop by Mesura that won the 2024 Dezeen Award for best interior.

Compound interest is often called the eighth wonder of the world, and for good reason. It is the mathematical force that turns consistent, modest investing into life-changing wealth — and it is the foundation of every financial independence plan.

Here is the core concept. Simple interest earns a return only on your original deposit. If you invest $10,000 at 7% simple interest, you earn $700 per year — every year, forever, on the same $10,000 base. After 30 years, you would have $31,000.

Compound interest earns a return on your original deposit plus all the interest previously earned. In Year 1, you earn $700 on your $10,000. In Year 2, you earn 7% on $10,700 — that is $749. In Year 3, you earn 7% on $11,449 — that is $801. Each year, your interest earns its own interest, and the growth accelerates.

After 30 years of compound interest at 7%, your $10,000 grows to approximately $76,123 — more than double the $31,000 from simple interest. And that is with a single $10,000 deposit and no additional contributions.

The difference starts small and then explodes. In the first 10 years, compound interest adds only $2,672 more than simple interest. In the last 10 years (year 20 to 30), it adds over $30,000 more. This accelerating curve is why time in the market matters more than almost any other factor in building wealth.

Investing $500 per month at a 7% average annual return — roughly the inflation-adjusted historical return of the S&P 500 — produces dramatically different results depending on how long you invest. After 10 years: $86,500. After 20 years: $260,500. After 30 years: $567,000. You contribute $180,000 of your own money over 30 years. Compound interest adds $387,000 — more than double your contributions. Time is the multiplier that no amount of additional savings can replace.

The compound interest formula is straightforward once you understand the components:

For a $10,000 investment at 7% compounded monthly for 30 years:

A = 10,000 x (1 + 0.07/12)^(12 x 30) = 10,000 x (1.00583)^360 = $81,165

Notice this is higher than the $76,123 from annual compounding — more frequent compounding produces slightly more growth, though the difference is modest.

The jump from annual to monthly compounding is meaningful. The jump from monthly to daily is negligible. Most bank accounts and investment returns compound daily or monthly, so you are already getting nearly the maximum benefit.

The Rule of 72 is the single most useful mental math shortcut in personal finance. Divide 72 by your expected annual return to estimate how many years it takes to double your money.

At a 7% real return, your money doubles every 10 years. A $100,000 portfolio at age 25 becomes $200,000 at 35, $400,000 at 45, and $800,000 at 55 — even with zero additional contributions. This is why starting early is the single most powerful financial decision you can make.

The following table shows how different monthly contribution amounts grow over time at a 7% average annual return (roughly the inflation-adjusted long-term return of the US stock market). These numbers assume you start with $0 and contribute consistently every month.

Notice the pattern: the growth in the third decade dwarfs the first two decades combined. At $1,000 per month, you accumulate $173,000 in the first 10 years but $613,000 in the last 10 years — with the same monthly contribution. This is compound interest in its most powerful phase.

The 7% figure used above is already adjusted for historical inflation (the nominal S&P 500 return has averaged roughly 10%, minus approximately 3% average inflation). This means the projections above represent real purchasing power — $567,000 in 30 years would buy roughly what $567,000 buys today.

If you use a nominal return of 10% instead, the numbers look even more dramatic, but they overstate your future purchasing power. Always use inflation-adjusted returns (6-7%) for retirement planning and real purchasing power comparisons.

Consider two investors. Investor A starts investing $500 per month at age 25 and stops at age 35 — investing for only 10 years, then letting it grow untouched until age 65. Investor B waits until age 35 and invests $500 per month every month from 35 to 65 — investing for 30 years.

Investor A contributes one-third the money and ends up with more at 65. The 10-year head start gave compound interest enough time to overcome the difference. This is not a trick — it is the fundamental math of compounding. Every year you delay costs you more than the money you eventually invest.

The single most important factor in compound interest is time, not amount. Even $100 per month started today beats $500 per month started five years from now over a long enough timeline. Open a brokerage account or increase your 401(k) contribution today.

Pro tip: Automate your contributions so they happen before you see the money in your checking account.

The historical 7-10% average return comes from broad stock market index funds. A total US stock market fund or S&P 500 fund with an expense ratio below 0.10% gives you the full benefit of compound growth without high fees eroding your returns.

When you get a raise, increase your monthly investment by at least half the raise amount. This prevents lifestyle inflation from consuming your additional income and accelerates compound growth.

Pro tip: A 3% annual raise invested means your contributions grow exponentially alongside your investment returns.

Set all your accounts to automatically reinvest dividends. Dividend reinvestment is compound interest within compound interest — your dividends buy more shares, which generate more dividends, which buy more shares.

Market downturns are not a reason to sell — they are the cost of admission for long-term compound growth. Every major market crash in history has been followed by recovery and new highs. Pulling money out during a downturn and reinvesting later is the most reliable way to destroy compound interest.

Pro tip: If seeing your balance drop causes panic, check your portfolio less frequently. Quarterly or annually is enough.

Simple interest is calculated only on your original principal. Compound interest is calculated on your principal plus all previously earned interest. Over long periods, the difference is enormous — $10,000 at 7% for 30 years grows to $31,000 with simple interest but $76,123 with compound interest.

More frequent compounding produces slightly higher returns, but the difference is small. Monthly compounding at 7% on $10,000 for 30 years yields $81,165 versus $76,123 for annual compounding — a difference of about 6.6%. Most investment accounts compound daily or when dividends are reinvested, so you are already receiving near-optimal compounding.

Yes. Compound interest (more accurately, compound growth) applies to any investment account where your returns are reinvested. In a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account invested in index funds, your gains generate additional gains. Tax-advantaged accounts like Roth IRAs are especially powerful because the compounding occurs entirely tax-free.

The S&P 500 has returned approximately 10% annually in nominal terms over the past century. Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7%. For conservative planning, use 6-7% to account for inflation. For nominal calculations (not inflation-adjusted), use 9-10%. Using rates above 10% for long-term projections is overly optimistic for a diversified portfolio.

Yes — and the math is surprisingly accessible. Investing $1,000 per month at a 7% real return reaches $1,134,000 in 30 years (you contribute $360,000, compound interest adds $774,000). At $500 per month, you reach $567,000 in 30 years. The key variables are consistent contribution, a reasonable return, and patience.

Compound interest is the mathematical engine behind financial independence. The FI community uses compound growth to accumulate 25x their annual expenses in invested assets (the 4% rule). By saving 50%+ of income and investing in index funds that compound at 7-10% annually, FIRE practitioners can reach financial independence in 10-17 years rather than the traditional 40-year career.

Compound interest is the most powerful wealth-building force available to ordinary investors. The math is unambiguous: $500 per month at 7% becomes $567,000 in 30 years, with compound interest contributing more than twice what you personally invest. The two factors you control — how much you invest and how long you stay invested — matter far more than picking the "right" stocks or timing the market. Start today, invest in low-cost index funds, reinvest all dividends, and do not interrupt the compounding. Time is your greatest asset, and every year you wait costs more than you think.

#9041. Rotterdam's Echo is a Tokyo-inspired listening bar inside the brutalist Groot Handelsgebouw

Photography by Sophia van den Hoek

Creative director Jeﬀ Hoogendijk, DJ and producer Khalil Ryahi and architect Paul Cournet have teamed up to open a listening bar in Rotterdam, featuring a bar made from shipping crates and ombré mirrors by Sabine Marcelis.

Inspired by visits to listening bars in Tokyo, the trio envisioned Echo as a flexible space that can host different events and activities, but primarily focuses on the experience of music.

Located on the ground floor of Groot Handelsgebouw, a post-war office block opposite Rotterdam Centraal station, the bar has an interior designed by Cournet’s architecture and design studio, Cloud.

Cournet said the idea was to adapt the concept of the listening bar to the creative energy of Rotterdam.

“We wanted to make it super local,” he told Dezeen.

The main bar, which functions as both a service counter and the DJ area, exemplifies this approach.

Built in collaboration with Barendregt’s Kistenfabriek, a company that manufactures wooden shipping crates, together with carpenter Simon Fitskie, it’s a reminder that Rotterdam is home to Europe’s largest seaport.

Its sides are printed with the words “handled with care”, which became Echo’s tagline.

“We thought it would be so cool make the bar an art crate because we treated everything, from music to hospitality, as if it were art,” said Cournet.

“We always wanted to do everything in the best way possible.”

The space features several works by Rotterdam-based designer Marcelis, who is Cournet’s partner.

Her signature ombré mirrors adorn the walls, reflecting shades of red and gold, while a linear resin lamp hangs above the bar.

Polish brand Tylko supplied much of the furniture, including the modular shelving that extends across the walls to create space for displaying vinyl.

Cournet previously worked with the furniture company on its Berlin showroom, a project that led to a collaboration with audio company Form Follows Frequency.

Together, they developed a colourful system of speakers and subwoofers that slot precisely into Tylko’s shelving, which launched earlier this year.

These speakers form part of the sound system for Echo, along with two sculptural speaker towers that stand either side of the bar.

“There’s a contrast between the rawness of the exposed concrete and the more refined elements, like the sound system or Sabine’s mirrors,” said Cournet.

“When you put them together, it creates a tension that I find interesting. The concrete feels a bit softer.”

ECHO is one of several listening bars to have opened recently – with others including Bar Bardo in Milan and Upstairs at Hausu in London – but it is the first of its kind in Rotterdam.

The space shifts from a coffee shop by day to a bar by night, and includes a curated retail offering.

It can also morph to accommodate exhibitions, listening sessions of 20 to 40 people, or seated dinners for up to 40 guests.

Since opening in early September, the team has invited various local record stores to contribute to the event programme.

“Rotterdam has this really long history with music, with a lot of famous DJs and people who were pioneers in the music scene in the 1990s and 2000s,” added Cournet.

“It feels like the project has really resonated with that community.”

#9040. Sophia Huitema "Prussian Blue" @ Harper’s Apartment

Harper’s is pleased to announce Prussian Blue, New York–based artist Sophia Huitema’s first solo exhibition with the gallery. The presentation features new works by Huitema and will be on view through April 25, 2026.

Across the seven oil paintings on view, the visual and chemical properties of the pigment Prussian Blue function as a metaphorical anchor, tying together a cast of watchful female figures within Huitema’s hazy, dreamlike worlds. Working within a restrained range of blue and green tones, the paintings evoke a moody atmosphere through cool harmonies and dimly lit interiors. Prussian Blue, derived from chemical processes historically linked to cyanide while also used as an antidote to certain forms of poisoning, embodies a rare duality in which toxicity and protection converge, mirroring the emotionally guarded, ambiguous presence of Huitema’s figures.

The tension between beauty and menace permeates Huitema’s subjects. Elongated figures with exaggerated limbs and slender necks slink through each scene, often directly confronting the viewer’s gaze. Set within opulent surroundings that recall Gatsby–era decadence, Huitema’s women bear the markers of high society themselves, dressed in elegant gowns and adorned with pearl necklaces or jewel-studded headdresses. Moving through film-noir settings with poise and a quietly calculating air, these femme fatales seem either to lure their audience into a seductive ruse or to deploy their own cunning to evade danger. In Sleeper Car, for example, a woman fitted in a backless evening gown tilts her head slyly over her right shoulder in a relaxed pose while her right hand appears braced and ready to strike. As rain streaks across the coach’s windows and the narrow aisle stretches into an uncertain depth, a moment of cinematic suspense emerges, evoking the apex of a psychological thriller. In this way, Huitema constructs a world of heightened atmosphere and theatrical tension that opens onto the broader visual traditions and painterly languages informing her work.

Huitema’s paintings draw on a range of art-historical and visual references while maintaining a distinct internal coherence. The attenuated proportions and stylized poses of her figures recall traditions of early twentieth-century fashion illustration and Art Deco design, where gesture and embellishment echo the streamlined finesse of illustrators such as Erté and the theatrical poise found in interwar couture and stage design. Her compressed spaces also suggest affinities with aspects of Symbolist and Surrealist painting, in which shallow interiors and phantasmagoric backdrops function less as coherent environments than as psychological realms shaped by subconscious experience. Rather than aligning with a single historical framework, Huitema synthesizes these influences into a contemporary visual language that moves fluidly between illustration, painting, and cinematic staging. Working outside formal academic training, she has developed this vocabulary through sustained studio practice and close observation, resulting in a body of work that situates itself in dialogue with art history while remaining grounded in a self-directed approach to image making. In this context, Prussian Blue operates not only as a chromatic throughline but also as a conceptual one, binding together Huitema’s historical references and recurring motifs of protection and threat in constant tension.

#9039. A 3,200-Pound NASA Observatory Is Crashing Down to Earth

A 3,200-Pound NASA Observatory Is Crashing Down to Earth

NASA’s longtime Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is expected to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere tomorrow, November 4. While most of the telescope will burn up as it careens through the atmosphere, NASA says it expects some components to survive and potentially even cause harm, although that outcome is exceedingly unlikely.

The Swift Observatory launched in 2004 to explore gamma-ray bursts throughout the Universe. These are the Universe’s most powerful explosions and second only to the Big Bang in terms of the most energetic and brightest phenomena known to science.

Swift’s initial prime mission was scheduled to last just a couple of years, but its scientific operations ultimately lasted much longer. The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has witnessed many incredible things over its lifetime, observing the Universe across a wide range of wavelengths.

“Swift has broadened our understanding of a wide variety of cosmic objects and events, from active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes and stars undergoing X-ray flares, to supernova explosions and comets and asteroids in our own solar system,” NASA says.

Just a few years ago, Swift captured the most powerful gamma-ray burst ever observed, which released a staggering 18 teraelectronvolts of energy. It was so powerful that even though the event was 2.4 billion light-years away, it shook Earth’s outer atmosphere.

Even earlier, in 2013, scientists built a 160-megapixel map of ultraviolet light in nearby galaxies using data from Swift. 13 years later, it remains beautiful.

Right now, NASA expects the 3,200-pound Swift Observatory to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere around 3:30 AM EST on November 4. However, there’s an 11-hour uncertainty, so that reentry could happen later today.

Re-entry locations of any components that survive the re-entry burn could land anywhere between 20.6 degrees south latitude and 20.6 degrees north latitude. NASA says the risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth from Swift’s re-entry is about 1 in 2,100.

While this risk is very low, NASA tried to avoid it altogether. NASA launched a $30 million rescue effort this past summer, but it ultimately failed.

Even after this failed attempt, Swift actually continued to do science. The team restarted observations and observed hundreds more targets, including remnants of stellar explosions and supermassive black holes. However, on October 20, Swift entered safe mode and prepared for the end.

Just a couple of weeks before that, NASA released a four-photo set of some of Swift’s last images. NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory and the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory teamed up to create these final photos, all seen below.

“NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory is one of the many telescopes that frequently teamed up with Swift to make important discoveries about the cosmos. Chandra and Swift have complementary abilities,” NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory explains. “While Swift can quickly capture rapidly-changing events in space in ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma-ray light, Chandra is able to gather more detailed data with its sharp X-ray vision. When combined, these two telescopes helped provide a more complete picture of events and objects in space than either could alone.”

Image creditsNASA. X-ray: NASA/CXC/SAO; UV: NASA/Penn State Univ./Swift; Optical: Mark Hanson; Image Processing: NASA/CXC/SAO/L. Frattare.

#9038. Former High Museum of Art executive sentenced to 12 months in prison for embezzlement

Auguste Rodin's The Shade at the High Museum of Art, Atlanta Photo: Marc Merlin, via Flickr

Brady Lum, a former chief operating officer at Atlanta's High Museum of Art, was sentenced to 12 months in federal prison on Monday (2 November) for embezzling more than $600,000 from the institution. The sentencing comes as the High celebrates its centennial and its parent organisation, the Woodruff Arts Center, conducts a major corporate fundraising campaign.

Federal prosecutors said Lum diverted museum funds to pay for personal purchases, including guitars, music lessons and woodworking equipment. He concealed the expenditures through falsified invoices, reimbursement requests and accounting adjustments. The scheme began in September 2019, less than nine months after Lum joined the museum, and continued until its discovery in November 2025.

Lum paid full restitution of $607,688.18 to the High and voluntarily paid approximately $500,000 more to cover costs the museum incurred while uncovering and investigating his criminal activity.

During Monday's hearing, US District judge Michael L. Brown focused extensively on the deterrent purpose of sentencing. Although Brown said he did not believe Lum was likely to reoffend, he emphasised the court's responsibility to discourage similar financial crimes by others in positions of trust.

The judge acknowledged similarities between his own professional and socioeconomic background and Lum's, discussing how sentencing structures have historically been shaped by educated, professionally successful individuals whose circumstances resemble those of many white-collar defendants.

Brown also considered Lum's prompt restitution after the misconduct was discovered, distinguishing between voluntarily returning stolen funds before detection and repaying them after being caught. The latter, he indicated, carried less weight in assessing accountability.

Lum addressed the court and apologised for his conduct, expressing regret for disappointing his family and community. The gallery appeared to consist largely of relatives, friends and supporters of Lum.

Contacted for comment following Monday's sentencing, a spokesperson for the Woodruff provided the following statement: "We respect the court’s decision and remain focused on fulfilling our mission, responsibly managing our resources and connecting deeply with the audience we serve."

Both the Woodruff and the High declined to provide substantive information about financial safeguards introduced following Lum's misconduct, or whether they intend to publish a remediation plan addressing financial controls, governance reforms and oversight procedures.

#9037. 13 Winning Shots From Tecno’s Smartphone Photography Contest

13 Winning Shots From Tecno’s Smartphone Photography Contest

Hong Kong smartphone maker Tecno has unveiled the winners of its third annual “Shot On CAMON” global photography contest. This year’s edition, co-hosted with Lonely Planet, received over 13,000 entries from 40 countries.

The theme of this year’s photo contest is “Seeing is Believing,” and it was open to any photographers using Tecno Camon series smartphones. Tecno most recently made headlines on PetaPixel for its Slim 5G smartphone, which borrows aesthetics and visuals from famous artists like Vincent Van Gogh, Piet Mondrian, and Henri Matisse.

Mobile photographers entered across five categories, competing for a total prize pool of $38,000. The top honor goes to Nigerian photographer @dominic_films, whose photo, Weightless Voyager, earned him the title “TECNO Photography Master.” Dominic got $8,000 for the victory.

Alongside the overall winner, there are also top three finishers across five categories, four of which are traditional photo categories. The fifth, not in this article, focuses on AI-generated images.

Another Nigerian photographer, @_shotbykene, took the Gold Prize in the Faces • Unfiltered: Stories Behind the Faces portrait category. Filipino photographer @dzxl_mxjid took second place, while Indonesian photographer @7ustalvin rounded out the top three.

Filipino photographer @mlpadecio won the Culture • Unscripted: Traditions in Motion category. This category focuses on celebrating local traditions, community celebrations, and craftsmanship. Photographers @kolkatarchobiwala_ and @reuflores finished second and third, respectively.

Nigerian photographer @amazing_haywhyclicks_ earned the top prize in the Night • Unveiled” After the Light Fades category. This category celebrates low-light photography, which is a key focus for Tecno and other smartphone manufacturers these days. @tanvirahmed_1415 from Bangladesh won silver, and @miinkooo_mobile of Malaysia took third.

Rounding out the photo-specific categories is Snapshot • Unspotted: The Moments in Between. This category celebrates “fleeting actions and unexpected encounters,” which Tecno says reflects its Camon smartphones’ ability to capture fast-moving subjects. Indonesian photographer @30secondtothemoon won the category with a striking skateboard shot. @aungkyawzaw.ig and @baganphoto rounded out the top three.

“We were consistently impressed with the creativity and quality of the images submitted for the Shot On CAMON contest. Much of travel photography isn’t just a straightforward shot of a destination, but capturing a real mood and feeling of a place and people in a destination. The winning photographers brought real inspiration, feeling and a lightness to their photography that is impressive for any photographer,” says Lonely Planet.

“Our goal is to make imaging technology work for people’s creativity, giving them the freedom to capture moments and bring their ideas to life,” adds Zhang Liankai, Tecno Imaging Expert.

Even more photos from the contest, including the winners from the AI category, are available to browse on Tecno’s website.

#9036. Molly Bounds "The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins" @ Mrs Gallery, Maspeth, NY

Mrs. is pleased to present The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins, Molly Bounds’ New York debut solo exhibition, on view at the gallery’s 6040 56th Drive location. This exhibition marks the Los Angeles-based artist’s second presentation with the gallery following The Armory Show in September 2025. The show will be on view through May 2, 2026.

Opening on the vernal equinox, a rare moment when the hours of daylight and night are equal, Molly Bounds offers light as the protagonist in her new series of paintings. It is versatile and ever-changing; it both conceals and reveals, and reminds us of the unrelenting forward movement of time. Depicting her subjects both in contemplation and in the midst of candid movement, Bounds continues her investigation into liminal moments where stillness and urgency shape the mood. Much like the transition from winter to spring, these figures appear on the threshold of a transformative shift.

There are also moments of escapism. In both It Sings in Me and Among of Green, Again a figure moves freely amongst rolling green hills, illuminated under the sun. The landscape appears bucolic and perhaps overly so - is this real or imagined? For Bounds this is less important; the ability to build optimism and a belief in renewal and rebirth is paramount. Contrasting with the scenes of pensive interiority, these landscapes communicate urgency, celebration, possibility, and fantasy. After the darkness of winter, spring wins.

#9035. Nextorage Debuts New 1TB SD Card for Pro Video Work

Nextorage Debuts New 1TB SD Card for Pro Video Work

Nextorage Corporation has announced the NX-F2AE Series, a trio of new UHS-II SDXC memory cards that promise high-end speed and reliability for demanding video workflows.

While a lot of attention in recent years has been on CFexpress Type A and Type B cards, many photographers and videographers still use SD cards in their cameras, either as their primary storage or as backup in case they fill up their CFexpress card. SD cards are an important tool for many creators.

Nextorage says the NX-F2AE Series is its Advanced Edition SDXC UHS-II card, which means the cards were designed specifically for professional video production applications.

“As high-resolution, high-bitrate video formats such as 4K and 8K continue to become increasingly common, the demand for memory cards capable of delivering both large storage capacities and stable long-duration recording has grown significantly,” Nextorage explains. “The NX-F2AE Series was designed to meet these requirements, providing reliable and uninterrupted recording performance for demanding video applications.”

As expected, given the billing, the new SD cards have a V90 rating, the highest video speed class for SD cards. This means the cards guarantee a minimum sustained write speed of 90 MB/s. Overall, the cards promise read and write speeds up to 300 MB/s.

Nextorage recommends using the cards alongside its NX-DF1CL Dual-Slot SD Card Reader. The card reader supports the UHS-II interface for both slots, meaning that each card can offload files at full speed.

“Whether shooting in 4K, 6K, or 8K resolution, or capturing high-frame-rate footage, the card delivers stable performance under heavy data workloads while minimizing the risk of dropped frames and recording interruptions,” Nextorage promises.

The new cards are available in 256GB, 512GB, and 1TB capacities. For video applications in particular, larger cards are often preferred as 8K footage can take up considerable space in short order.

Professionals have rigorous reliability demands as well, and Nextorage says its new SD cards have passed a series of seven durability and protection tests. Specifically, the cards are rated to operate in temperatures from -25° to 85° C (-13° to 185° F), shock-resistant for drops from heights up to 1.5 meters (4.9 feet), and bend-resistant up to 10 Newtons. The cards are also tested for 10,000 connector matings and are resistant to X-rays, magnets, and electrostatic discharge.

The Nextorage NX-F2AE Series SD cards start at $299.99 for the 256GB size. The 512GB card is $529.99, while the 1TB one is $999.99. All three cards are available today.

#9033. Adobe Is Bringing Licensed Music to Premiere Mobile

Adobe Is Bringing Licensed Music to Premiere Mobile

Adobe Premiere mobile, which recently launched on Android after releasing last year on iOS, will soon include music from Universal Music Group (UMG) and Warner Music Group (WMG).

“Music has the power to turn an everyday moment into an unforgettable story. It’s the beat behind a viral trend, the track to a favorite memory, and the spark that inspires you to pick up your phone and start creating. For millions of you, inspiration starts with music,” Adobe’s Mike Polner writes.

Polner says that Adobe is working directly with Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group to bring fully licensed music clips from leading, famous artists directly into Adobe Premiere mobile on iOS and Android. Adobe is confident that with leading music, Premiere users will be able to create even better videos more easily inside Premiere, which remains a free app on mobile.

“Music has always been a powerful way for people to express themselves and connect with others. By bringing licensed music from UMG artists into Adobe Premiere mobile, we’re giving creators new ways to build their stories around the songs they love for the first time, while helping our artists and songwriters reach new audiences,” says Bryan Stone, SVP, Business Development at Universal Music Group.

“The way people experience and engage with music extends far beyond traditional listening platforms,” adds Rachel Scarpati, VP, Digital Strategy and Business Development, WMG. “Our partnership with Adobe Premiere mobile integrates WMG’s catalog directly into the creative process, opening up new possibilities for creative expression and deeper fan engagement.”

Premiere mobile users will be able to browse, search, and preview trending music, filter by genre and duration, bookmark favorites, and explore curated collections. Licensed music clips will be available up to 60 seconds, and Adobe is developing new music-friendly video templates for its mobile video editing app.

“You can also take advantage of Premiere mobile’s powerful editing capabilities, including professional-quality video tools, studio-quality audio tools like Enhance Audio to reduce distracting background noise and Adobe Firefly-powered AI features to generate unique creative assets,” Adobe adds.

Music from UMG and WMG, which is “coming soon” to Premiere Mobile, will be licensed only for personal, non-commercial use. Those who require music for commercial-friendly video projects can stick with Adobe Stock Audio or create new music themselves.

Adobe Premiere mobile is available for free on iOS and Android.

#9032. Where to Find the Small Worlds Most Photographers Walk Past

Where to Find the Small Worlds Most Photographers Walk Past

Peter Baumgarten was looking for centimeter-tall mushrooms when he spotted a cluster of orange caps on a rotting log. A few warm, rainy days had encouraged mushrooms to emerge in Canada’s McLean’s Park, a forest on Ontario’s Manitoulin Island where he regularly walks his dog. At six feet two inches tall, Baumgarten could easily walk past mushrooms that small if he weren’t specifically looking for them.

Full disclosureThis article was brought to you by OM SYSTEM.

Peter Baumgarten is just one of a number of OM SYSTEM ambassadors who specialize in macro photography and shared with PetaPixel their favorite places to look for small subjects and the encounters that keep them returning time and time again. For Lisa and Tom Cuchara, that includes the meadows and woodland around Little River in southern Maine. Chris McGinnis searches the rainforests of Costa Rica and Panama, while also expanding his macro photography portfolio in Maine and his own backyard.

Their photographs show the miniature world that can turn up on a rotting log or a garden stem. Baumgarten gets low on the forest floor to photograph mushrooms and the slugs that feed on them. The Cucharas and McGinnis have both made some of their favorite finds after dark, the Cucharas in a garden in the Northeast and McGinnis at a pond in Panama.

In one of Baumgarten’s favorite macro photographs, a garden slug stretches along rotting wood beneath a cluster of orange mushrooms, its head raised toward one of the caps.

“What excited me the most was the garden slug getting ready to chow down, which isn’t a common shot,” he says.

Baumgarten takes many of his macro shots at a park close to home. McLean’s Park has several kilometers of trails through mixed forest, which he uses for hiking, biking, cross-country skiing, snowshoeing, and photography.

“It is about a 15-minute drive from my home,” he says. “I go there several times a week to walk my dog. As a mature forest there are plenty of fallen trees and branches that make for the perfect environment for a bunch of different types of mushrooms.”

“What I love about the park is the variety of photographs I can take there,” he notes. “One day I might photograph a person walking their dog in autumn along a leaf-covered trail, with tall trees and yellow foliage all around. Another day, I might be down among the fallen logs and branches photographing mushrooms.”

Baumgarten likes to shoot most of his mushroom macro photos below eye level. “I love capturing them from underneath,” he explains. “For me, the gill structure is perhaps the most interesting and photogenic part of the mushroom. I want a soft background that doesn’t pull focus from my subject. By shooting from just below the mushroom I can usually include the more distant, lush greenery of the forest.”

“While mushrooms don’t move, when I’m photographing a slug in the low light of the forest, I have to be aware that even its slow movement can cause blur,” he continues. “Shooting handheld, I might use a shutter speed of around 1/100 second to keep it sharp, raising the ISO if I need to.”

Bumping up the ISO, the camera’s sensitivity to light, lets him shoot at a faster shutter speed when the light on the forest floor is dim. With a mushroom, he can usually keep the ISO low and slow the shutter down instead. The image stabilization in his OM SYSTEM OM-3 lets him handhold exposures as long as half a second, even while using in-camera focus stacking, which combines the sharp areas of photographs focused at different distances to keep more of a close-up subject in focus.

“I capture mushrooms in a very similar way to how I photograph wildlife,” Baumgarten says. “For many wildlife shots I prefer to use my long lens. This gives me great close-up images of my subject. But a great close-up is not always the best way to showcase the animal. Showing the animal in its environment helps me tell more of the story about where it lives. That’s when I turn to using a wider lens. I will often do the same when photographing mushrooms.”

Mushrooms can appear quickly and may not stay in good condition for long, so Baumgarten recommends watching the weather to help decide when to go looking.

“Mushrooms need warm, moist conditions, so I recommend exploring one or two days after a good rain,” he advises. “I have had great success from late spring to late autumn. I recommend avoiding bright sunny days. The dappled sunlight on the forest floor can work for some shots, but often it is more of a hindrance than a help.”

A subject that stays put gives photographers new to macro more time to experiment with focus and composition.

“Photographing mushrooms is a great way to get into macro shooting,” he adds. “I love the geometry of most mushrooms and the infinite patience they have. I’ve never had a mushroom run away from me as I sneak up on it.”

Those quiet searches are also part of why he keeps returning to the forest.

“I often turn to macro photography to get me out of a rut,” Baumgarten says. “I primarily shoot landscapes and wildlife and over the years there have been many stretches of time where I just couldn’t capture shots that I was happy with. It’s at these times, when I feel a bit down, that I grab my macro lens and head into the forest for a bit of exploration and de-stressing. I slow down, observe carefully, and invariably find something in the macro world to photograph. And the best part is, I don’t have to go far. Macro subjects are everywhere, and a local park or garden can be a great place to start looking. I’m lucky to have McLean’s Park just a short drive from home.”

For Lisa and Tom Cuchara, some of the strangest subjects turn up after dark.

“One evening I headed into the garden to look for tiny nighttime wonders,” Lisa Cuchara recalls. “Imagine my surprise when I found a bright green hornworm sporting what looked like dozens of tiny white marshmallows. Those little white blobs weren’t eggs or fungus, though. They were the silken cocoons of tiny parasitoid wasps. The wasp larvae had developed inside the living caterpillar before coming out to spin their cocoons. It was creepy and fascinating at the same time.”

Gardeners don’t like hornworms, since a hungry one can make a massive amount of tomato foliage disappear overnight. The wasps, most likely a Cotesia species, are another matter.

“This was a perfect example of nature’s own pest control,” Lisa explains. “Unlike regular parasites, which generally don’t kill their hosts, parasitoids kill the animal they develop in. These tiny wasps help keep hornworm numbers down, which makes them real allies for gardeners.”

“When I saw this scene, I knew that the challenge was getting the detail of both the caterpillar and those wonderfully wonky white cocoons while working handheld in the dark,” Lisa recalls. “Even at f/11, there just isn’t enough depth of field to get everything sharp in a single exposure.”

An aperture of f/11 is a small lens opening that would normally extend depth of field, the zone of a photograph that looks sharp. In-camera focus stacking, used with the Cucharas’ OM-1 Mark II and the M.Zuiko Digital ED 90mm F3.5 Macro IS PRO lens, got around the problem.

“I was able to shoot a focus-stacked image handheld, without setting up a tripod or disturbing my subject,” Lisa notes.

For insects, the Cucharas use a small flash fitted with a diffuser.

“A bare flash gives you harsh highlights and deep shadows, especially on an insect’s shiny exoskeleton,” the Cucharas explain. “Using a diffuser turns that small flash into a much larger, softer light compared to a tiny subject. The flash also helps freeze movement, whether it’s a slight breeze moving a leaf or an insect shifting position.”

“Without a flashlight and a willingness to explore the garden after sunset, I might have walked right past an extraordinary biological story unfolding just inches away,” Lisa adds.

On other outings, the Cucharas have photographed a moth laying eggs at night and a crab spider grabbing an unsuspecting bumblebee. They’ve also watched a caterpillar that had just shed its outer skin, known as a molt.

“A black swallowtail caterpillar will eat its own molt for energy,” they add. “Those spontaneous moments of seeing something so unique are just one reason we enjoy macro photography so much.”

The Cucharas have turned their own yard into a wildlife habitat, replacing most of the lawn with the goal of mainly native plants grown without pesticides or herbicides. They also lead macro and close-up photography retreats at Little River in North Berwick, Maine.

“We love places where you can move just a few feet and find a whole different world,” they say.

Insects are cold-blooded, so how active they are depends on the temperature and conditions around them.

“Pick a rainy, drizzly, or overcast day,” the Cucharas advise. “Insects like to hang out under the leaves and they’re less likely to move. And get there early, because a lot of insects are cold and slow in the early hours, which gives you more time to photograph them.”

“Slow down and look under every leaf,” they continue. “Don’t rush from flower to flower; pick a small area and explore it from a few angles. You start to see a jumping spider on a stalk, holes in a leaf from insects eating, or a curled leaf with a caterpillar inside.”

“If you’re just starting to practice macro photography, a stationary flower with some personality, pollen, or water droplets is a wonderful starting point,” the Cucharas note. “A flower past its prime, a crooked stem, a curled petal, or an oddly shaped mushroom can be a far more compelling story than a flawless blossom. And learn to notice the background, because it’s just as important as the subject.”

“At one of our retreats, six groups rotated through my session to photograph a swallowtail chrysalis on its host plant,” Lisa recalls. “It gave me a chance to talk about fennel and other host plants, and about how to photograph it without disturbing the spot or making it more obvious to predators. No photograph is worth possible harm to the subject, including insects and the plants they’re on.”

Lisa also says that it’s not necessary to have a large piece of land to start creating your own macro photography sanctuary. “I always recommend planting more native and host plants everywhere, even if it’s just a few planters at your condo. Native plants are what attract the insects that look fascinating in a photograph.”

Even with their own garden, the Cucharas still head out to other spots for macro photography. However, unlike static landscape overlooks, macro photography is always delivering something new. “We often visit the same places again and again, and we always come home with different photographs,” the Cucharas explain. “Flowers open and fade, insect species change from month to month, and the light and weather change. Macro photography might be the best genre for photographers who are always looking to shoot, and learn, something new.”

Chris McGinnis has captured some of his favorite macro photographs after dark, in the rainforests of Costa Rica and Panama.

McGinnis says that one of the most interesting subjects in the Central American rainforest is the red-eyed tree frog. “With these frogs, I am constantly surprised with the variety of moments I am able to capture them in, and maybe my favorite moment was on a trip to Panama with fellow OM SYSTEM ambassador Lee Hoy,” McGinnis remembers. “We had some workshop clients with us, and they faded one by one and went off to sleep, but Lee and I stayed out shooting. We were on this little pond, looking for frogs, and we’d found and photographed several. All of a sudden Lee says, ‘Red-eyed tree frogs in amplexus.’ I said, ‘What? What do you mean?’, not knowing what amplexus meant. Lee pointed to a branch and there were two red-eyed tree frogs with the male on top of the female. I’ve photographed hundreds of these frogs before, but I had never seen them do this. The shot was a unique addition to my portfolio, and I learned a new word in the process.”

According to McGinnis, red-eyed tree frogs spend the day higher up in the trees and come down toward the water as the sun goes down, which is why he looks for them at night. But whether it’s day or night, he often chooses to shoot macro photographs with a non-macro lens.

“That night with the frogs was a time when I could have used my M.Zuiko Digital ED 90mm F3.5 Macro IS PRO,” he recalls. “I wanted to be up really close, but I wanted a wider view so the story was the frogs in their environment, as that can make a more interesting shot.”

Instead, he had the M.Zuiko Digital ED 8-25mm F4.0 PRO on his camera that night. It’s a wide-angle zoom that can focus close enough to fill the frame with a frog while still showing the branch the pair was sitting on.

“I don’t think I could ever get tired of searching for red-eyed tree frogs,” he adds. “It’s an addiction for me. I find one, I photograph it until it jumps away or I’ve exhausted every angle I can get. Then I could go back to my room and go to sleep, or I could try to find another one. And I have a really hard time walking away, because that next one might be something I’ve never seen before, like capturing two red-eyed tree frogs in amplexus.”

“The biggest challenge of the rainforest at night is getting lost,” McGinnis warns. “So I always get a guide, as there is incredible value in going out with someone who knows their way around the rainforest. Not to mention the danger hiding on the ground and in the trees. Central America has lots of venomous snakes. You grab the wrong thing, you step in the wrong place, and you could be in trouble. A local guide knows how to keep you from accidentally running into one of them.”

Rain is a given in a rainforest. “Photographing in the rain is challenging because it can be harder to find subjects or keep your clothing dry, but luckily I never have to worry about my camera gear in the rain, which eliminates one of the challenges,” he notes. With IP53-rated weather sealing, his OM-1 Mark II can keep shooting through snow, dust, and rain. “I’ve been shooting days on end in pouring, torrential rain in Central America, and I’ve never had a problem with my gear.”

When McGinnis isn’t finding small subjects in the Central American rainforest, he also helps lead multi-day macro retreats with Lisa and Tom Cuchara and other OM SYSTEM ambassadors, on fellow ambassador Steve Morello’s property in southern Maine, as well as other locations. One of his favorite subjects on Morello’s property is dragonflies.

“If you find a dragonfly as the sun’s coming up, they’re not warm yet,” McGinnis advises. “They are cold and they might have dew on their wings, making it harder for them to fly. They’re almost like sitting ducks at that time, and much easier to photograph than in the heat of the day, when they’re busy hunting.”

He also searches his own backyard after dark, where wolf spiders and other hunting spiders give themselves away. Their eyes have a reflective layer that bounces a flashlight beam straight back, a glint known as eyeshine.

“In my own backyard, I love to photograph spiders and praying mantises after dark,” he continues. “Spiders hunt at night, and they are easier to find than most people realize. If you hold your flashlight up to the side of your head and scan the grass about 10 to 15 feet ahead of you, the eyeballs of a spider will flicker back at you. In the pitch black, all you’re looking for is those little diamonds in the grass. Having the flashlight right to the side of your eye keeps your line of sight in line with the beam of the flashlight.”

Some of McGinnis’s favorite discoveries don’t happen until he’s back at his computer. “I was trying to get this mantis to cooperate, and I ended up with tons of shots of it in different poses.”

“As I was reviewing them, I noticed a little something else in the shot that was invisible to my naked eye,” he continues. “That mite on its head is very, very tiny, just one or two millimeters. That’s actually happened to me many times, and finding those tiny surprises when I zoom in on the computer is one of the best things about macro photography.”

McGinnis says this is a great way for both beginners and seasoned macro photography veterans to practice and capture unique photos. “Go outside with a flashlight and scan the yard, and you’re bound to find something. No matter where you live, especially in the summertime, go out after dark with your camera and a light. On a nice, warm summer night, it’s just really fun. I’m exploring this small world, and through that exploration, new things reveal themselves. That’s what keeps me going back. Even if it’s my backyard, a local park, or a tropical rainforest, I’m always discovering new things and finding interesting stories in the small world that most other photographers walk by.”

#9031. Nat Meade's "Franklin" @ HESSE FLATOW, NYC

HESSE FLATOW is pleased to announce the opening of Franklin, an exhibition of paintings and works on paper by Nat Meade, marking his third solo presentation with the gallery. The show is on view through April 18, 2026.

The emotional arc of life’s struggles and triumphs take shape within Meade’s figurative works, reflecting the artist’s everyday experiences as he navigates being a father, son, partner, and academic. Far from portraits of actual individuals, his protagonists mirror timeless archetypes. At times, we encounter a lone traveler searching for existential validation; at other times, we see through intergenerational dynamics. This allegorical distance via painting provides a realm for Meade to explore personal challenges through absurd, somber, and humorous tropes, while also furnishing a space rife with human nature that bears unequivocal resonance.

Meade’s reflections on his relationship with his father after his recent passing, and subsequent reevaluations of his own role as a parent percolate throughout the works in the exhibition. Vulnerability, pain, and mortality are themes Meade does not shy away from, yet the introduction of younger males in this body of work casts a sense of hope, acceptance, reconciliation, and renewal.

Faced with a pair of dangling legs from a cloud in Poise, we question whether a figure is ascending or descending from the heavens, a suggestion perhaps on the interchangeability of birth and death, be it physical or spiritual. Ghostly specters hover over certain individuals – a metaphor for inherited trauma and release. In the same way that a soul peels away from an expiring body in classic cartoons, we observe a spirit looking back on itself with what might be  happiness or regret. The exhibition’s title Franklin is a subtle nod to the 1974 horror film Texas Chainsaw Massacre, known for its portrayal of a deranged patriarchal family. Meade embraces this inner turmoil of contending with one’s violent and antagonistic impulses as his characters are visibly sublimated or put in their place. A vulture picking away at a corpse recalls the eternal punishment of Prometheus by Zeus, while a bearded figure on his hands and knees echoes William Blake’s portrayal of Nebuchadnezzar, condemned for his lust for power.

In contrast to the adults, Meade’s younger figures appear more harmonious. A young boy charts his own path as he steers a boat with a radiant torch, unclouded by societal and familial pressures. A sense of childlike wonder and adventure beholds an adolescent ankle-deep in a secluded cove, reaching in to touch the sea floor brilliantly covered in starfish, anemones, and mussels. In a related work, we observe two pairs of legs belonging to father and son in the same shallow pool, one tenderly guiding the other. Having in the past shown his figures wrestling with or victims of forces of nature, physically being overtaken by turbulent wind and crashing waves, Meade’s focus on calmer seas signals a turning point. He recognizes the need to acknowledge one’s rocky histories in order to heal and release future generations from similar burdens. Despite what may seem like an insurmountable heaviness, he reminds us of the stubborn resilience of human nature, making progress attainable.

#9030. Apple takes "monumental step forward" with first touchscreen MacBook

Apple has revealed its latest MacBook Pro model, which features the technology brand’s first laptop touchscreen and what it claims is “the world’s best laptop display”.

Sixteen years after Steve Jobs described touchscreen laptops as “ergonomically terrible”, Apple has ventured into the market with its new MacBook Pro, which is available from 6 November at prices ranging from £2,899 to £14,549.

As well as being touchscreen, the laptop features a PROLED XDR display, which Apple said is “the world’s best laptop display”, M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, 128 gigabytes of memory, 16 terabytes of storage, up to 24 hours of battery life and a thinner, lighter design compared to previous models.

It comes in 14- and 16-inch models, weighing three and four pounds respectively. The laptop was designed to be both portable and a powerful tool for professional creatives on the go, whether they’re working on 3D models or playing musical instruments onscreen.

“The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display is a monumental step forward for the Mac,” said Apple chief hardware officer Johny Srouji.

“PROLED XDR is the world’s best laptop display,” he continued. “And with the magic of Touch coming to MacBook Pro, combined with the game-changing performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max, we’ve created a whole new way for pros to interact with their content, taking their workflows to a completely new level.”

“The new MacBook Pro is the result of the deep integration between Apple silicon, hardware, and software, and there’s simply nothing else like it.”

Aiming to provide an intuitive experience, the Touch technology allows users to scroll through a webpage by swiping, zoom in on a photo by pinching, drag and drop slides in presentations and double-tap a window to fill the screen.

The touch sensor is built into the display panel rather than layered over it, to give the feel of touching the displayed content itself.

To support the Touch feature, Apple redesigned the laptop hinge for better stability and created real-time video stabilisation to smooth the camera feed when using the touchscreen on a video call.

Apple said that the macOS operating system automatically translates touches into clicks, meaning multiple existing apps will work with Touch right away. These include Adobe Lightroom, Blender, Maxon Cinema 4D, Maxon ZBrush, Notion, Canva, Zoom, Microsoft Word, Excel and PowerPoint.

“Graphic designers can now use the entire display as their canvas, no longer constrained by the area of the trackpad when drawing,” said Apple.

“Musicians can play software instruments right onscreen, and app developers can test how Touch performs in their iOS and iPadOS apps directly on the MacBook Pro display.”

Apple said the new PROLED XDR display offers “true-to-life colour and unparalleled brightness and contrast”, made possible by combining OLED technology with algorithms that control light across the display.

“The PROLED XDR display offers tandem OLED technology unlike any other, with deep innovations in its layers that keep brightness and grayscale uniform across the entire display, while minimising internal reflections common in traditional OLED designs,” said Apple.

“It’s all backed by advanced algorithms in the display engine that precisely control each pixel in real time, plus a meticulous manufacturing process and precise calibration of every panel for consistency from display to display.”

The MacBook Pro also has a six-speaker sound system, designed for deeper bass and improved sound clarity compared to previous models, and the Dynamic Island search and notification feature currently used in iPhones.

Other recent releases from Apple include its first folding smartphone, the HomeView dashboard for home controls and the budget-friendly MacBook Neo.

#9029. November Book Bag: from a book about broken art to a collection of Zanele Muholi’s LGBTQ+ portraits

This ancient Greek Colossal Head of a Youth (around 200BC-100BC) features in The Power of the Fragment in Sculpture Antikensammlung, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, inv. AvPVII 283. bpk Bildagentur / Antikensammlung/Staatliche Museen zu Berlin / Ingrid Geske / Art Resource, NY

The Power of the Fragment in Sculpture explores the enduring fascination with fractured statues, focusing on the “power dynamics of iconoclastic dismantling and defacement, and how various cultures treat broken statues”, says a publisher’s statement. Highlights include Michelangelo’s terracotta Model of a Nude Woman (around 1533), which new research suggests may have been intentionally created incomplete. The publication accompanies a wide-ranging and eclectic exhibition spanning more than 4,500 years of global history, which opened in September at the Palazzo Strozzi in Florence before it travels to the National Gallery of Art in Washington DC next year.

This newly revised and expanded edition assesses the relevance today of the influential conceptual artist Felix Gonzalez-Torres who died from an Aids-related illness in 1996. “Almost two decades after its original publication, the monograph accompanying Gonzalez-Torres’s 1995 retrospective at the Guggenheim Museum is still the canonical text on the artist,” says a publisher’s statement. Gonzalez-Torres is known especially for his famous sweet installations, which are usually mounted in piles in the corner of rooms. “The candy pieces, like all his works, encourage a wealth of meanings, and can be everything from stridently political to gently lyrical,” writes the critic and host of The Art Newspaper’s podcast, Ben Luke.

This publication grew out of a video project devised by the cultural producer Gabriela Galcerán in which 26 artists chose a word, one for each letter of the alphabet, and responded to it in their own way. The five thematic chapters, including “Power + Politics” and “Agency + Language”, subsequently draw connections between their ideas. Contributors include Lynn Hershman Leeson, Lawrence Abu Hamdan and Gary Hill. “They all made me flinch, each for a different reason. I love the wide range of tones and registers that make up this choral effort. Some are intimate, some political, some humorous or oblique,” says Galcerán in a statement.

For more than 20 years, the South African artist and activist Zanele Muholi has been documenting Black lesbian and bisexual women, along with queer, trans, non-binary, and gender fluid people for the project Faces and Phases. This new volume of the work, released to mark the project’s 20th anniversary, has been updated to include new sitters in locations such as São Paulo, Salvador, London, Porto and Los Angeles. “These striking photographs are often accompanied by participants’ testimonies, sharing their personal stories, feelings, and lived experiences,” says a publisher’s statement. #9028. The Nikon ZR’s First Major Firmware Update Improves Video Quality and Adds More Control

The Nikon ZR’s First Major Firmware Update Improves Video Quality and Adds More Control

Nikon has unveiled more details about the Nikon ZR’s first major firmware update. Firmware 2.00, slated to arrive before the end of the year, brings major improvements to Nikon’s popular video-first camera.

Nikon first announced the new firmware back in September, sharing a few details while simultaneously promising Open Gate recording and in-camera anamorphic desqueeze sometime in 2027. While those two big features aren’t coming in firmware 2.00 this year, Nikon ZR owners still have plenty to be excited about in the meantime.

As promised, the upcoming firmware update will add support for Log3G10 gamma when recording in H.265, which enables shooting with RED’s color science in the lightweight video codec. Nikon notes that RED’s color science in Log3G10 gamma has a lot of latitude for color grading, promising smoother tonal gradations and a wide color gamut.

Another new feature is the ability to select the level of High ISO NR (noise reduction), giving users more control over the look and noise levels of their video.

On the usability side, Nikon notes that more functions are now assignable to the camera's command dials and function buttons. New options include ISO, exposure settings, white balance, and white balance color temperature (WBK). Further, when assigning 3D LUT/View Assist to an Fn button, users can switch between their 3D LUT settings with a single operation.

"This enables the operator to adjust settings without taking their eyes off the monitor, allowing them to stay focused on capturing their intended shots," Nikon explains.

Other new features coming in the Nikon ZR firmware 2.00 update include focus peaking support even when a 3D LUT is applied when recording in R3D NE format, support for applying a 3D LUT to HDMI video output for easier previewing, and new processing that "suppresses frame-by-frame fluctuations in black level, reducing flicker that tends to occur in low-light conditions."

This isn't the first time flicker has shown up in recent years with video recording on Nikon cameras. Nikon Z6 III owners may remember issues with shadow noise performance on the Z6 III when recording RAW (N-Log) video. Nikon addressed that issue with firmware shortly after launch. Nikon doesn't say today whether the ZR's "frame-by-frame fluctuations" are related at all to the issues it fixed on the Z6 III. However, the two cameras do share the same 24.5-megapixel partially stacked image sensor and image processing engine.

Nikon says the ZR's big new firmware update, version 2.00, will arrive "before the end of the year."
