#9027. Photographer Risks It All to Capture Extreme Images Around the World

Photographer Risks It All to Capture Extreme Images Around the World

A photographer’s relentless pursuit of extraordinary images takes him from remote landscapes to some of the world’s most dangerous places.

Paul Bride began his career capturing climbers on towering cliffs and frozen peaks, where he developed not only a remarkable eye but a sky-high tolerance for risk — and an addiction to its rewards.

Over the past 25 years, his relentless pursuit of extraordinary images has led him to striking locales and sketchy situations around the world, from reef breaks in Tahiti to armed checkpoints in the tribal regions of Ethiopia, frozen waterfalls in the Rockies to cartel shootouts in Panama.

In his first monograph, Bride tramples genre conventions to share a thrilling selection of more than 200 photos from all these places and more, uniting the kaleidoscopic array with often-harrowing stories of how they were made and reflections on the uncommon power they hold.

These are photographic dispatches from the chase — the product of a lifelong obsession with finding indelible moments that seem to exist outside time, and that produce images as difficult to forget as they are to make.

Most of these photos have never been posted or published. Organized into five sections (Climbing, People, Water, Travel, Storms), each of which includes a double-page foldout, they include a mix of dizzying action shots, jaw-dropping landscapes, and stirring portraits.

In his foreword, legendary climber Sonnie Trotter speaks to the passion that sustained Bride through his self-proclaimed “dirtbag” days; in his introduction and extended captions, Bride wrestles with the demons and motivations that have shaped his career.

Paul Bride: Until the Light Dies (Figure 1 Publishing) is an extraordinary collection that reveals how a passion verging on madness can create images you didn’t know were possible.

Paul Bride is a professional photographer who has devoted nearly three decades to capturing the intersection of beauty and grit in spectacular locations all around the world. His many clients have included Arc’teryx, Black Diamond, KUIU, Lowepro, MEC, Mitsubishi Canada, Patagonia, Redbull, Whistler/Blackcomb, and Yeti; and his editorial work has appeared in the New York Times, the Globe and Mail, and dozens of magazines, including Climbing, Explore, Mountain Life, National Geographic Adventure, Outside, Photo News, Powder, and Skier. His work has been shown at the Banff Mountain Film Festival and galleries across Canada, and among his many awards and honors he is a two-time Redbull Illume finalist and winner of the International Photography Award. When he’s not chasing wild experiences across the planet, Bride lives in Britannia Beach, British Columbia.

#9026. Chris “Daze” Ellis "Orchid Rain on the Underground" @ PPOW Gallery, NYC

PPOW are pleased to present Orchid Rain on the Underground, Chris “Daze” Ellis’s third solo exhibition with the gallery. The show is on view through April 25, 2026. Featuring a new series of paintings, multimedia installation, and a site-specific mural, the exhibition harnesses the passion and spontaneity of the graffiti movement of the 1970s and 80s while demonstrating a thoughtful and meticulous practice honed over the past five decades. While the version of New York City that fostered Daze’s beginnings as a fine artist may feel like a bygone era, the works in this exhibition are evidence of its enduring legacy. By revitalizing that foundational energy for the present moment, Daze affirms the continued relevance of those figures and places, and their profound influence on the creative spirit that persists throughout the city today.

Born in Brooklyn in 1962, Daze became inspired by early graffiti writers like Blade, Lee Quiñones, and PHASE 2 while attending High School of Art and Design in the mid 1970s. As he began to establish his own name as an artist, he was also a frequent visitor to what would become historic landmarks of the city’s nightlife, including the Lit Lounge in the East Village, Danceteria on West 21st Street, and the Mudd Club in Tribeca. These nightclubs, which often doubled as art galleries and performance venues, functioned as generative sites of social and artistic experimentation and part of the driving force behind Daze’s early works. By the early 1980s, he had begun transitioning from tagging subway cars to developing a studio practice that encapsulates the ethos of the city.

Inspired by early 20th-century urban realist artists, including John Sloan of the Ashcan School and Reginald Marsh of the WPA era, Daze’s works honor New York City’s streets and subways as important sites of his creative evolution. Simultaneously influenced by the lyrical abstraction of works by Joan Mitchell and Willem De Kooning, Daze combines gestural swaths of acrylic and spray paint with detailed renderings of train car interiors, tunnels, and stations. In Gem Spa In the 80s, 2025, Daze depicts the now iconic newspaper stand and candy store that once operated on the corner of St. Mark’s Place and Second Avenue. Gem Spa was a central destination and meeting place for members of the city’s subcultures and is referenced by literary figures like Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg (who called it a “nerve center” of the city). Important people from Daze’s life can be found throughout the composition, among them critic and curator Carlo McCormick as well as artist Martin Wong, who both emerge amongst the crowd in the painting’s foreground. In other works, technicolor throngs of flowers ascend from heaps of urban rubble, representing optimism amidst inequality and the beauty that can arise out of destruction. Throughout the exhibition, these varied combinations of tropical flora and local flowers from the artist’s home in upstate New York function as poignant memorials to what has been lost and hopeful testaments to the beauty and creativity that can still be found around every corner.

The exhibition will also include a site-specific mural, bringing an aspect of Daze’s practice often relegated to the outdoors into the interior setting of the gallery. Covering the walls of a hallway, the mural gives way to the final room of the gallery, featuring a multimedia installation that transports viewers into a composite scene from the artist’s youth. Combining a light-up dance floor and disco ball, actual subway car seats, and a curated track fusing house, disco, hip-hop, and club music, the installation emphasizes the freedom and creative inspiration that arose from these settings, and their importance to Daze’s personal and artistic development. Combining elements from throughout his career, Orchid Rain on the Underground showcases Daze’s never-ending exploration of daily life in New York City while paying homage to the people and places that comprise its vibrant cultural heartbeat.

#9024. Lomography Launches Gold-Plated Point-and-Shoot Film Camera

Lomography Launches Gold-Plated Point-and-Shoot Film Camera

The Lomography MC-A 35mm point-and-shoot camera is celebrating its first birthday in style with a pair of new limited-edition designs, including one plated with real gold.

“One year, twelve months, 365 days, and at least 15,872 film rolls later, we’re unashamedly proud of this creative tool that has grown progressively with its community. Learning and growing with experience, the Lomo MC-A is the camera made BY, FOR and WITH film photography lovers all around the globe. The same pocket-sized rebel, just a little wiser and a lot more YOU!” Lomography says, with the company’s emphasis preserved.

Inside, the new limited-edition designs are about the same as before. They are full-frame film cameras with a built-in 32mm f/2.8 multi-coated glass lens. The lens includes five elements across five groups and can be stopped down to f/16. The lens can automatically focus or zone focus from 0.4 meters (1.3 feet).

The MC-A is designed to be accessible and approachable while also supporting manual controls and creativity. To that end, it has automatic, aperture priority, and fully manual shooting modes. It also has a built-in Xenon flash, enabling the popular, nostalgic flash look many photographers covet these days.

The camera has a tripod mount, runs on a single CR2 battery, and supports multiple exposure photography.

Lomography says it has learned a few things from the community over the past year, though, including ways to improve the MC-A. The new versions promise easier film loading, can preserve settings after powering off, are more likely to shoot at f/3.5 in automatic mode, and the built-in LCD info panel shows settings “a little longer at every half-press” of the shutter.

However, it’s on the outside where the two new cameras differ even more from the MC-A that Lomography launched just over a year ago.

The new Lomo MC-A 35mm Film Camera Gold Plated is, as its name suggests, genuinely gold-plated. Lomography doesn’t say much more about the gold, but notes that the camera also features a rich brown leather cover, ships with a free glass lens filter set, and works with a new, matching leather half-case.

The other new MC-A edition is the Film Camera Noir. It features a glossy, chunky, textured black leather reminiscent of snakeskin. How reptilian. It’s a starkly different look than the golden MC-A, but no less old-school.

Lomography says both new MC-A limited-edition cameras are slated to ship in December and are available to preorder now. The Noir one is $599, while the Gold Plated version is $649. The standard Lomography MC-A, available in black and silver, is $549.

#9023. "Lady in Blue is as fitting a monument to our era as any I can imagine"

Tschabalala Self’s sculpture is far from being out of place in Trafalgar Square, writes Priya Khanchandani.

Who belongs in public space? How should public art represent who we are? And who deserves to be celebrated, cast in bronze and placed on a pedestal? These are some of the questions that Tschabalala Self’s commission for the Fourth Plinth, Lady in Blue, has raised in recent months, since it was unveiled in September.

I was there that cloudy morning in Trafalgar Square – a space I’d always crossed, probably like most Londoners, without thinking much about what it symbolises. When the black cloth was pulled away, we saw the figure of a Black woman caught mid-stride, one leg pushing through the fabric of her bright blue dress.

Like most of the admirals and generals monumentalised around her, she is cast in bronze. But unlike them she isn’t posed in command, she’s on her way somewhere. Her head, hair piled high, looks straight out into the city towards Whitehall, her left arm and fingers outstretched, moving with intention.

My Instagram post about the unveiling alarmingly attracted more than 6,000 comments, many of them either subtly or openly racist

I couldn’t help but feel satisfaction that a sculpture of a Black woman was there, taking up space in the city, on what is probably the most visible public plinth in Britain, and assumed this sentiment would be widely shared. It turns out I was wrong; my Instagram post about the unveiling alarmingly attracted more than 6,000 comments, many of them either subtly or openly racist and often suggesting the sculpture doesn’t fit its context.

I feel the need, therefore, to address the notion of what and who belongs in public space, and particularly in a space like Trafalgar Square.

Before Trafalgar Square existed, the site was used for the royal stables that served Whitehall Palace. Designed in 1840 by Charles Barry, the square was conceived as a stage for Britain’s image of itself, articulated through the grandeur of neoclassicism, and statues were central to its story. If you linger, you’ll spot George IV in Roman robes, sitting valiantly astride his horse. The generals Henry Havelock and Charles James Napier, whose reputations were made in the violent consolidation of British rule in India (the latter for the conquest of Sindh, where all four of my grandparents happen to be from) stand on two further plinths.

Admiral Horatio Nelson himself, the Royal Navy officer whose victory at the Battle of Trafalgar gave the square its name, overlooks them from 50 metres high atop a granite Corinthian column, guarded by four bronze lions. This composition represents a particular vision of 19th-century imperial power, reflected in the monuments and civic spaces rolled out across the Empire.

The square might be beautiful, and a fitting monument to its time, but it is also a living, breathing entity formed not only through its monuments and buildings, but also through the way it has been used.

Its function and meaning as a civic space keep being shaped by the people who have held festivals, memorials, gatherings here – or even simply walked through it on their daily commute. After it was built, Trafalgar Square quickly became a place for public assembly. From Bloody Sunday to the suffragettes to Black Lives Matter and the Palestine Coalition, it has a long tradition as a space of protest.

The square has been redesigned over and over, most significantly by Foster + Partners and Atkins in a 2003 scheme that closed the road along its northern edge, adding a terrace and turning what was essentially a traffic island into a pedestrianised space.

For some, in recent years the commission has merely settled into a pleasant biennial ritual

Lady in Blue is in dialogue with this context. She echoes the other figures here through her medium, bronze. And yet while the other figures are rooted to their respective plinths, she looks frozen in motion, echoing the movement of the people in the square below rather than the stillness of statues. The vivid blue of the figure’s dress – evoking lapis lazuli, the stone that has been ground into pigment since antiquity – is far from an attack on the Western canon, but rather in conscious conversation with it.

Once intended for an equestrian statue of William IV, the Fourth Plinth stood empty for more than 150 years before it became a space for contemporary sculpture in 1998. Unoccupied, it was always suggestive of a history waiting to be told or – given that the sculptures around it were all commemorating a contemporary moment – a future moment waiting to be solidified in bronze.

The absence of a statue suggested the question of who belongs on a pedestal was always open. Its dedication to contemporary art has allowed for redefinition and offered a chance to bring a quite spectacular historic space, a space of democracy, protest and celebration, into sync with the present.

The Fourth Plinth has become a space where identities are made visible and histories challenged, from Marc Quinn’s powerful Alison Lapper Pregnant, to Yinka Shonibare’s sculpture of Nelson’s own ship in a bottle. Works like these have also, at times, provoked arguments about how the square should be used, and yet each of them has become a part of its changing meaning.

For some, in recent years the commission has merely settled into a pleasant biennial ritual – and yet, this year’s sculpture underscores why it exists and why it’s so necessary right now.

In 2026, when a Black woman crossing this space is one of the most ordinary sights imaginable, Self’s statue validates her as worthy of belonging, not just in the city but here, in a culturally and politically charged public space dominated by white men sculpted by other white men.

Any notion that she doesn’t belong isn’t an aesthetic judgement, so much as a claim about who the city is for

That elevating such a woman into the visual language of the monument should provoke rage is telling, especially when all the figure has done is walk. Any notion that she doesn’t belong isn’t an aesthetic judgement, so much as a claim about who the city is for.

Self has said her work is meant to speak to human experience beyond racial identity. She has described the sculpture as depicting “everywoman”, implying that an ordinary person merits acknowledgement.

In other words, she hasn’t put it into the world simply as a statement about race – though its reception shows how readily the presence of a Black woman in this setting becomes about who is allowed to stand for the universal.

It’s as fitting a monument to our era as any I can imagine. At such a fractured time, I can’t help but feel relieved she is there, elbowing her way through the noise, making room for all of us.

Priya Khanchandani is a writer and curator specialising in contemporary design and visual culture. She was formerly head of curatorial at the Design Museum, where she curated the exhibition The Offbeat Sari and an accompanying book. She was also previously editor-in-chief of Icon, while her writing has appeared in the Financial Times, Frieze, The Guardian and The World of Interiors, as well as numerous books.

#9022. New York Studio School revamp unearths long-forgotten murals

Back in 1907, Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney established her sculpture studio in a converted stable and hayloft on MacDougal Alley in the heart of Manhattan’s Greenwich Village. The heiress and artist then proceeded to procure four neighbouring brownstones one by one, with the Lincoln Memorial sculptor Daniel Chester French being the last holdout.

The five buildings that now comprise 8 West 8th Street are some of the New York art world’s most storied. It was here that Whitney promoted US artists at a time when they were widely denigrated, and where she opened the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1931. After the museum relocated uptown, the nascent New York Studio School (NYSS) moved into the compound in 1967.

Over the past century Edward Hopper sketched, John Cage lectured and Philip Guston taught within these walls. Countless other greats practised, exhibited or, in the case of Marianne Faithfull, lived in what is now a National Historic Landmark. “This building has been the incubator for American art for 120 years,” says the artist Matthew Ritchie, sitting in a bare-bones conference room on a warm September afternoon. It has also been sorely in need of a makeover at least since he was a student here in the 1990s.

When Ritchie was named the school’s director last year, the roof and studio skylights—coveted by students for their diffused natural light—leaked, the nearly century-old cloth-wrapped wiring had deteriorated dangerously and wheelchair access was extremely limited. His priority was renovation. The first phase—including doubling the public exhibition space and creating a new accessible lecture and performance hall in wood with stepped seating—is set to be completed this autumn, and phase two will begin in the spring.

Prior to Ritchie’s arrival, the school had obtained public grants for the necessary work, but they required matching funds and their expiration date was fast approaching. He quickly marshalled forces. The board agreed to donate the required money, he says, and the school tapped Matthew Baird of Baird Architects to helm the overhaul.

The renovation work uncovered an early work by the British-born artist Cecily Brown painted on the wall when she was a student there in the 1990s

Ritchie and Baird’s history of collaboration dates back 17 years and across two other local institutions. In 2009, they teamed up to consider the effects of rising sea levels on the built environment as part of the interdisciplinary Rising Currents project at the Museum of Modern Art. Just a few years later, they put their theories into practice after Hurricane Sandy tore through the city, its storm surge flooding much of downtown. Ritchie was on the board of the beloved alternative art space The Kitchen when it enlisted Baird to rehabilitate its waterlogged lobby and black-box theatre.

The architect’s sensitive execution on that project—he preserved visual evidence of flood damage, for example—made him an obvious choice for the NYSS project, which presented a similar challenge. “You have this really cool building that’s got this patina of great artists that have moved through it,” Baird says. “How do you not erase that?”

Thanks to Baird and Ritchie’s handle-with-care edict, the construction crew was on the lookout for treasures buried beneath layers of plasterboard. The artist Cecily Brown had told Ritchie that she painted her first mural on a school wall when she was a student in the 1990s but could not remember where. And the school archives held numerous photos of murals Whitney had commissioned from the artist Robert E. Locher for the original carriage house.

Sure enough, the crew uncovered the work of both artists within a 24-hour period. Brown’s piece—featuring disembodied penises, two of them appearing to kiss—is in the newly expanded gallery space on the main floor. To prevent it from potentially distracting from exhibitions, the design team installed a shallow cabinet in front of the mural.

Ritchie jokes that the set-up resembles a gabinetto segreto, or secret room, the most famous of which was a locked vault of erotic artefacts from Pompeii and Herculaneum. “Who doesn’t want a Cecily Brown mural? And then, who doesn’t want pornography in your brand-new public gallery?” he says with a laugh. “It’s the perfect combination.”

A recently uncovered mural by the artist Robert E. Locher, commissioned by Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney

Workers discovered the two Locher murals where a bathroom and a hallway leading to it will be built. Intended to be viewed in the candlelight of Whitney’s dining room, one is a glimmering green, the other a trompe l’oeil image of doric columns. Baird tweaked the layout but not the location of the restroom. “Now it will be the most historic bathroom in New York,” Ritchie says.

A less fortuitous surprise: the beams beneath Robert Winthrop Chanler’s flame-motif fireplace in Whitney’s original second-floor studio were cracking, requiring emergency shoring up to stop the ceiling from collapse—together with the priceless fireplace. “This is the urgency of renovation,” Ritchie says. “You can wait too long, and then you lose it all.”

Because of the grant deadlines for the first phase of the project, Baird needed to work at warp speed, condensing three years of planning, permitting, bidding and execution into one. Owing to New York City’s complex building code, he approached the $2.2m renovation as “100 small projects” rather than gutting the 59,000 sq. ft building. The landmark-restoration specialist Jonathan Raible is overseeing the new roof.

In addition to enhancing the first floor’s public spaces, Baird rewired the building, renovated the wreck of a kitchen and improved accessibility by adding a wheelchair lift to the performance hall. “You can’t have a public programme if you don’t provide correct facilities for the public,” Ritchie says. “You’re not really welcoming them.”

Climbing the narrow staircases to the maze of studios where the school’s 27 full-time, in-person students work, Baird speaks enthusiastically about the second phase of renovations, which will include a student coffee bar. In keeping with his preservationist instincts, he plans to relamp with LED bulbs the elegant Fresnel recessed box lighting that Whitney installed for evenly washed walls, and he hopes to restore the system of baffles that modulated direct light in the studios as well as undertake other restoration while safeguarding the landmark’s character.

Ritchie already has his eye on another, likely longer-term fix for the school: free tuition. “That would require a very large endowment from extremely generous single or multiple donors,” he says, giving his best impression of a silver-tongued salesman, “which we’re eagerly awaiting with an entirely unique naming opportunity.”

The 82nd edition of the most closely-watched recurring exhibition in the United States will open in spring 2026

The institution's revamped third and fourth floors present reconfigured galleries, expanded education spaces and a luminous display of more than 100 menorahs from around the world

The building, just a few blocks from the museum, will be renovated and used as a permanent home for the Whitney’s Independent Study Program

#9021. From Spreadsheet to Studio: Inside a Commercial Production for Tempur-Pedic

From Spreadsheet to Studio: Inside a Commercial Production for Tempur-Pedic

I ’ve photographed campaigns in some pretty unusual places over the years, from the highlands of Ethiopia to the plains of Iraq, and I’ve been fortunate to be part of projects that were both challenging and incredibly rewarding. Somewhere along the way, I got used to the idea that the complicated jobs would probably involve an airplane, a passport, unpredictable weather or some combination of all four. So when an 12-day studio project for Tempur-Pedic and Tempur-Sealy came across my desk, I didn’t necessarily expect it to become one of the more complicated and formidable productions of my career.

It essentially started with a spreadsheet. There were roughly 30 products spanning pillows, mattress toppers and bed-in-a-box mattresses, along with references and priorities that would eventually need to bex captured, selected, retouched and delivered. Some of the photography would be clean product imagery silo on white, some would be styled-bedroom without talent, and some would feature talent in that styled-bedroom. Then within those categories were multiple compositions. When you add it all up, we were photographing thousands of individual images across a fairly rigid set of requirements.

I had worked with Tempur-Pedic previously, so I had a good understanding of what they typically needed and the usage for their deliverables. Rather than receiving a fully developed treatment and locked production plan, we were working primarily from a product list, references, and the knowledge we’d built from previous projects. The work also had to function across multiple retailers, including Amazon, Home Depot, Walmart and Wayfair.

During estimating and pre-production, my producer Bryan Sheffield and I found ourselves working backward from that spreadsheet and trying to translate it into something that could actually happen inside a studio. How many days would we need? How many days required talent? What crew would be necessary? How quickly could we move between products? How would motion and still photography share the space? And once we had thousands of images, how were they going to move through client review and post-production quickly enough to hit the final deadline?

When I started doing the math, the schedule wasn’t “mathing.” A more conventional one-camera approach looked like it could require somewhere in the neighborhood of 30 days of production time which equated to hundreds of thousands of dollars in crew fees, talent fees, studio time and equipment rental. Moreover, simply adding overtime to already long days wasn’t a real solution and I wasn’t interested in building a production plan around the assumption that everyone would simply work faster. We needed to work smarter.

That thinking led directly to the five-camera setup.

Rather than continually repositioning one camera for straight-on, three-quarter, profile, overhead and tighter compositions, I designed the studio around four static camera positions that could remain in place and hard-wired, with a fifth camera able to float handheld. Once we committed to that idea, the cameras began dictating almost everything else. Each bedroom environment was built around a relatively tight footprint, so furniture, product, talent, lighting, grip and crew all had to work around those predetermined viewpoints. A combo stand that was perfectly fine from one camera might suddenly be visible from another, which meant we had to think of the entire room as one interconnected system rather than a series of individual setups.

The lighting had to follow the same philosophy. We couldn’t light one hero angle beautifully and then rebuild everything when we moved to another camera. We needed a larger lighting environment that could remain soft, natural and consistent across several compositions at once. On paper, the diagram looked organized and relatively simple. In reality, the studio became a controlled maze of large diffusion, scrims, flags, cameras, monitors, digital carts and crew surrounding what ultimately looked like a very simple bedroom in the final photograph.

At the same time, the photography was only one part of a much larger production. Nadus Films handled the broader infrastructure around the project, including production design, set building, talent casting, wardrobe, hair and makeup, craft services and all of the logistics required to keep something of this scale moving.

We had two separate styled environments, one for Walmart and one for Wayfair, which became another important part of the efficiency plan. By the time all of this was coming together, the original spreadsheet had turned into a much larger production ecosystem. The finished photographs were intentionally simple, but there was nothing simple about what was happening behind the scenes. That’s one of the things I love about commercial photography. The final image should often feel effortless, even when everything surrounding it is anything but.

Before we got further into the pre-production weeds, we had to figure out what this thing was actually going to cost. We took the scope we had built and started putting real numbers against it: 11 production days, a dedicated pre-light day, the two bedroom sets, photography and motion, equipment, location, post-production, retouching and everything else required to keep the production moving. Once we had a realistic first pass, the client came back with a working budget and we started figuring out where we could tighten things up without cutting something we were going to regret later.

By the time everything was accounted for, it was the single largest studio production of my career, with a six-figure production budget. On December 23rd, we landed on a scope and budget that worked for everyone, and the contract and statement of work were signed. Merry Christmas!

Fast forward one month, on January 23rd we had welcomed our daughter Celeste into the world, so I was deep in pre-production while also adjusting to life with a newborn at home. My wife and family stepped in in a huge way, and I genuinely couldn’t have taken on a project of this scale without their support. It added another layer of pressure, but it also forced me to be disciplined with my time, trust the preparation and really lock in when it was time to work.

Before the first official production day, we dedicated an entire day to pre-lighting and testing. That gave us the opportunity to work through the camera system, refine the lighting, solve technical issues and figure out how mobile different parts of the set needed to be before the full production was underway. On a project this complicated, that day was incredibly valuable because every problem we could solve in advance was one less problem we had to solve while the client and full crew were waiting.

It also gave me time to think through the balance between creativity and what the photography actually needed to accomplish. At the end of the day, these were mattresses, pillows and mattress toppers. The images could be elevated and visually interesting, but they still had to accurately communicate the product.

Moving between the Walmart and Wayfair sets also meant recreating the same camera compositions and lighting as precisely as possible. My second assistant Ryan Grant and I spent a meticulous amount of time documenting lighting ratios for each camera position, marking tripod locations with color-coordinated spike tape, and measuring both the distance and height of every camera. If Camera A needed to be 48 inches off the floor and 13 feet from the bed, we wrote it down. If a light needed to be at a certain power level for a particular angle, we documented it, even if it was sometimes our own personal chicken scratch. When it came time to transition from one environment to the other, we wanted to recreate the system instead of relying on memory.

That preparation mattered because a major transition could still take close to three hours. Once a set came apart, we needed to know we were truly finished with it, or at the very least know exactly how to put it back together.

By the time the first production day arrived, I felt prepared. Then, naturally, things started changing. Some products were coming from overseas, and there were times when we weren’t entirely sure something would arrive before its scheduled day. Shots were added, others were removed and products shifted.

That’s where our line producer, Kelsey Forren, became critical. There were simply too many moving pieces for me to concentrate on directing, lighting and photography while also managing the client, product, crew, schedule and every production conversation happening around us.

The schedule became a living document. As the shot list continued to change, Kelsey was the one helping us navigate those hiccups. If we started losing time, we had to determine whether similar setups could be grouped together or whether another department could work simultaneously somewhere else.

She also became an important bridge between the client and the crew. A lot of the feedback happened conversationally and in real time rather than through formal written notes, and over the course of the project she became very good at understanding the client’s shorthand and translating that feedback into clear direction for the team.

Concise communication, responsiveness and making sure the client feels heard and supported are just as important as what happens behind the camera. Having Kelsey managing so much of that communication allowed me to stay focused on the photography while knowing that the client relationship and production itself were being taken care of.

I was thinking about the client experience in the physical studio as well. Between pre-light and the 11 production days, we were spending a lot of time together in a space where the main overhead lights often needed to remain off because of the photography. A large dark studio can start to wear on people after several days, so we brought in rugs, lamps, comfortable chairs, candles and essential oils and created pockets of warm ambient light around the client area.

I wanted the client and the crew experience to be calm and coordinated. For me, that was part of the job. I’ve always believed that customer service is a huge part of commercial photography. The photographs obviously matter, but so does the experience of making them.

Once we were fully into the production, another challenge started to become more apparent: visual variety. Much of my lifestyle work naturally gives me a lot of variables to work with, whether that’s different environments, people interacting or movement within the scene. Here, we were deliberately working inside a much more controlled framework. Even with the introduction of different props and doing my best to create micro-stories, it was still one person with one mattress, one pillow, or one mattress topper. So I had to get creative.

I started paying more attention to small changes. We could move the talent to the opposite side of the bed, alter a gesture or slightly adjust the composition without disrupting the entire setup. Occasionally I would unlock a camera from the tripod and shoot around the set looking for another perspective, but I also had to keep reminding myself why those cameras were locked in place in the first place. We weren’t trying to create endless variations of every image. We needed the required photography, enough variety across the overall library, consistency from product to product and a production that kept moving.

The products themselves demanded another kind of patience. Still photography is incredibly unforgiving. A wrinkle, fiber, fold or shadow that disappears instantly in motion becomes permanently frozen in a photograph. A pillow being manipulated by a stylist might look perfect from three feet away, but completely wrong through the camera. Because we were primarily lighting with strobes, we couldn’t always judge the final result in real time. We would adjust the product, take a frame, review it on the monitor, adjust it again, take another frame and repeat. Sometimes the difference between a photograph that looked “almost right” and one that was approved was extraordinarily small. That process, multiplied across dozens of products and hundreds of final images, is where an enormous amount of the work actually happens.

Meanwhile, another production was effectively happening inside the production: post.

With approximately 300 final images moving toward a tight delivery deadline, there was no realistic way to wait until the 11 production days were complete before beginning retouching. We needed photography, client selects and post-production to happen at the same time.

Our digital tech, Adam Mescan, carried a massive amount of that responsibility. As images were captured, he was naming files according to retailer, product, camera angle and image number, exporting them from Capture One and uploading them into the proofing gallery. The client could begin making selects while we continued working through the shot list, and once those images were selected, they could move directly to the retoucher.

Adam and I were communicating with our retoucher Jordan Hartley throughout the production, often through video calls, passing along notes and working through client feedback while we were still on set. Instead of photography ending and post-production beginning, the two processes overlapped almost completely.

Toward the end of production, client selections began to slow down. When selects slowed, retouching slowed, and suddenly something happening in one corner of the workflow had the potential to affect the final delivery.

That was another reminder that a production like this is never really about one task. You have to understand what today’s decision does to tomorrow’s workload. By the time we finished the final production day, I was exhausted, relieved and already thinking about what I would change the next time.

When I think back on the project now, I keep coming back to that original spreadsheet. On paper, it was roughly 30 products, hundreds of images, retailer requirements and references. By the time those rows and cells became photographs, dozens of people had brought their experience, judgment and craft into the room.

That feels especially important at a moment when our industry is having a larger conversation about artificial intelligence. AI can already generate a convincing bedroom, a person lying on a mattress or a perfectly shaped pillow, and those tools will only get better. What they don’t replicate in the same way is the process that created this body of work. These were real products that needed to be represented accurately. Real sets had to be built. Real talent had to be directed. Real people had to make decisions, respond to problems, communicate with one another and find solutions together.

To me, that human part of commercial photography is still incredibly important. The work has never only been about the final image. It’s about collaboration, problem-solving, customer service, trust and creating something together that accurately represents a real product and a real brand. The photograph is the visible result, but all of those decisions, conversations and experiences are embedded in it.

AI will continue to change how images are made, and I’m sure it will become another tool in the creative process. But it can’t replicate a client, photographer, producer, art department, talent and crew standing in the same room, solving real problems together and responding to one another in real time.

A project of this scale is never the work of one person. A huge thank you to everyone who brought their time, talent and attention to this production, and especially to the Tempur Sealy team for the trust and collaboration throughout the project. I’m incredibly grateful to Nadus Films and the entire crew for helping turn a spreadsheet and an ambitious production plan into something real.

Client: Tempur Sealy International (Liz Layne, Rachel Dame) Photography: Clay Cook Production: Nadus Films Producers: Ryan Galanaugh, Mark Minnery Line Producer / 1st AD: Kelsey Forren Production Assistant: Blake Peterson Digital Tech / DIT: Adam Mescan First Photo Assistant: Luke Franke Second Photo Assistant: Ryan Grant Set Construction: John Travisano Production Design + Art: Jo Hall Art Assistant: Jacob Weaver Art Assistant: Emma Anderson Hair, Makeup & Wardrobe: Lauren Sutton Wardrobe: Kate Roach Casting: Helen Wells Agency

#9020. Canon Marks 15 Years of Its Cinema EOS System With Big Firmware Updates

Canon Marks 15 Years of Its Cinema EOS System With Big Firmware Updates

It’s a very busy day for Canon. In addition to marking the 15th anniversary of the Cinema EOS System, which began when the Canon 5D Mark II DSLR arrived with Full HD video recording, Canon has announced new Cinema EOS firmware updates and new Cinema EOS camera kits.

Looking first at the new firmware updates, they are arriving for the Canon EOS C400, Canon EOS C80, Canon EOS C50, and Canon EOS R5 C cameras. Canon says the updates “solve production challenges faced by filmmakers, live broadcast crews, and virtual production technicians.”

Canon is bringing Multi Matrix Color Axis Control to the Cinema EOS lineup. Matching color profiles and overall color rendering across different cameras can be tricky, so Canon's new Multi Matrix support will let camera operators and engineers adjust the phase and gain of specific color axes remotely or directly within a dedicated camera menu.

"For example, a live broadcast crew running a multi-camera setup can make rapid in-camera color adjustments to match the Canon EOS C400, EOS C80, and EOS C50 feeds with existing studio cameras on the fly," Canon asserts.

Typically, high-frame-rate Slow & Fast (S&F) recording requires people to give something up, often live audio monitoring or subject tracking autofocus. Canon's new firmware updates add autofocus at more frame rates in S&F mode, including 72, 75, 90, and 96 frames per second. There's also new external audio transmission via SDI and HDMI.

On the C400, C80, and C50, users can now change sensor modes via an assignable function button, so operators can quickly change the angle of view without changing lenses. For example, users can switch from a full-frame sensor mode to a cropped one with the press of a button.

The EOS C50 also gets a new 1/8000s shutter speed option. This provides filmmakers more control over exposure in bright environments. The C50 also supports external flash in photo mode.

Finally, Canon has announced a free Camera Control Center app for its PTZ, select Pro Video, and Cinema Cameras. Launching later this year on Windows and later on macOS, the app provides multi-camera control, device management, and more in a single tool.

Firmware updates for the Canon Cinema EOS cameras are scheduled to be available by December. The new Camera Control Center is coming to Windows in January 2027.

Canon U.S.A. Inc. has also announced new Cinema EOS Lens Kits and an EOS C50 Videographer Kit.

There's also a new Canon EOS C50 Videographer Kit that ships with the C50 camera, the RF 20-50mm f/4L IS USM PZ lens, an Azden SGM-250LX-C Shotgun Mic, Azden MH-787-C headphones, a Hoya Variable Neutral Density II 67mm filter, and two years of CarePak Pro coverage. This entire kit is $5,999, meaning that customers are effectively paying an extra $900 for the mic, headphones, filter, and extra protection coverage.

#9019. This New E-Paper Lens Chart Is Built for Cinematographers

This New E-Paper Lens Chart Is Built for Cinematographers

Video productions can quickly become very complicated. A startup has a new e-paper display designed to keep things organized on set.

As reported by CineD, the Barcelona-based startup, Offbit, has announced M1. It’s a small e-paper display designed to replace a traditional paper lens chart that filmmakers put on cameras.

The M1 works with an iOS app and lets cinematographers label camera setups, lenses, and settings, organized by crew with space for notes. An Android version of the companion app is in development.

“Camera departments still run on paper: lens charts, crew lists folded in a pocket, notes scribbled between takes. On crews of around 30 people that change every week, even names slip,” Offbit says.

The company hopes M1 will fully replace that old-school paper approach, delivering the same information in a cleaner, more compact, more consistent device that is readable in all conditions and has a long battery life. E-paper displays are typically very power efficient, and Offbit says the M1 runs “for weeks” on a single charge.

The M1 and its app already have a database of more than 2,500 lenses, although it also supports custom lenses. It works offline without an account and only needs a connection for app and firmware updates. The app sends entered information to the M1 device itself via Bluetooth.

The M1 machined aluminum device has a matte-black design and attaches to cameras via Velcro or, in the case of cameras without a flat enough surface, an optional backplate add-on. The M1 is 85 x 60 x 10 millimeters (3.35 x 2.36 x 0.39 inches) and weighs just 71 grams (2.5 ounces). The e-paper screen is 3.1 inches diagonally and has a 320 x 240 resolution. It has a Gorilla Glass panel.

The device also has three buttons along its top edge to switch between lens, crew, and “notes.” A long press on a central button opens up the “patch gallery,” which holds 25 custom images, like production logos or crew photos. A fourth button on the left edge controls pairing and settings.

“M1 saves prep time, but the real difference is on set: lenses, crew, notes and the shooting plan, all in one place. You stop looking for the paper that went missing,” says Bernat Eguiluz, a working cinematographer and founder of Offbit.

The first batch of Offbit M1 devices, limited to 100 units, will be available to preorder on November 11 for €199. The first batch will begin shipping in December and will be available only to EU customers. Global release, including in the United Kingdom and United States, is expected in Spring 2027.

#9018. Olaver unveils multi-purpose Laneway Studio with "lantern-like" glass-block facade

In the garden of a Melbourne family home, a facade of glass blocks set within recycled white brick and a concrete band beam tops this two-storey studio by Australian architecture practice Olaver.

Olaver designed Laneway Studio to appear as a “beautiful object” reflecting light into the garden in the day and glowing like a lantern at night. The multi-purpose building was designed in response to the growing needs of the family of five, offering a practical alternative to renovating the existing home.

It houses a study-cum-guest-room with an en-suite and terrace on the first floor and an open-plan living area below, fitted with concealed laundry facilities and a bar.

The new studio block was constructed behind the main house and its newly configured garden, designed by landscape architect Penny Starr to include a pool and areas of planted foliage.

Large glass-panelled sliding doors leading into the garden from both the house and studio create a seamless flow between the interior and exterior living spaces.

Another sliding door on the opposing wall of the studio, made from oak with a steel-clad exterior, connects the studio’s living space with the titular laneway behind the property.

“With large sliding doors on opposing walls, the ground floor can open right through, so it works as an extension of the garden and pool terrace to the laneway rather than a closed room”, Olaver director Emlyn Olaver told Dezeen.

“Open, the space feels far bigger than its footprint, and the family can spread across the house, the pool and the studio as one connected space when entertaining”, she continued.

Inside, the ground floor was designed to be minimal and open-plan to ensure its multi-functionality. It features neutral terrazzo flooring throughout. Oak cabinetry conceals storage, laundry facilities and a TV nook and frames a central bar area with a stainless-steel sink and surround.

“We wanted the studio to be calm, with joinery doing the heavy lifting so each space can change roles without feeling cluttered”, Olaver explained.

“Every space had to do more than one job; a laundry, a living room or a bar depending on the day. That flexibility also gives the building a longer life, because the family’s needs will keep changing as the kids grow up, move out and come back.”

On the first floor’s east-facing wall, overlooking the garden, a facade of glass blocks was installed above a concrete band beam to bypass planning restrictions on the use of conventional windows.

The first-floor interiors were also designed to be multi-functional, comprising a combined study and guest bedroom with an en-suite and small roof terrace. Red wraparound tiling in the bathroom is echoed by red panelling in the nook of the foldable bed, itself concealed behind more oak joinery when not in use.

“The new studio’s interiors echo the existing home’s rich but calm textures,” Olaver said. “Natural materials and tactile elements exist in both spaces, but the studio is slightly more playful in its approach.”

The project tasked Olaver with extending the home of a family rapidly outgrowing their existing space.

“In Melbourne, the usual answer is yet another extension that eats into the backyard,” she said. “Laneway Studio goes the other way, keeping the garden at the centre of the site and showing how a well-designed studio can add flexibility and density to an existing lot.”

More studio developments recently featured on Dezeen include a Camber Sands studio made using waste materials and a green-tiled studio in a London garden.

#9017. Canon Technology Used to Perform World’s First Coral ‘Pregnancy Test’

Canon Technology Used to Perform World’s First Coral ‘Pregnancy Test’

Coral Spawning International (CSI), in partnership with Canon Medical Systems UK and Canon EMEA, has successfully conducted the world’s first ultrasound scan of living coral to identify developing eggs.

At a time when coral conservation is of paramount importance, this is the first non-invasive ultrasound scan on living, submerged corals that has been completed. It was conducted with the Aplio i700, an advanced Canon ultrasound platform. Scientists explain that accurately detecting egg development in living colonies allows researchers to better predict spawning windows, accelerating lab-based propagation, selective breeding, and reef restoration efforts.

In ultrasound technology, ultra-high frequency provides a sharper, high-resolution picture. However, this sharpness sacrifices the depth the sound waves are able to travel. As such, a mixture of both high (deeper but lower resolution) and ultra-high (shallow but high resolution) frequencies is used to gain a complete picture of the corals’ internal structures.

“Corals still hold so many secrets, particularly when it comes to the complex processes that drive their reproduction. Being able to look inside a living coral and see these processes unfolding in such remarkable detail is an extraordinary moment. This experiment has given us a new perspective on these animals and, as we continue monitoring them through spawning, we hope to build an increasingly detailed picture of how different coral species reproduce,” Dr. Jamie Craggs, Co-Founder of Coral Spawning International, says.

“This experiment showcased just how powerful ultrasound technology can be. Moreover, that the experiment was successful opens opportunities in fields such as minimally invasive surgery and diagnosis of dermal conditions,” Sally Davey, Clinical Product Specialist, Canon Medical Systems UK, adds.

Using Canon’s Aplio i700 hospital ultrasound system with a mix of high and ultra-high frequency probes, researchers successfully imaged internal egg structures in six large polyp stony (LPS) coral species underwater, which eliminates the traditional need to cut open or sacrifice living corals to check their reproductive state. The scan findings were verified on Trachyphyllia geoffroyi coral by cross-referencing the ultrasound images with macro photography.

While this achievement is impressive on its own, Canon says that the success of high-resolution underwater ultrasound provides valuable insights for human medical fields, including minimally invasive surgery and dermal diagnostics.

“This experiment demonstrates that imaging innovation has the power to show us what was previously unseen, creating deeper understanding of the world around us. By unlocking this knowledge, we hold a fundamental belief that imaging has the power to transform the world,” Peter Bragg, Sustainability and Government Affairs Director at Canon EMEA, explains.

Canon adds that the corals used in this experiment will continue to be monitored for six months, with recordings taken when gametes (mature reproductive cells) are released. This will allow CSI to better understand the coral reproductive cycle, helping identify spawning windows more accurately and support future coral conservation and restoration efforts.

#9015. Last Days to See Kate Meissner's New Paintings @ Lyles & King's Project Space, NYC

Lyles & King presents new paintings by Kate Meissner in our project space, on view through April 4. Kate Meissner writes: "These works are an exploration of the human body's elasticity and capacity to metamorphose. Informed by my own experience of pregnancy and the birth of my first child last year, these paintings are a meditation on physiological transformation and the body's underlying animalistic and mammalian nature."

Kate Meissner (b. 1995, Sacramento, CA) lives and works in Los Angeles, CA. Her work is in the permanent collections of Denver Art Museum, Denver, CO; Xiao Museum of Contemporary Art, Rizhao, CN; The Mer Collection, Madrid, ES; and Abroms-Engel Institute for the Visual Arts, Birmingham, US. She received her MFA from Yale University. Meissner is represented by Lyles & King, New York.

A primary beneficiary is the person or entity you designate to receive an asset — such as a life insurance policy, 401(k), IRA, or bank account — when you die. If you name multiple primary beneficiaries, they split the asset according to the percentages you specify. A contingent beneficiary (also called a secondary or backup beneficiary) receives the asset only if all primary beneficiaries are unable to inherit, either because they predeceased you, disclaimed the inheritance, or cannot be located.

This layered system exists because life is unpredictable. If you name your spouse as primary beneficiary on your life insurance and you both die in the same accident, the contingent beneficiary ensures the proceeds go where you intended rather than into your general estate where they become subject to probate.

You can name individuals, trusts, charities, or even your estate as a beneficiary. However, naming your estate is generally a poor choice because it forces the asset through probate, exposing it to creditors, delays, and court costs. The entire purpose of a beneficiary designation is to transfer assets outside of probate — naming your estate defeats that advantage.

When naming multiple beneficiaries, you must choose a distribution method that determines what happens if one beneficiary dies before you. This choice is critical and frequently misunderstood.

Per stirpes (Latin for "by the branch") means each branch of your family tree receives its designated share. If your son predeceases you, his share passes down to his children (your grandchildren) in equal portions. The family branch stays intact.

Per capita (Latin for "by the head") means assets are divided equally among surviving beneficiaries only. If your son predeceases you, his share is redistributed among your other surviving beneficiaries — his children receive nothing.

For most families, per stirpes is the safer default because it prevents accidental disinheritance of grandchildren. If you want surviving beneficiaries to absorb the shares of those who predecease you, per capita achieves that — but make sure that outcome aligns with your actual wishes.

Some financial institutions also offer per capita at each generation, which distributes equally among the nearest living generation first, then passes remaining shares equally to the next generation. This hybrid approach is less common but available at some custodians.

Beneficiary designations are deceptively simple forms that create binding legal consequences. The most expensive mistakes happen not from malice but from neglect.

In most states, a divorce does not automatically remove your ex-spouse from beneficiary designations on retirement accounts or life insurance policies. Federal law (ERISA) governs employer-sponsored plans like 401(k)s, and ERISA does not recognize state divorce revocation statutes. If you divorce and never update your 401(k) beneficiary, your ex-spouse can legally claim the entire balance — even if your will leaves everything to your new spouse.

Minor children cannot legally receive life insurance proceeds or retirement account distributions. If you name a 5-year-old as beneficiary, the insurance company will not release funds until a court appoints a guardian or conservator of the child's property. This process costs $2,000 to $5,000 in legal fees, takes months, and requires ongoing court reporting. Instead, name a trust for the benefit of the child or use your state's Uniform Transfers to Minors Act (UTMA) custodial designation.

If you leave the beneficiary field blank or all named beneficiaries predecease you without a contingent, the asset typically defaults to your estate. This triggers probate, adds 6 to 18 months of delay, and exposes the asset to estate creditors. Always name at least one contingent beneficiary.

Your beneficiary designations and your will can contradict each other. The beneficiary designation always wins. If your will says your daughter gets your IRA but the IRA beneficiary form still names your brother, your brother gets the IRA. Review both documents together annually.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Set a recurring calendar reminder to review every beneficiary designation once per year — ideally alongside your tax preparation. Pull statements from your 401(k), IRA, life insurance, bank accounts, and brokerage accounts. Verify that primary and contingent designations match your current wishes. This 30-minute annual review prevents the kind of outdated-beneficiary disasters that lead to costly litigation and assets going to unintended recipients.

Yes. You can name multiple primary beneficiaries and assign a percentage to each. For example, you could name three children as primary beneficiaries at 33.3% each. The percentages must total 100%.

If all primary beneficiaries predecease you and no contingent is named, the asset typically defaults to your estate. This forces the asset through probate, where it is subject to creditor claims, court costs, and delays of 6 to 18 months.

For state-law-governed accounts like IRAs and life insurance, some states have revocation-upon-divorce statutes — but not all. For ERISA-governed accounts like employer 401(k)s, federal law does not recognize state divorce revocation. You must manually update the beneficiary form after divorce to be safe.

Yes. A beneficiary can file a qualified disclaimer within 9 months of the account holder's death. The disclaimed asset then passes to the contingent beneficiary or according to the plan's default rules. Disclaimers are sometimes used for tax planning purposes.

Naming a trust provides control over how and when assets are distributed — especially useful for minor children, spendthrift beneficiaries, or blended families. However, trusts named as IRA beneficiaries must meet specific IRS requirements to qualify for stretch distributions under the SECURE Act. Consult an estate planning attorney before naming a trust as retirement account beneficiary.

A POD designation on a bank account functions exactly like a beneficiary designation. The named person receives the account balance upon your death without going through probate. You maintain full control of the account during your lifetime and can change the POD beneficiary at any time.

Primary and contingent beneficiary designations are among the most powerful — and most overlooked — estate planning tools. They transfer assets instantly upon death, bypass probate entirely, and override your will in every state. The 30 minutes it takes to review and update your designations after every major life event can save your family months of legal proceedings, thousands in attorney fees, and the heartbreak of assets going to unintended recipients.

#9013. Canon Announces Timer Remotes for Astrophotographers and a Compact Hotshoe Mic

Canon Announces Timer Remotes for Astrophotographers and a Compact Hotshoe Mic

Alongside new Cinema EOS firmware, Canon has announced some new accessories for its mirrorless EOS R System cameras, including timer remote controllers and a hotshoe microphone.

The new Timer Remote Controllers, the TC-N3 and TC-E3, build upon the legacy of Canon’s Timer Remote Controller TC-80N3 for film and digital SLR cameras. Timer Remote Controllers are designed for specialized photographic applications, including precisely capturing long-exposure photos in bulb mode and automating and customizing long-interval photography for things like star trails and timelapses.

Compared to the TC-80N3, the new TC-N3 and TC-E3 controllers feature a 20% larger LCD panel with bigger numbers and icons, a new orange illumination backlight for better visibility at night, a new clock function to schedule shooting sessions, and tripod compatibility. It still includes dedicated shooting controls, and the remotes run on AAA batteries.

The Timer Remote Controller TC-N3 is compatible with the Canon EOS R1, EOS R3, EOS R5, EOS R5 Mark II, and EOS R5 C, and other cameras with an N3 remote terminal.

The TC-E3 works with cameras with an E3 terminal, including the EOS C50, EOS R6 Mark III, EOS R6 V, EOS R6 Mark II, EOS R8 Mark II, EOS R8, EOS R7, EOS R10, EOS R50 V, and EOS R100.

“The remotes offer photographers great flexibility and precision when capturing landscapes, astrophotography, and self-portraits, particularly in low-light environments or when composing a group photo or self-portrait from a distance,” Canon says.  The new remote controllers will begin shipping in early January. The TC-N3 is $189.99 while the TC-E3 is $209.99.

Canon TC-N3Buy new on B&HCanon TC-N3Buy used on KEH.comCanon TC-E3Buy new on B&HCanon TC-E3Buy used on KEH.com

Canon has also announced the DM-E10D, a new monaural digital microphone for use on Canon’s Multi-Function Shoe.

Compatible with a wide range of Canon cameras, including the EOS R1, R3, R5 II, R6 III, R6 II, R8 II, R8, R7, R10, R50 V, R6 V, and more, the DM-E10D features a super cardioid polar pattern mic that prioritizes sound from the front while reducing unwanted noise from the sides. It also picks up sound from the rear, so it can capture conversations between the camera operator and a subject.

The compact on-camera mic features cable-free operation and has a Menu button for easy access to audio settings. It draws power directly from the camera and includes a built-in shock mount and wind cover.

Canon notes that the DM-E10D is its smallest and lightest DM-series microphone to date. It will begin shipping by the end of December and is $209.99.

Canon has also announced new Cropping Guide firmware for the EOS R6 Mark III full-frame mirrorless camera. The firmware update has four different guides, including top and bottom guidelines to fit different head sizes and guidelines for positioning props in the frame.

This firmware is designed for high-volume photographers, like school and sports photographers, to consistently capture photos with the same framing of many subjects in a short time. It also includes color-coded guides for common print sizes, including 5×7 and 8×10 aspect ratios.

Canon will begin selling the EOS R6 III with the Cropping Guide firmware already installed for $2,919 in early December. It will also be available separately as a $120 service charge for existing owners.

#9012. Vienna Recession? Four galleries in Austrian capital shut shop amid a tougher market

MYMOVE (pink) by Lena Henke on the roster of Layr Gallery, which is moving to a more flexible gallery model Nils Jorgensen/Alamy Stock Photo

Vienna’s contemporary art scene seems to be collapsing. Three of its galleries—Layr, Exile and Zeller van Almsick—are either closing or “evolving”, all citing the unsustainability of running increasingly costly businesses in an unpredictable market. Meanwhile Eva Presenhuber, who opened a space in Vienna in 2022, has confirmed she is also leaving the Austrian capital amid a downturn in sales.

Those that have confirmed they are closing for good—Exile after 18 years and Zeller van Almsick after nearly ten—are clear-eyed. “There is no point in sugarcoating the fact that the past two years have been financially extremely challenging,” says Magdalena Zeller, a co-founder of Zeller van Almsick. For Christian Siekmeier, the founder of Exile, “there are simply no new collectors emerging”.

Emanuel Layr, who is closing his corner-hugging Layr gallery in favour of a more nomadic, project-based business (including a smaller, by-appointment space in Vienna), says: “The gallery model as we know it is increasingly reaching its limits.” The relentless commitments, to art fairs and the customary six-weekly exhibition, are not paying off. “It’s harder to sell some things, costs are getting higher, then there’s a big art fair coming and taking another €100,000,” he says. “I had to be more realistic, and think, ‘How much profit do I get? How much does the artist get?’.”

A historic garage was the venue for the Astoria Artshow, which debuted in September © Carmen Alber/Astoria Artshow

Yet Layr and his Viennese counterparts identify a groundswell of enthusiasm from younger generations. September’s new Astoria Artshow, an event held in Europe’s oldest garage (founded in 1918), was a hit, and notably from a young crowd. Its cash tills might not have been ringing, but galleries paid only €500 to participate so had much less to lose. The gallery-led gathering, which returns as a “fair” next year, seemed a breath of fresh air in the slot of previous events, such as Viennacontemporary, which is not showing any sign of returning.

Long-time collectors were also fans of Astoria Artshow. “This will be the future,” says Eva Frey, who with her husband Manfred has been buying contemporary art for more than 30 years, and who sits on the board of Mumok, another bright spot in Vienna’s cultural offerings. Frey points out that the gallery closures will come after the city’s unique, month-long Curated By festival, supported by the city and state and which has been a boon to the contemporary art scene since it launched in 2009.

Frey says that the issue for Vienna’s cutting-edge galleries is that collectors of her vintage (which she defines as “over 70”) are not enough to keep business going. The problem, she says, is not so much the youngest generations, but that “there are fewer people between 45 and 55, who are established in a profession, and who used to be the main collectors in the market”. Layr finds too that “for middle-income professionals, there is less money around, so they are more careful”.

Many of the issues might be Vienna-related. It’s a small market and Zeller identifies “a significant gap between the cultural importance of the city and the depth of its local collector base”. But the middle-income strains seem a microcosm of what is happening in the wider art market, namely plenty of enthusiasm from the younger generations and a relative handful of older buyers keeping the top end just about managing. This requires a holding pattern of flexibility, at best, from the galleries who stick it out. For those that do, and can, hope rests on the juniors, but we just might have to wait a while to know if they can fill the gaps.

#9011. Atelier Zébulon Perron draws on metabolist influence for Montreal bistro

A monochrome palette and influences from Japanese metabolism characterise Bistrot à Franky in Montreal, Canada designed by local outfit Atelier Zébulon Perron.

The restaurant is a home base for local chef Francis Blais in the city’s hip Mile End neighbourhood.

Atelier Zébulon Perron took what it views as the standard design language of a Montreal bistro – bright lighting and lots of activity – and translated it into a more contemporary design.

For studio founder Zebulon Perron, the monochrome whites and beiges, interspersed with milled aluminium accents and a large zinc bar top, allowed the studio to experiment with textures and lighting to create visual interest and contrast in the dining space.

“With the monochromy of the restaurant, we experimented with textures – shiny versus matte, tile nd and stucco – and how light reacts to those surfaces in different ways,” Perron told Dezeen.

The studio emphasised the postmodern and “retrofuturist” elements of the design, pointing to the custom chandeliers with their illuminated Pyrex tubes and exposed wiring, fabricated by Perron’s long-time collaborators, local lighting design studio Lambert & Fils.

Perron highlighted the milled aluminium wine cellar that sits above the bar face, interspersed with portholes that are a direct reference to Japanese metabolist architecture.

“There’s a postmodern, 1980s aesthetic that naturally rose from everything we were doing,” said Perron.

Visitors enter the restaurant through a red-painted hallway and a metal door and handle carved from butcher block by local cabinetmaker Olivier Doray.

Inside, only the terrazzo floor was a holdover from the building’s former use. Granite tabletops cover some of the larger tables, while the classic bistrot white tablecloths are draped over the smaller tables.

Blond leather banquettes were placed below large mirrors on the wall opposite the bar, and these larger seating arrangements are centred by large butcher block tables, also fabricated by Doray.

Custom walnut chairs were designed by local industrial designer Guillaume Sasseville.

On the walls, white tile is interspersed with stucco and works of art, curated by local filmmaker Xavier Dolan. These artworks give pops of colour and Perron said that the monochromatic design elements allow both the food and the artworks to stand out in the space.

“Since the canvas is pretty neutral, the food and the artwork take centre stage,” he said.

A set of windows opens up the kitchen space to the dining room.

Custom bar seating features white columns with seats informed by transportation design, and Perron noted that the metal details and clean lines of the bar space, as well as the metal fans, also give the interior a streamlined look.

Atelier Zébulon Perron has designed some of the most interesting interior spaces in the city, including Café Constance and the dining areas for the city’s Four Seasons hotel.

It also helped create the pop-up bar staged during the city’s inaugural design week earlier this year.

#9010. The Motorola Signature 27 Has a Dedicated Action Sensor and Ludicrously Bright Screen

The Motorola Signature 27 Has a Dedicated Action Sensor and Ludicrously Bright Screen

Motorola debuted its brand new flagship phone, the Signature 27, at Qualcomm’s annual Snapdragon Summit in September. However, at the time, Motorola unveiled just a few key specs and left much to the imagination. That changed this week, with the company revealing more information about its new phone.

As PetaPixel previously reported, the sleek Signature 27’s main camera is the 50-megapixel Sony Lytia 910, a relatively large Type 1/1.28 LOFIC image sensor. It promises excellent low-light performance, expanded dynamic range, and gorgeous color.

It’s paired with a 200-megapixel Sony Lytia 901 image sensor for the telephoto camera. This is an even bigger sensor, measuring at Type 1/1.12. The periscope telephoto camera has 5x optical zoom and, through AI image processing, can reach 100x equivalent zoom with Super Zoom Pro. As Motorola notes, this uses generative AI to create new pixels. This is similar to other super zoom features seen on competing Android smartphones.

It also has a third standard rear camera: a 50-megapixel ultrawide with a Type 1/2.76 sensor.

However, in an exclusive hands-on video with Motorola, YouTuber creator Danny Winget revealed more details about the Signature 27, including a special sensor on the rear camera module.

Describing the camera system as “insane,” Winget explains that a dedicated “action sensor” on the back of the Signature 27 helps with high-speed photography. It’s not entirely clear what this sensor actually is, but as Winget shows, it looks effective with the camera’s dedicated “action mode.” It’s worth keeping an eye on.

Winget also discussed the Signature 27’s large 6.8-inch display, which is a Tandem OLED that Motorola claims tops out at 12,000 nits, which is absurd. The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra doesn’t even hit 3,000. While 12,000-nit peak brightness will likely be limited to specific situations and only part of the screen, it is still a pretty wild spec.

Tandem OLED display tech recently made news elsewhere in the tech space, as Apple’s brand-new, redesigned touchscreen MacBook Pro also features a new Tandem OLED.

As PetaPixel noted in September, the Signature 27 runs on Qualcomm’s newest Snapdragon 8 Elite chip, features a refined, fashion-forward design, and includes Bang & Olufsen audio.

Motorola is definitely targeting a premium market here, although it’s not known yet just how premium. It’s also still unclear exactly when the Motorola Signature 27 will launch. The company is slow-rolling the reveal. It is expected to fully launch sometime this month, though, so prospective buyers shouldn’t have to wait much longer for all the details.
