#9009. William N. Copley "X-Rated (1972–1974)" @ Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin

Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin, is pleased to announce X-Rated (1972–1974), a solo exhibition of paintings and works on paper by William N. Copley. This is the fourth presentation of the artist’s work at the gallery, and the show will be on view through April 22, 2026.

Copley came to painting from an unusual position. He had ambitions to become a writer before becoming a painter, and, for a brief period in the late 1940s, he co-founded and operated a gallery in Beverly Hills that focused on the Surrealists. The Copley Galleries – which he ran with his brother-in-law, the artist John Ployardt – brought him into close contact with exiled Surrealists such as Man Ray, Max Ernst and Marcel Duchamp, as well as the dealer Alexander Iolas, who encouraged him to pursue his nascent art practice. Adopting the signature CPLY around the time the gallery closed, he debuted his first exhibition at a bookstore in Los Angeles in 1951, shortly before he moved to France.Even though he was a generation younger than the Surrealists, Copley’s work is deeply informed by the movement on a conceptual and personal level. While his bold black outlines and self-taught figurative style recall comics and Pop art, Copley approached painting with a literary sensibility, using narrative strategies that both embodied Surrealist principles and drove the structural evolution of his compositions. Like many Surrealists, Copley embraced humour, psychology and eroticism as fundamental to his creative process, yet his engagement with overtly sexual subjects went far beyond the playful eroticism of his peers.On view in the exhibition are works from Copley’s prolific ‘X-Rated’ series, created between 1972 and 1975, and first exhibited in 1974 in an eponymous show at the New York Cultural Center. This body of work draws on erotic imagery and ritualised motifs from adult magazines, seeking, in the artist’s own words, to ‘break through the barrier of pornography into the area of joy.’ 1In a decade when the sale of hardcore pornography was still illegal in the United States, Copley would buy ‘adult magazines’ under the counter, using them as a source for inventive figurative and narrative paintings that explored eroticism, sexual politics and the pursuit of pleasure. The artist was able to convey a wide range of tone in the ‘X-Rated’ paintings: some, such as The Seven Year Itch, 1973, are tender; others, including  Viridiana, 1973, are exuberant; and almost all of them are openly humorous. Underscoring the open-endedness of sexual expression, Copley stated: ‘That’s what makes sex so much fun: since nobody really understands it, the possibilities for originality are endless.’ 2Copley typically produced two stages of preparatory drawings before starting a painting: an initial, small-scale study, followed by a larger version in which he refined the composition, introduced changes, and heightened the work’s pictorial dynamism. The resulting paintings maintain a deliberately slapdash style, with figures treated loosely rather than meticulously rendered. The exhibition makes this developmental process visible through multiple pairings of preparatory drawings and completed paintings, including Calcutta, 1973, and its counterpart Untitled, 1973.Scenes of copulations and orgies are set against vivid, brightly coloured backgrounds animated by bold, geometric patterns, making them almost ‘too artful to be libidinous, let alone lascivious’, as critic James R. Mellow has remarked. 3 It is both this treatment of the backgrounds and the contorted, entwined bodies with their attenuated limbs and schematic outlines that has prompted critics to draw a link between Copley and Henri Matisse more than once. Yet, while depictions of the nude and sexual imagery throughout art history have traditionally relied on suggestion and idealisation, Copley presents the sexual act directly, leaving nothing to the imagination.With titles borrowed from Hollywood movies such as Les Quatre Cent Coups, The Exorcist or Tobacco Road, Copley tempered the shock of the pornographic image through comic playfulness and pop cultural sensibility. Manifesting a Surrealist disjunction, the movies rarely align explicitly with the images’ content, but the titles nevertheless set in motion a cascade of associations for the viewer. The title of the series, likewise, draws on terminology from the film industry: until the 1990s, the film-classification term ‘X-rated’ was used in the US for films only suitable for adults. Despite the cautionary notices that some visitors might find the subject matter offensive, the 1974 exhibition at the Cultural Center – curated by the newly appointed and strikingly progressive director Mario Amaya – received a notably positive critical response. Art in America writer Peter Schjeldahl hailed the presentation as a ‘uniformly gorgeous exhibition,’ noting that it marked ‘a highly satisfying development in Copley’s work’. 4The ‘X-Rated’ series represents a singular chapter in Copley’s oeuvre, deliberately set apart from the prevailing currents of the early-1970s art scene. Even in today’s uncensored and image-saturated world, Copley’s suggestive canvases retain a subversive charge. By merging art and eroticism, Copley challenged conservative norms and rejected the notion of artistic neutrality, clearing away moralistic constraints in favour of directness and humour.

#9008. The Art of the Panoramic Aspect Ratio

Panoramic compositions offer another way to present a scene, preserving its horizontal breadth and giving the frame a different sense of scale, movement, and visual balance. They can be extremely powerful.

The proportions of a photograph influence how it is viewed. A conventional landscape frame provides a relatively balanced relationship between horizontal and vertical space, while a panoramic crop places considerably more emphasis on width. This changes the viewer’s experience, encouraging the eye to move across the image and take in the composition progressively.

That extended viewing experience is one of the format’s greatest strengths. Rather than concentrating attention within a relatively compact frame, a panoramic photograph gives visual information more room to unfold. The viewer can follow changes in light, examine relationships between foreground and background elements, and appreciate the full extent of the scene. This can make the photograph feel expansive without relying on dramatic processing or exaggerated perspective.

Panoramic images also have a distinctive sense of balance. Their proportions can create a feeling of openness and continuity, especially when the composition has a strong horizontal structure. The format can be quiet and understated or dramatic and imposing, depending on the subject, light, and arrangement of elements. It is not simply a way to include more of a scene. It changes which parts of the photograph receive emphasis and how the viewer moves through it.

The panoramic format works best when a scene’s horizontal breadth is an important part of its visual appeal. Landscape photography is an obvious application, but the format can also work well for architecture, cityscapes, environmental portraits, and other subjects where the surrounding space contributes to the image.

Before choosing a panoramic composition, consider what makes the original photograph compelling. If the subject depends on vertical elements or a strong relationship between foreground and sky, removing too much of the image’s height may weaken it. If the strongest visual information is distributed horizontally, however, a wider frame may create a more cohesive composition.

The format can also help simplify a photograph. Cropping away unnecessary sky or foreground reduces competing information and emphasizes the remaining elements. This is particularly useful when the original image contains substantial areas that contribute little to its visual impact. However, removing space simply to achieve a wider aspect ratio is not necessarily an improvement. Open areas can provide balance, establish scale, and give important details room within the frame.

It is worth comparing several aspect ratios before deciding on a final composition. A moderately wide image may preserve enough vertical information to maintain depth, while a more elongated format can create a stronger emphasis on horizontal movement. Neither is inherently better. The right proportions support the composition without sacrificing the information that matters.

A panoramic composition requires attention across the entire width of the frame. In a conventional photograph, the viewer may be drawn quickly toward a central subject. With a panoramic image, the extended proportions create more opportunity for visual movement, but they also make balance particularly important. A strong focal point should work with the rest of the frame rather than simply occupy the center.

Horizontal lines and directional elements can help establish that movement. The placement of the horizon, the alignment of natural or architectural features, and the distribution of contrasting areas all influence how the viewer moves through the photograph. Consider whether the composition has a clear visual starting point and whether the remaining elements support or interrupt that progression.

Negative space plays an equally important role. A wide frame does not need to be filled with detail from edge to edge. Open areas can provide visual relief, separate competing elements, and establish the atmosphere of the photograph. Removing too much space during cropping can make an image feel crowded, particularly when important subjects sit close to the boundaries.

Pay as much attention to the left and right edges as to the center. Small distractions become more noticeable when the composition is stretched horizontally, and an element that seems insignificant in the original frame may disrupt the finished image. Review the entire composition before releasing the shutter, and make small adjustments to camera position when necessary. The goal is not to fill every part of the frame, but to make each area feel intentional.

A wide aspect ratio can communicate a scene’s breadth, but width alone does not create depth. The relationship between elements at different distances remains essential. Overlapping forms, changes in contrast, and variations in light help establish separation and give the viewer a sense of how the scene extends into the distance.

Atmospheric conditions can be particularly effective in this regard. Haze, fog, rain, and changing light create tonal differences between near and distant elements. Preserving those transitions across a panoramic composition can give the photograph a strong sense of depth without requiring an exaggerated foreground.

Scale also benefits from thoughtful composition. Including recognizable elements within an expansive environment provides a reference point that helps viewers understand the size of the surrounding space. The challenge is to retain enough context for that relationship to be clear without allowing secondary details to compete with the main subject.

When editing, consider how much of the original foreground and background needs to remain. A panoramic crop that removes too much of either can flatten the photograph or change its sense of scale. The goal is to retain the relationships that give the image depth while letting the wider proportions emphasize the overall scene.

You can create panoramic photographs with almost any focal length. The choice depends on how much of the scene you need to include and how you want the different elements to relate to one another.

Wide-angle lenses capture a broad field of view and can preserve a strong relationship between foreground and background. They are useful when the composition depends on including substantial environmental context, although perspective becomes increasingly pronounced as the camera moves closer to foreground subjects. This can make nearby elements appear much larger in relation to the background.

Standard and telephoto lenses offer a different approach. Longer focal lengths isolate a narrower portion of the scene and can make distant elements appear more prominent within the composition. They are useful when the visual interest is concentrated in a particular section of the landscape or when the photographer wants to emphasize layers without including much foreground.

Camera position is just as important as focal length. Changes in height and direction can alter the alignment of elements, the amount of foreground visible, and the relationship between different parts of the scene. Take time to assess the composition before settling on a viewpoint, especially when working with a longer lens.

If the intention is to create a panoramic crop from a single exposure, leave sufficient room around important details. Cropping reduces the available resolution and may remove more of the original frame than expected. A little extra space gives you flexibility in editing and helps prevent important elements from being cut off.

There are two primary ways to create panoramic photographs: cropping a single exposure or stitching multiple frames together. Each approach has advantages, and the best choice depends on the scene, the available resolution, and whether anything within the frame is moving.

Cropping a single exposure is often the simplest option. It works particularly well when the camera’s native field of view already includes the necessary horizontal information and the resulting file retains enough resolution for the intended output. High-resolution cameras offer more flexibility, but it is still important to consider how much of the original image you’ll remove.

Stitching multiple photographs together can produce a much larger file with additional detail. This is useful when photographing a scene that extends beyond the camera’s field of view or when you intend to print a particularly large image. For consistent results, use a tripod when practical, keep the camera level, and overlap consecutive frames by approximately 25 to 30 percent. The overlap gives stitching software enough shared detail to align the images.

Manual exposure and a fixed white balance help maintain consistency throughout the sequence. If the camera changes exposure or white balance between frames, visible variations can appear in the finished image. Focus should also remain consistent. Consider focusing once and switching to manual focus before capturing the remaining frames, particularly when photographing distant subjects.

Stitching is not always the best choice. Movement within the scene can create alignment problems, duplicated details, or visible inconsistencies. Waves, foliage, clouds, and moving subjects may change position between exposures. In these situations, a single image may produce a more natural result. When stitching, also be mindful of nearby objects, since parallax can cause alignment errors if the camera rotates around the wrong point.

Post-processing shapes the final proportions and balance of a panoramic image. Most editing programs allow photographers to select a custom crop ratio or enter specific dimensions. Ratios such as 2:1 or 2.35:1 provide useful starting points, but there is no need to force every photograph into the same proportions.

Begin by identifying the visual information that needs to remain. Consider whether the sky, foreground, and surrounding details contribute to the photograph or simply occupy space. Adjust the crop gradually and compare different proportions. A relatively small change in height can have a significant effect on the image’s balance.

Check the position of the horizon and other prominent horizontal lines. Their placement should reflect the visual importance of the areas above and below them. Also review the edges for distractions, and make sure important details aren’t positioned awkwardly close to the boundaries.

For stitched panoramas, cropping also removes the uneven edges created during alignment. Leave enough room during capture to account for this, particularly when important details extend close to the edges of the frame. Once you’ve established the composition, inspect the full-resolution image for stitching errors, uneven transitions, and inconsistencies in exposure or color.

Avoid making the crop so tight that the image loses its sense of openness. One of the advantages of the panoramic format is the space it provides. Removing too much of that space can undermine the very quality that makes the format appealing.

Large prints are one of the most compelling applications of panoramic photography. The extended proportions make effective use of horizontal wall space, creating a presentation that feels distinct from a conventional landscape print. They are particularly well suited to areas where a standard rectangular photograph might appear too small or visually contained.

The viewing experience also changes with print size. A panoramic image encourages the viewer to move their attention across its length, taking in details and relationships that might be overlooked when viewing a smaller image on a screen. At a larger scale, subtle changes in tone, texture, and light become more apparent. The photograph can become something viewers return to rather than an image they take in at a glance.

The format is also versatile in interior spaces. Its proportions can work above furniture, along hallways, in offices, or across larger uninterrupted walls. A carefully composed panoramic print can provide a strong focal point without requiring an elaborate arrangement of multiple images. Its visual impact comes from the photograph itself and the space it occupies.

Preparing an image for a large print requires more consideration than simply selecting a wide crop. Resolution is particularly important. Cropping a single exposure reduces the available pixel dimensions, so check the final file against the print lab’s recommendations before ordering. If the intended print is especially large, stitching multiple frames may provide the additional resolution needed to retain fine detail.

The viewing distance should also inform the final output. A print intended to be seen from across a room does not necessarily require the same pixel density as one that will be examined from close range. Consult the printer’s specifications and consider the physical dimensions of the finished image before making final sharpening and output decisions.

The print surface influences how the photograph is presented. Matte papers reduce reflections and suit images with subtle tonal transitions, while luster and semi-gloss finishes add more surface sheen and can emphasize contrast. Canvas offers a different aesthetic, with visible texture and a softer rendering of fine detail. Choose a finish that complements the photograph rather than treating it as an afterthought.

Framing and presentation matter, too. Panoramic aspect ratios don’t always match standard frame sizes, so custom framing may be necessary. A mat can separate the photograph from its surroundings, while a frameless presentation gives the image a more continuous appearance. Consider the available wall space and the intended viewing distance when deciding on the final dimensions.

The strongest panoramic photographs aren’t necessarily the widest or most dramatic. Their success comes from the relationship between the subject, the composition, and the proportions of the finished image. The format should give the photograph a reason to extend horizontally, whether that means preserving the breadth of a landscape, emphasizing visual relationships, or creating a more immersive viewing experience.

When composing, look beyond the central subject and consider the entire width of the scene. Pay attention to balance, negative space, depth, and the placement of important details. Leave room to refine the crop, and consider the intended presentation before removing a substantial portion of the original image.

A panoramic photograph offers more than an alternative aspect ratio. It lets you control how a scene is experienced, giving the viewer space to explore the image and allowing the photograph to take on a distinctive presence when displayed at a larger scale.

#9007. One Dead and Two Critically Injured After a Helicopter Crashed During a Photography Flight

One Dead and Two Critically Injured After a Helicopter Crashed During a Photography Flight

One person has been killed while two others were injured after a helicopter crashed during a photography flight in Miami, Florida.

As ABC News reports, three people were aboard the flight. Passengers were reportedly filming boats on the water when the chartered helicopter crashed into Biscayne Bay, just south of downtown Miami.

“Preliminary information indicates it was a photography flight,” the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) reports. NBC 6 South Florida reports that the helicopter is owned by Global Aerials, a Miami-area aerial media services company, and took off from North Perry Airport, just north of Miami.

One man died as a result of the crash, despite the heroic efforts of a good Samaritan who was providing life-saving assistance, according to Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz. The same good Samaritan also sent a mayday call to authorities and may have saved the lives of the other two passengers due to their quick thinking.

The two other men who were aboard the crashed helicopter were rescued from the water and transported by air to Jackson Memorial Hospital’s trauma center, where they are both in critical but stable condition. Authorities say that their conditions after being removed from the water were so severe they required life-flight transportation.

Authorities do not yet know the cause of the crash, although it is under investigation. Heavy storms have hit the area over the last few days, but authorities cannot yet say whether weather conditions contributed to the crash. The helicopter had been flying south in the bay before looping back north shortly prior to crashing.

The Robinson R44 helicopter crashed at around 11:15 AM ET. Rescue workers from various local agencies, the Coast Guard, and even Customs and Border Protection (CBP) all responded to the crash scene, NBC News reports.

Television news video, like the one seen above from NBC 6 South Florida, shows the helicopter upside down in the water, surrounded by rescue personnel.

Less than two months ago, aerial photographer and reporter Eliana Moreno died after an NBC Los Angeles helicopter crashed in L.A. suburbs while the news crew was filming a fatal bus collision scene. Alongside Moreno, the helicopter pilot, George Marciniw, and a person on the ground, Edy Gutiérrez Mejia, who was visiting Los Angeles from Guatemala, also perished.

#9006. In uneasy times, Bangladesh launches its first art fair

The Bangladeshi capital is a city of nearly 37 million people but has few commercial art galleries, despite a rich artistic tradition Towfiqu Barbhuiya

The Bangladeshi capital of Dhaka is set to stage its first commercial art fair this month, which aims to transform the city’s private art sector and encourage a new generation of Bangladeshi collectors.

Art Dhaka, staged under the tagline “Art for All”, will take place at Aloki, a popular multidisciplinary cultural hub and former garment factory.

Though Dhaka is increasingly recognised on the global stage for its non-commercial exhibitions, the city has a limited number of traditional commercial art spaces, with only a few private galleries.

The fair’s founding members—Durjoy Rahman, Nahar Khan, Aumia Khundkar and Fahd Sattar—are addressing the city’s lack of commercial infrastructure by staging a curated fair of emerging and established Bangladeshi artists. Those whose work will feature in the first edition include Dhali Al Mamoon, Mojahid Musa, Najmun Nahar Keya, Bishwajit Goswami, Ayesha Sultana and Dinar Sultana Putul.

The new fair is being curated by Najmun Nahar Keya and fellow Dhaka-based artist and curator Zihan Khan, both of whom have guest curated Dhaka’s international festival for photography, Chobi Mela. The fair will feature gallery presentations, public programming and dedicated spaces for emerging artists.

“This is not like Frieze or Art Basel—it is with the ambiance of an art biennial,” says Rahman, a collector and the founder of the Durjoy Bangladesh Foundation (DBF). “We wanted to stage an event to showcase the art, culture and architecture in Bangladesh through a platform which caters to a wider ecosystem, with a commercial aspect.”

Bangladesh, emphasises Rahman, is a country of around 178 million people, making it the eighth most populous nation in the world, and one in which art has long played a key role. “Culture and art have always been important to everyday life,” Rahman says. “Craft is a part of everyone’s household. We grew up going to cultural events. But over the years, because of industrial development, art became a subject for just a few. Art Dhaka attempts to fill this gap.”

“We don’t have a strong gallery system,” Rahman says. Besides his own foundation, Dhaka is home to a handful of other private foundations, including the Bengal Foundation, Brihatta Art Foundation, Cosmos Foundation and the Samdani Art Foundation. The latter was founded in 2012 and has organised the Dhaka Art Summit (DAS) since 2012, arguably the most influential event in attracting international attention to Dhaka’s art scene.

The handful of commercial art galleries include Drik, internationally known for championing photography and multimedia storytelling; Galleri Kaya and Gallery Chitrak, showing Modern masters and contemporary Bangladeshi painters; and Abinta Gallery of Fine Arts, a non-profit cultural centre that opened in 2012 and shows established and emerging Bangladeshi artists.

“In a city with 36.6 million people, how do we stage something that will lure even 2% of the population when we have such few art spaces?” asks Rahman. “We want to balance the display of both Modern and contemporary art and encourage new and younger Bangladeshi collectors to invest in art.”

A rendering of Aloki, the venue for the Art Dhaka fair Courtesy of Aloki

“For the first edition, I think we want to establish the fact that we have local patronage. We do have the calibre of artists and we have the organisational ability within ourselves and our curators to put on this show,” says Fahd Sattar, the founder of Aloki.

“We need to have cultural infrastructure between South Asian countries,” he adds, emphasising how future editions of the fair will incorporate the wider region. “This year we are focusing on Bangladeshi artists and the diaspora. Next edition, we could also venture out of Aloki to other areas of the city, and may open to international galleries and artists.”

While there is much hope the new hybrid-format fair will provide a needed boost for Dhaka’s art scene, it is taking place as the country continues to navigate a challenging socioeconomic and political landscape.

Following a historic general election on 12 February—which marked the first contested presidential election since October 1991 and resulted in a landslide victory for Tarique Rahman’s Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP)—the nation is still finding its footing. The last few years in Bangladesh have been characterised by intense political turbulence and economic strain, particularly during the challenging democratic transition under an interim government following the ousting of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in 2024. Against this backdrop, Bangladesh’s art scene is undergoing a profound post-uprising transformation. Following the fall of Hasina’s government, the creative community has experienced a surge in politically engaged expression, alongside institutional restructuring and the formation of new international partnerships.

Globally, the Bangladesh art scene garnered much international interest due to the DAS, a biennial event staged by Bangladeshi collectors and patrons Nadia and Rajeeb Samdani. But the country’s challenging political landscape has created difficulties in staging the summit, with the last edition taking place in 2023.

Collector Durjoy Rahman, a founding member of the fair Courtesy of Durjoy Rahman

“We have never censored any artist; you can’t censor artists,” says Rajeeb Samdani, emphasising that DAS cannot be staged in Bangladesh’s current political climate.

Most recently, transgender and feminist human rights activist Ho Chi Minh Islam was dropped as a speaker from the fifth Bay of Bengal Conversation in Dhaka, scheduled to take place on 5 October, following an intense online backlash. The event is an international forum on geopolitics, technology and governance, organised by the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS).

Rajeeb Samdani, who praises the inaugural Art Dhaka for the wealth of opportunities to be had for the Bangladeshi art scene, says he and Nadia hope to return to Bangladesh with the DAS in the next few years, once the challenging political landscape dissipates.

“It’s great an art fair is taking place in Dhaka as I think it is important for the city’s art ecosystem and the wider development of the art scene,” he says.

In the meantime, the Samdanis have been busy maintaining their programming abroad. This includes a multi-year partnership with the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford, which includes a solo exhibition of Soma Surovi Jannat and the appointment of Munem Wasif as the inaugural visiting artist at the UK museum.

On 27 November the Kunsthalle Basel will present works by eight shortlisted finalists for the Samdani Art Award from Bangladesh alongside 16 artists from the wider Basel region in the exhibition Far Reach (until 2 January 2027).

The Samdanis’ much anticipated permanent space, Srihatta Samdani Art Center and Sculpture Park in Sylhet, will include permanent galleries and residency facilities. “We haven’t announced it publicly yet, but we started operations at the beginning of this year,” says Rajeeb.

During a period of uncertainty in Bangladesh, Samdani is hopeful. “It’s wonderful everyone is coming together during this period of transition,” he said, “We are looking forward to doing the summit sometime soon.”

Collaboration between Samdani Art Foundation in Dhaka and Delhi's Kiran Nadar Museum of Art brings the institutions—and the powerful collectors behind them—closer together

The non-commercial Dhaka Art Summit is helping to raise the international profile of South Asian artists

Modernist paintings by artists such as Zainul Abedin and Mohammad Kibria soared past their estimates at recent sales in New York

#9005. Ten products that upgrade office interiors

The following products for offices published on our Showroom section allow for streamlined workplaces that don’t compromise on aesthetics.

These include desks, sit-stand tables as well as those with integrated outlets, modular seating systems and ergonomic task chairs.

Global designers and brands aimed to boost productivity through these items, whether that be by reducing desktop clutter, providing spontaneous opportunities for meetings and light work, or correcting posture to make long periods of sitting less taxing on the body.

Read on to find out more about this selection of workplace furniture.

TOT table by Isern Serra for Omelette Editions

A bisected tabletop with electrical outlets tucked neatly inside characterises this co-working desk by Spanish designer Isern Serra for furniture brand Omelette Editions

Supported by cylindrical legs, the TOT table provides a 12-socket power board, allowing wires to be neatly concealed to eliminate excess visual and physical tabletop clutter.

Muku task chair by Foster + Partners for Okamura

Japanese furniture brand Okamura has released a sleek office chair designed by eminent British studio Foster + Partners.

Muku comes in a sober trio of colourways – light grey, dark grey, red and black – all partly made from recycled materials: recycled aluminium for the frames, and recycled fishing nets for the mesh seat upholstery.

Pullman Modular seating system by NaughtOne

All three segments in the Pullman Modular system feature high backs, creating visual seclusion, sound-dampening and room division in open plan interiors.

Dynamism is given to steel and plywood in this task chair by designer Alina Schnizler for German brand Wilkhahn.

WiChair features a thick, strong spring beneath its seat, which gives bounce to the structure and encourages active sitting.

Indoor landscapes are created via this undulating modular sofa system created by designer Francesco Rota and Italian brand Lapalma.

HUB aims to create islands of activity in open plan spaces, creating space for working, meeting, conversing and waiting.

TNK500 Aurea task chair by Alegre Design for Actiu

Spanish brand Actiu worked with design firm Alegre Design on this task chair, which has a distinctively metallically-finished frame.

TNK500 Aurea supports healthy posture when working, and is made from almost 60 per cent recycled materials.

Konzert office furniture system by Paolo Dell’Elce for Knoll

Complete private office fit-outs are made cohesive with US furniture brand Knoll and Italian designer Paolo Dell’Elce’s new furnishing system.

Konzert comprises configurable wall panels, tables, seating and storage that come in various curated colourways and finishes.

Seated and standing work and meetings alike are made possible by this series of tables by office furniture brand Actiu.

Menssula sit-stand work tables come in various sizes and formats, all containing an electrically-powered height raising mechanism.

Norwegian designers Andreas Engesvik and Jannicke Grung have created a compact and lighthearted task chair for Flokk-owned furniture brand HÅG

HÅG Minu comes in seven designer-curated curated colourways and aims to bring the comfort and casualness of residential furniture to workplaces.

British furniture brand Boss Design aimed to bring adaptability and personalisation to this range of office booths.

Eden pods can be fitted out with lounge furniture, tactile cladding and finishes, and planters on their roofs to bring the health and wellbeing of plants into workplaces.

#9004. An Interview with Surreal Salon 18 Winner, River Reishi

We are so excited to share our interview with Surreal Salon 18 winner, River Reishi, selected by guest juror, Swoon. On the occasion of the win, we spoke with Reishi about the work in the show, the history of Surreal Salon, and her upcoming travels.

Juxtapoz: Congrats on the big win! Talk about the winning work, what the story behind it is, the process, and even the process of submitting it to the Surreal Salon?River Reishi: The piece is called Surface Tension. It shows a figure emerging from dark water, her hands reaching forward as if she is about to break through the surface and step into our world. She is half submerged, suspended in that strange moment between two realms. Around her is an ephemeral field of black sand and amber.

From land, the surface of water looks smooth and transparent, almost empty. But of course it hides an entire world that is not ours. I have always been fascinated by that threshold. The installation tries to hold that exact moment where the two worlds meet.

The sculpture also glows faintly from within, which was a little hard to see in the bright gallery lighting but becomes visible as you approach. I like that quiet surprise. The piece looks still at first, but there is a sense that something is about to happen. Water is often a symbol of life, but it also carries danger and power. Louisiana and the Gulf region know that reality very well. I think some of that tension found its way into the work.

The black sand surrounding the sculpture is loose and hand-drawn into patterns, so the installation only exists in that form for a short time. Even small vibrations change it. I am interested in that fragility, in works that cannot quite stay fixed.

It was already an honor to be included in a show curated by Caledonia Curry (Swoon). When I arrived to install the piece and saw the other works for the first time, I remember thinking how haunting and memorable every single one was. So hearing the piece announced as Best in Show later that night felt surreal in the truest sense.

Had you followed the Surreal Salon in past years? What did you know about it? I had heard about the Surreal Salon through the pop surrealist art community for years, but this was the first time I lived close enough to attend in person. I kept hearing that it felt a little like an unofficial kickoff to Mardi Gras season, that people came in elaborate costumes and that the whole evening had this celebratory, slightly otherworldly atmosphere.

What I did not realize until participating this year was that some people actually design their costumes based on the artwork in the exhibition. That was amazing to see. At one point someone came up to me wearing a costume inspired by my piece, and getting to watch him model it and explain how the sculpture influenced the design completely made my night. It felt like the work had briefly stepped out of the gallery and into the room!

Also, it was a wonderful addition to have SWOON be the juror for this year's contest. I have done it in the past, and it was hard, fulfilling work. What did you know of SWOON's work and did that inform your submission at all? I have admired Swoon’s work for a long time, especially her installations and the way she moves between sculpture, architecture, and public intervention. I first heard about her in 2009 when she brought the Swimming Cities of Serenissima project to the Venice Biennale. A fleet of sculptural rafts floating into one of the most formalized spaces in the art world was such an unforgettable gesture.

The act of arriving that way, without waiting for institutional permission, became part of the artwork itself. That kind of boldness has always stayed with me. It is difficult to break into the art world, especially in spaces where voice is carefully selected and curated. Seeing an artist carve out space for herself so creatively was incredibly inspiring.

I also love the direction her work has been taking recently with the Sibylant Sisters project. My own work is deeply inspired by myth and storytelling, so it has been fascinating to watch her develop that world, creating her own oracle cards and building a living mythology around the work. There is something powerful about artists inventing symbolic languages that people can enter into. So having the chance to meet her and have her encounter one of my installations was a very meaningful moment for me.

You work in a few different mediums, and sculpture and installation seem to be your focus. Talk a little bit about your process and where you feel most comfortable as a maker? I am not sure I feel comfortable in any single medium, and I think that is probably a good thing. I tend to move toward whatever material feels necessary for the idea at hand. In many ways my practice grew out of practical constraints. For a long time I did not have a large studio, so I had to find ways of making work that could expand into a space temporarily and then disappear again. Sand, modular sculptural elements, and ephemeral materials all emerged from that reality.

Over time those limitations became part of the language of the work itself. I am drawn to materials that hold a sense of fragility and transformation. Installation allows me to build an environment around the sculpture where those ideas can unfold more fully, where the viewer is not just looking at an object but stepping into a moment or a story.

What sort of artists influenced you as you began to find your own voice? And, sort of as a nice anecdote, what is the last work that made you stop in your tracks and get back into the studio and create?

Voice is an interesting concept to me as a woman, because women often face particular obstacles when it comes to the emergence of voice. It takes a certain measure of audacity to say something and commit it to art. In a way you are asking the world to listen. Because of that, I am especially inspired by women who make art without asking permission.

I mentioned earlier how powerful it was for me to learn about Swoon bringing her Swimming Cities project to the Venice Biennale. That gesture has always stayed with me, not only because of the work itself but because of the confidence behind it. The willingness to claim space in a world that does not always easily offer it. Moments like that remind me that voice is not only about what you say as an artist, but about allowing yourself to say it at all. That idea continues to shape the way I approach my own work.

As for the last artwork that made me stop in my tracks, I recently visited the Museo Nacional de Antropología in Mexico City. Walking through the galleries of figurative ceramics from different regions of Mexico was completely mesmerizing. The Mayan ceramics in particular took my breath away. There is so much spirit in them, such a sense of presence. I encountered one ceramic face that affected me deeply. I have gone back to see it several times now, and each time I leave feeling more inspired to return to sculpture.

What else do you have lined up this year? Are you someone who likes to work in a gallery situation, or do you prefer alternative means to show your work? This summer I will be working with Raf Gallery in Reykjavik, Iceland during the month of August. A total solar eclipse will pass directly over Reykjavik on August 12, and later that month the city celebrates Menningarnótt, a large citywide festival of arts and culture.

Raf Gallery works with both artwork and Baltic amber jewelry, and I have always been drawn to amber as both a material and a mythological object. For the exhibition I will be installing sculpture and a sand installation that tells the myth of the birth of Baltic amber while also reflecting on eclipse mythology and the relationship between darkness and light.

The sand will come from the local shoreline, and at the end of the exhibition I invite the community to dismantle the installation with me. We carry the sand back to the ocean and return it with a wish, prayer, or intention.

I love Iceland deeply. The black sand I often use in my installations was inspired by the volcanic beach at Reynisfjara, so being able to create work there during such a rare celestial moment feels very meaningful.

As for where I like to show my work, I enjoy many different contexts. My installations have appeared in galleries, museums, empty storefronts, and even city halls. But my favorite place for ephemeral work is the beach.

When I lived near the sea in Washington State, friends and I would sometimes build temporary altars from flowers, driftwood, shells, and plants as offerings to the water. The tide would slowly carry everything away. There is something very special about building something together that only exists for that one night.

What did you like about the whole Surreal Salon experience? What were some of the highlights?The whole evening had an incredible energy. The costumes alone were extraordinary, and everywhere you looked there was another small moment of creativity unfolding. Music, conversation, artists reconnecting, people discovering work for the first time. It felt celebratory in the best way.

There was also an unexpected moment early in the night. Someone accidentally backed into the platform holding my installation, and when the platform shifted the sand vibrated and many of the detailed designs disappeared. Thankfully the person who tripped was completely fine, which was the most important thing. But in a strange way the moment also revealed something essential about the work. Some people had assumed the sand had been glued down or painted in place. When it shifted, it suddenly became clear that the entire surface was loose and hand-drawn. I sat beside the piece and carefully repaired it, re-drawing the patterns into the sand and amber while people watched.

For me that moment captured the spirit of the work. The installation only existed in that exact form on that particular night. It could be recreated, but it would never be exactly the same again. Everyone there was witnessing something temporary, something that belonged only to that moment in time. And in a way that felt very fitting for the Surreal Salon itself.River Reishi is a multidisciplinary artist whose sculptures and ephemeral sand installations explore myth, grief, and the mysterious threshold between worlds. Drawing on feminine water deities and ancient storytelling traditions, she works with materials such as sand, amber, and light to create environments that exist only briefly in time.See more at riverreishi.com and on Instagram @riverreishi.

#9003. The Laowa 24mm f/2 Zero-D Tilt-Shift Is the Fastest Tilt-Shift Lens Ever

The Laowa 24mm f/2 Zero-D Tilt-Shift Is the Fastest Tilt-Shift Lens Ever

Laowa has officially announced the 24mm f/2 Zero-D Tilt-Shift lens. Built for architectural and commercial photography, the full-frame lens also works on Fujifilm GFX and Hasselblad XCD medium-format cameras thanks to its large image circle.

With its f/2 aperture, the new Laowa 24mm f/2 Zero-D Tilt-Shift is an especially fast tilt-shift lens. Canon’s 24mm TS-E Tilt-Shift Lens for EF-mount cameras, for example, is an f/3.5 lens. Nikon’s F-mount PC-E 24mm lens is also f/3.5. Fujifilm’s GF 30mm f/5.6 T/S, which is effectively equivalent to about 24mm, is clearly much slower than the new Laowa lens.

Laowa says that thanks to the 24mm f/2 Zero-D Tilt-Shift’s fast f/2 aperture, the fastest aperture of any tilt-shift lens ever made for any format, it is significantly better-suited to low-light and night-sky photography than any other tilt-shift lens before it.

Despite its fast aperture, it’s also a relatively compact and lightweight lens for its class. The lens is 119 millimeters (4.7 inches) long with a maximum diameter of 93 millimeters (3.7 inches). It weighs 860 grams (1.9 pounds) and accepts 77mm front filters.

The lens features 13 elements arranged across 10 groups. It promises to minimize distortion through optical corrections, hence the “Zero-D” in the model name, and keep lines straight throughout the frame, from center to edge. Laowa also promises high resolution, strong contrast, and minimal reflections and ghosting. PetaPixel will be putting the lens to the test in real-world situations to verify these claims.

The manual focus lens can focus as close as 0.25 meters (9.8 inches), resulting in a maximum magnification of 0.19x. It’s not quite a macro lens, but it should work well enough for foreground elements in a scene.

The shift range is ±12 millimeters, while the tilt range is ±10 degrees. However, Laowa notes that the precise tilt and shift range may vary “slightly” depending on the selected camera mount. Tilt-shift lenses like this often offer reduced ranges on medium-format cameras because of their larger image sensors. However, in this case, Laowa says that the lens retains “its full” range on Fujifilm GFX and Hasselblad XCD medium format cameras.

The Laowa 24mm f/2 Zero-D Tilt-Shift lens is available for Sony E, Canon RF, Nikon Z, L-Mount, GFX, and XCD mirrorless camera systems. It is available now for $1,249.

Further, Laowa has also announced that its 55mm and 100mm f/2.8 Tilt-Shift 1x Macro lenses are now available for Hasselblad XCD cameras as well. They are also $1,249 each.

#9002. iMac With M6 Review: The Best All-in-One Computer for Photographers

iMac With M6 Review: The Best All-in-One Computer for Photographers

The updated iMac with M6 may not bring a new design, display, or major new features, but it is still a competent, straightforward Mac with a lot to offer.

It does its job, looks good doing it, and is about as fuss-free as any computer can be. PetaPixel Score 8/10 ProsPractical and stylish designGood built-in screen for photographyPowerful enough for photo editing and some video editingColor-matched accessoriesConsNo Thunderbolt 5 or SD card slotScreen isn't very bright

It does its job, looks good doing it, and is about as fuss-free as any computer can be.

The first Mac I ever used was an iMac. It wasn’t just just any iMac, either; it was the very first iMac model ever, a graphite iMac G3 with its matching “hockey puck” mouse. At the time, it was running Mac OS 8, I was about eight years old, and I had no idea how computers worked. But importantly, I was hooked. I’ve had Macs ever since.

When it was finally time for me to get my own computer, rather than bogart my older brother’s machine to play games (yes, Macs can play games) and browse the very early web, I ultimately went for a Power Mac and didn’t have any more iMac experience until my parents bought an Intel-powered 21.5-inch unibody iMac over a decade ago. I helped set it up, but that was about it.

Much has changed about the iMac since I puttered around frankly dangerous message boards and forums on the iMac G3 and handled IT on an Intel iMac in the 2010s. In many ways, I think the iMac has lost most of its prominence in the Mac lineup. Older iMac computers were iconic, in homes and school computer labs everywhere. But consumer preferences shift. A lot of people go for laptops now, and I understand why. Professionals and power users might go for a desktop, but typically something like a Mac Studio.

I’m here to tell you that while the iMac may never reclaim its elevated position on the Mac totem pole, people should definitely take a good, long look at the newest M6-powered iMac. It’s relatively affordable and powerful, gorgeous to look at, and very convenient. What’s not to like?

Speaking of “affordable,” while the iMac with M6 starts at $1,499 with two Thunderbolt/USB 4 ports, that’s not the machine I have here for testing. I’m using the iMac with four Thunderbolt 4 ports, which starts at $1,699. The move to more ports also means going from the 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU M6 chip to the M6 with 12 CPU and 12 GPU cores.

It still starts with 16GB of unified memory and a 256GB SSD either way, but the four-port iMac also supports up to 32GB of RAM instead of 24GB and up to a 2TB SSD instead of 1TB. The higher-end starting iMac also has 2.5Gb Ethernet on its power brick.

The exact configuration I’m testing is the four-port iMac with M6, 16GB of unified memory, and a 512GB SSD. It has a beautiful blue finish. It is $1,899.

As mentioned, the iMac can come with either two or four rear Thunderbolt 4 ports. Unfortunately, there’s no Thunderbolt 5 here. While I admit Thunderbolt 5 ports are probably overkill for many prospective iMac buyers, it would be nice to have at least a couple on the higher-spec machine.

If I had to keep levying complaints against the iMac, I might also say that it’d be nice to have a built-in SD card slot somewhere, as we get on the MacBook Pro and Mac Studio. It’d also be nice to have a couple of USB-A slots for older accessories. That’s about where the knocks stop.

There’s a lot going for the iMac, not least of which is that it is pretty pretty to look at. It comes in six different bright colors and a seventh silver option for those who hate fun. In all seriousness, all seven colorways look great. I think the blue version that Apple sent for review is among the best options.

The front has a soft blue finish with a color-matched Touch ID Magic Keyboard (without a number pad) and a blue Magic Mouse. You can also get a color-matched Magic Trackpad instead for an extra $50. I’m generally a Trackpad man, but I wanted to use the blue Magic Mouse to feel fashionable. There’s also an optional color-matched keyboard with the number pad. It’s an extra $30.

The side and rear of the main chassis are a much darker blue, creating a lovely contrasting two-tone look. It even ships with a light blue USB-C cable for charging the keyboard and mouse and a color-matched power cord that connects to the big ol’ power brick.

I suppose I also don’t like that there’s a separate power brick. It houses the 2.5GbE port and is the classic glossy white plastic Apple uses for its bricks. I put the brick on the floor, as I suspect many people will, and it got very scratched almost immediately. Oh well. The cord that connects the iMac to the brick attaches to the computer via magnets, which delivers a super satisfying snap. I thought that might mean the cord would quickly release if I stumbled over the power cable, but it’s too strong a magnet for that. Don’t think of it like MagSafe on a MacBook; it’s not that.

The baby blue stand is well made. It’s very easy to tilt without ever feeling loose or wobbly. Unfortunately, the stand doesn’t have any height adjustment, which some users may find limiting. You can buy the iMac with a VESA Mount Adapter at no additional charge, but that means you don’t get the stand at all.

The iMac has a six-speaker sound system with force-canceling woofers. While not my area of expertise or focus, I find the overall sound quality good, though a bit lacking in the lows. There’s not a lot of bass here, if that’s something you’re into. Fortunately for me, I don’t like bass-forward speakers or sound profiles, so I really enjoyed listening to music on the iMac while working. The speakers don’t sound quite as nice as the ones on the Pro Display XDR I use primarily, but that’s a reasonably high, expensive bar to clear. The iMac’s speakers can also get impressively loud, if that’s what you’re into. The iMac also has a standard 3.5mm headphone jack with high-impedance headphone support on the side.

The iMac has Apple’s fairly standard 12MP Center Stage camera with Desk View and 1080p resolution. I’ve used this camera quite a bit over the years, and it’s serviceable enough for FaceTime and meetings. The same goes for the “studio-quality” three-mic array on the iMac. I’m not sure what “studio-quality” really means, but the mic quality is fine for typical daily use cases. If you want to make high-quality podcasts or videos, you’ll likely want a dedicated external camera and mic setup.

Now to the display. That’s a huge part of why you get an iMac, right? A Mac mini can certainly deliver better value, but you need to get all the accessories and screen. The iMac simplifies things greatly. You unpack it you’re off and running. Baby, you’ve got a stew going.

The iMac has the same 24-inch 4.5K Retina display as before. It has 4480 x 2520 resolution, an LED backlight, 500 nits of maximum brightness, and Wide color (P3) color gamut. This is where the iMac can either win someone over or arguably lose some people.

For me, a photographer, 500 nits of brightness is plenty. Arguably, for those who like to print, like me, even that is way too bright. Something I hoped to be able to do with the iMac is set it to a specific nits brightness, say 120 nits, a good value for printing workflows. However, while you can customize the white point, you cannot set a specific brightness. You can obviously just adjust the screen’s brightness until it seems right or calibrate it with an external device, but with some Mac displays, you can just pick a value and go.

For video editors, especially those working with HDR content, the iMac will prove insufficiently luminous. This is not one of Apple’s high-end panels in terms of brightness.

It’s also not a high-end panel in terms of color rendering, but it’s a genuinely good built-in screen. Black levels leave a bit to be desired compared to a higher-end MiniLED screen or especially an OLED, but the iMac’s Retina display looks good. It’s sharp, vivid, and you can absolutely enjoy looking at photos and watching movies on it.

If you are very serious about photography, I would recommend a dedicated calibration device to really dial things in, but otherwise I’ve had no issues.

By the way, while I don’t mind Apple’s glossy displays in controlled environments like my office, if you do want a nano-texture glass display instead, that’s available on configurations with at least 24GB of unified memory for an extra $200.

Overall, the iMac with M6 looks and feels great. While there are some areas where I think Apple could improve the iMac’s usability, I have zero issues with its aesthetics. Ultimately, style matters, and Apple hits all the high notes there.

Ultimately, the only real upgrade here with the newest-generation iMac is what’s inside. The design and display match the M4 version released in 2024, but the M6 chip is new. I’ve already discussed the M6 quite a bit in my recent Mac mini review, but the gist is that the M6 has Apple’s fastest CPU cores to date and improved performance for AI tasks.

That’s generally great news for photographers because many tasks in industry-standard software like Adobe Lightroom Classic and Photoshop are CPU-reliant and increasingly use AI. Win-win, right?

Generally, yes. Overall, Adobe Lightroom performance is good, about 10% better than the M5 MacBook Pro I tested last year. What’s notable here is that the MacBook Pro in question has twice as much unified memory as this iMac, which does matter. It’s not an entirely fair fight, and yet the M6 chip comes out on top by a healthy margin.

Looking at the category breakdown, we also see something interesting compared to the M6 Mac mini. Whatever was going on with that computer and JPEG exporting is not an issue here on the M6 iMac. To make the charts easier to read, I’ve included one in the gallery below with the Mac mini outlier result removed.

Ultimately, the M6 iMac is really good in Lightroom. It doesn’t export quite as fast as Apple’s higher-end Pro- and Max-series chips, but it barely trails elsewhere. Real-world use feels snappy across the board, too.

Over in Adobe Photoshop, the story remains good. The iMac with M6 is even a bit better than the Mac mini with M6, although not by a huge margin. It’s hard to say whether the iMac’s thermal design is just a bit more efficient under extreme stress than the ultra-compact Mac mini, or whether software is just a little more optimized now than when the Mac mini launched. After all, that was the first M6-powered Mac, and I tested it before public launch. That’s just speculation, though.

What’s not speculative is that the iMac is testing better than the Mac mini in some applications. That’s still true in Premiere, although only barely, and by such a small margin that it falls healthily within the margin of error.

The M6 is a better chip than the M5, all else equal, so you can really see the difference memory can make here, given that the M5 MacBook Pro with 32GB of RAM outperforms the M6 with 16GB in Premiere. If you’re serious about video editing and use Premiere a lot, it is worth considering upgrading to 24GB or 32GB of unified memory.

In our last benchmark, DaVinci Resolve, the M6 iMac really struts its stuff. Again, this could be optimization-related, because Blackmagic Design has updated Resolve since the Mac mini launched, and there’s no big reason the results should be this much better. But hey, don’t stare a gift horse in the mouth, right? These results are impressive.

During all my normal tasks, like importing and editing photos, the iMac stayed entirely silent. The fan never kicked on. It only ever spun up during Premiere and Resolve benchmark tests, and only some of the time. Even then, it was pretty quiet.

The iMac just works. It performs well, handles a wide variety of tasks, and never causes friction. Is it the most performant Mac ever? No, definitely not. I mean, look at the M5 Ultra Mac Studio. Holy cow. But that costs many times more than an iMac, and very few users will ever realize any of the benefits.

The iMac with M6 arrives with everything you need in a single, unified, sleek package. It performs well enough for most photographers, and I suspect many video users, too. It’s not a “professional” Mac, but most of us aren’t professionals with exacting demands at the very cutting edge of computing.

The new Apple iMac with M6 is a quintessential Mac. You unbox it, plug it in, and it works. It does its job, looks good doing it, and is about as fuss-free as any computer can be.

Nearly 30 years ago, when I used my first Macintosh computer, I entered the world of computers as a woefully ignorant child. But the iMac welcomed me in with its friendly, bulbous face, colorful design, and straightforward operating system. It won me over.

And while I eventually graduated beyond the iMac lineup, I truly enjoyed my time with the iMac with M6. It was like sitting down for a coffee with an old friend. We’ve both gone our separate ways, lived our lives, and yet found it so easy to pick up right where we left off.

At their best, Macs always feel accessible and familiar. The iMac certainly does.

While I have zero doubt whatsoever that the iMac is the best all-in-one computer on the market, and certainly the best for photographers, the big PC makers do have some options out there.

HP’s OmniStudio lineup is well respected and offers bigger screens than the iMac. Those are definitely great choices for those who enjoy Windows. Some are extremely cheap but have really subpar processors, so be wary.

Dell makes some that frankly kind of look like knock-off iMac computers. That’s not necessarily a bad thing, and Dell certainly has a wide range of models available at different price points. They are all called “All-in-One Desktop” computers, so you need to carefully look at exactly which model you’re considering.

Other manufacturers, including Acer and Lenovo, are in on the game, too.

Yes. The iMac with M6 is a great all-in-one for people who greatly value simplicity and performance.
