Malika Favre and Kumkum Fernando blend music, mythology and '60s flower power.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Forty years ago, Montreux Jazz Festival brought together the great US pop artists Andy Warhol and Keith Haring to create the poster design for the annual event. The result was a vibrant fusion of styles celebrating jazz music and rhythm. Now, the festival has repeated the experiment for just a second time, uniting two acclaimed contemporary artists for a dream collaboration.

The 2027 poster design was created by the French illustrator Malika Favre and the Sri Lankan sculptural artist and designer Kumkum Fernando. The former's distinctive geometric graphic style merges with the latter's colourful retrofuturism in a striking maximalist design that channels diverse influences into the form of a divine being that represents music as a joyful, spiritual journey.

Montreux has a long history of artist-designed posters. Other previous contributors have included David Bowie, Jean Tinguely, Yoann Lemoine (Woodkid), Lakwena, Kévin Germanier and Christian Marclay.

Keith Haring designed for the festival twice. For his second commission, in 1986, he worked with Andy Warhol as a collaborator. The festival invited Malika to adopt a similar approach for her second contribution, ten years after her first design for Montreux.

While her 2017 poster stood out for its minimalism, the new design goes in the opposite direction. A densely packed arrangement of colour and shapes creates a fantastical figure that looks like a cross between a robot, sacred altar and a jukebox. In fact, the design is also being turned into a sculptural vinyl cabinet (see further below).

“I fell in love with the festival on my very first visit in 2017. The poster I created for that edition remains one of my personal favourites to this day. I knew it would be hard to match, so I wanted to take the opposite approach: to create a work bursting with colour, as maximalist as the first one was minimalist. Kumkum was the ideal artist for this,” Favre says of the collaboration.

The design draws on diverse influences, including South Asian traditions, retro-futurism and '60s counterculture. The flowers evoke the lakeside quays of Montreux but also the flower power movement of the hippie era, a nod to the fact that Montreux Jazz Festival was founded during the 1967 Summer of Love. The floral patterns also subtly outline lips, kisses and female faces – symbols of love, pleasure and sexuality that recur throughout Malika's artistic universe.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

“I had this vision of music blooming in Montreux, this feeling of the entire town coming alive during the festival,” Favre adds. “I wanted to convey that joy. The world is going through strange times, and a festival like Montreux is an opportunity to celebrate. For me, flowers also symbolise eroticism, an explosion of the senses and the pleasures found in music. I always like to tuck in something a little cheeky, and I thought I could bring that touch of a feminine sensuality. When I sent the first flowers to Kumkum he said, ‘Oh yes, that’s sexy!’”

From the outset, the idea was also to bring the poster’s divine entity into the world as a three-dimensional object, following Kumkum’s practice of creating futuristic, geometric sculptures. The result is a made-for-order vinyl cabinet with a dedicated turntable compartment and pull-out drawers for record storage.

“The spark came when we noticed the resemblance between the shape of certain religious altars and that of a jukebox, both sharing the same sense of symmetry,” Fernando says. “We imagined a kind of gateway into a sacred realm of music, a timeless entity, part retro-futuristic robot, part mythological being, that embodies music as a joyful, universal experience.”

The 61st Montreux Jazz Festival will take place on the Lake Geneva shoreline from 2 July to 17 July 2027.

#8916. John Tree forms sculptural Hoop lamp from pine for Vaarni

Designer John Tree has created the monolithic Hoop Table Lamp for Finnish brand Vaarni, combining an “almost brutalistic block of solid pine” with a hooped shade of thin pine veneer.

Vaarni, which is known for its pine furniture and accessories, used Finnish pine from a sustainably managed forest for the lamp.

Tree‘s design for the light, which was made locally in Jurva, Finland, combines two different pieces of pine to create a sculptural shape.

“One is this heavy, almost brutalistic block of solid pine that forms a stable structural element through which a single cut is made to support the second element – a hoop of thin veneer which forms a diffuser and allows light to come through in an almost magical way,” he told Dezeen.

The hoop has an integrated light source to create a diffused glow, with Tree basing the thickness of the pine used on its ability to let the light through.

The designer also let the materials lead the way when it came to the size of the shade.

“It was in some ways an exercise in reducing the two elements to their simplest geometric forms, yet governed very much by what material would allow,” he said.

“For example, we discovered that if the thin veneer hoop became any bigger, it started to distort under its own weight,” he continued.

“Thickening it was not an option, as this stopped light from going through so we naturally arrived at an optimum form defined by the material.”

While Tree has worked with pine before, he said he hasn’t previously had the opportunity to explore the material’s properties to the extent he did for this project.

“The expertise that Vaarnii have with this material meant that we could do some very precise and complex technical details,” Tree said.

“It was interesting to see how much a material can be elevated with care and precision in its manufacture,” he continued.

“Hoop is a little celebration of pine, a humble material that can do some amazing things.”

Vaarni has previously showcased “brutal and sophisticated” furniture at 3 Days of Design and designed a chair and footstool with Faye Toogood.

#8914. this installation by jakob kudsk steensen considers the origins and agency of life

years of extensive underwater documentation comes together to question human-centered ideas of nature and the exploitation of ocean resources.

Artist Jakob Kudsk Steensen worked on the installation Psychosphere for five years. Exhibited at Cisternerne, The Frederiksberg Museums, Denmark, in 2025, the installation is an amalgamation of deep-sea footage shot both by Steensen himself and the research groups involved in the project. In the work, a collaborative effort between sculptors, scientific researchers, and composers brings to life near-mystical footage of a world bubbling beneath the surface of the vast oceans. In this visual, quasi-speculative recreation of some of the most mysterious parts of planet earth, Steensen explores what it means to be a living being, starting at the volcanic sites of where it all began. By looking at the evolution of life through this lens, the artist puts into question who, or what, has agency and how we as a collective of species on this Earth should go about protecting it.

The elements of Steensen’s exhibition come together to create an image of the earliest forms of life, when gases spewed from ocean rocks and, under intense heat and compression, formed the initial material of DNA, the genetic material that is the backbone of life. In collaboration with writer and theorist Melanie Challenger, they worked within her original concept of ‘psychospheres,’ or the idea that the psyche is what separates living beings from matter. In a text for the exhibition, she writes, ‘So, what makes life unique? The most obvious answer is that living beings do things for reasons.’ She gives examples of how animals have different mechanisms for survival, unlike matter such as rock or water, which reacts, degrades, and grows passively in response to other forces.

Moving from the theory of how DNA was created to the personal agency of organisms, she comes to the conclusion that perhaps we should see ‘the world not as a biosphere of genetic resources but as a psychosphere (my word) of diverse agents alters our perspective and thereby our values and priorities.’ With this sentiment, Challenger offers a model for viewing interspecies interactions that doesn’t prioritize humans—which she acknowledges have been the source of terrible environmental destruction—but one in which ‘every living being becomes a self – a locus of meaning.’ It is from this idea that Steensen starts to build his world in the dark, dank depths of the Cisternerne, materializing the ideas within Challenger’s psychosphere through both his captured images and his sculptural imaginings of the worlds that exist deep beneath the ocean’s surface.

installation view of Jakob Kudsk Steensen’s Psychosphere at Cisternerne in Copenhagen, 2025 | image by David StjernholmJakob Kudsk Steensen’s Psychosphere, 2025, still, commissioned by Cisternerne, The Frederiksberg Museums, Denmark

The Cisternerne, part of The Frederiksberg Museums, is an old water reservoir located beneath the Copenhagen’s surface. The space is cold and humid, creating puddles of water that have condensed on the ground. Traversing the pockets and archways of the space puts the viewer in another wet world, not too dissimilar from the ones that glow on the screens in Steensen’s installation. The videos that play are reflected in the water that sits still on the floor. In an interview with the museum, Steensen remarks on how this mirroring creates ‘a parallel world beneath.’ He remembers his own experience diving, where the bubbles released from his breath would float above him and create a mirror that reflected the world he was diving in.

Steensen captured some of these videos himself while diving from the Azores to the Aeolian Islands. Additionally, through a collaboration with the research vessel REV Ocean/REV Aurora, he was able to create a view of underwater volcanic landforms and marine fossils. Dotting the Cisternerne space were three forms of sculptural work. Abiogenesis is the central, freestanding piece near the center of the exhibition. Orogeny, a series of interactive glass sculptures, draws inspiration from the artist’s expeditions to deserts that were once sites of massive bodies of water. The Amorphous series is made of resin and fiberglass and takes its form from the artist’s sketches and the shapes of extinct sea lily specimens.

interview with Jakob Kudsk Steensen for the exhibition ‘Psychosphere’ | video by Frederiksbergmuseerne

Following the Copenhagen show, Psychosphere was brought to the 2025 United Nations Ocean Conference with ArtExplora. Adapted into an immersive LED tunnel, this iteration of the exhibition was presented to expand the ongoing dialogue about how to protect the deep sea. With renewed interest in deep-sea mining, there has been a movement to expand the rights of the organisms that live in this environment, moving toward an understanding that there is a duty to protect all species and not to prioritize resource extraction over environmental protection.

Ultimately, Psychosphere is a project about abiogenesis, or, as Steensen puts it, ‘the belief in the origin of life as something that evolved from non-organic matter billions of years ago, under the high pressures and gases of deep-sea volcanoes.’ It invites us to reconsider our understanding of life and our place within it with Steensen asking us to recognize the agency and significance of organisms beyond the human. Here, the installation offers a vision of the ocean as a world of interconnected beings, each with its own form of existence and meaning.

commissioned by: Cisternerne, The Frederiksberg Museums, Denmark | @frederiksbergmuseerne

A Brighton studio of Northerners, a 25-hour RPG and a free game engine. It’s set in 2002, so nobody has a smartphone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Plenty of Pokémon imitators have come along over the years, with the most brazen in recent years being Palworld. But look at 2023's Cassette Beasts, and you see how a creature-collecting game can offer a unique twist without following the same mascot-based formula. For one, it wasn't really about catching creatures but recording and then transforming into them yourself. Speaking to Bytten Studio's co-founder, art and game director Jay Bayliss, it had been important very early on to consider how Cassette Beasts would distinguish itself.

"We had the idea of fusion as a central mechanic, which Pokemon can't tap into because Pikachu is a mascot that you can't dilute by merging it with a thousand other beasts to get new beasts," he explains. "We also thought about focusing on the human characters, so maybe the beasts could be a reflection of the human characters, which led to the idea of transforming into them."

It also helped that Cassette Beasts aimed itself at a slightly older audience compared to every Pokemon game always having you start out as yet another schoolkid, though its British humour and sensibilities also stood out, which is something the Brighton-based studio is leaning even more directly on with its upcoming sequel.

Cassette Beasts 2002 is set in London (as well as its alternate world of Nodnol), but it aims not to give the tourist version of the capital, but a quieter Zone 6 suburb version of it, with the town of Elmwich.

"We don't lean into a certain Paddington-esque twee Britishism about it," Bayliss explains. "Crucially, we're Northerners living down South in Brighton; we don't really play with that twee Britishness. We enjoy portraying quite a mundane, crappy version of suburban English life. We're so bored of the Harry Potter-esque upper middle-class boarding school fantasy take on it. I think this version's more fun."

As the title's palindrome suggests, Cassette Beasts 2002 is also set in 2002. That appeals to me personally, much like one of my favourite indie games released earlier this year, Perfect Tides: Station to Station, because it taps into my formative teen years. "The early 2000s also mark this crossing point between the analogue and digital age," Bayliss explains. "The internet exists, but you don't have smartphones. People do have mobile phones in the game, but we haven't got the Panopticon of social media. For artists younger than me, they reflect on this ethereal time they just missed out on, just before we had the baggage of the modern world overwhelming you."

It was also important to reflect the era's aesthetic and fashion. "Skewing male, game developers often don't appreciate fashion, but if you go on TikTok and social media, people are very interested in noughties fashion," Bayliss explains. "There's a lot of interest in exploring that time that we don't discount, and that's reflected in the fashion sensibilities of the characters and the character designs themselves as well."

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Perhaps a major visual shift with this sequel is a more 3D one. Well, it's a case of perspective, literally. The original Cassette Beasts, while presented in the traditional top-down perspective of classic Pokemon and other 8- and 16-bit RPGs, was actually made in a 3D engine, albeit with environments given pixelated textures to match its 2D character sprites. In Cassette Beasts 2002, the camera drops down so things are presented as a third-person 3D game, except its characters are still pixel-art sprites presented with a billboarding technique.

"We were like, what if we can design this game with higher resolution sprites, with eight directions so when you pan the camera around, it feels less awkward?" Bayliss explains. "From a technical point of view, you have to rethink how you're designing worlds, but suddenly the perspective and scale you have in these worlds is very different. If you took the first game and dropped the camera down, it would probably feel very small, so it changes how we sculpt and design the world."

Cassette Beasts 2002 is also developed with the open-source Godot engine, which more indies are turning to. Although Bayliss recalls the challenges of porting the game's predecessor, which was developed with Godot 3, the latest iteration, Godot 4, that the studio is using has greatly improved features, including porting and performance, that make it a more viable alternative to Unity.

"If you sign up to Unity, you're kind of on the hook for any changes that Unity makes, whereas with an open-source engine, if you don't like changes, you can change the engine," Bayliss explains. "I think the flexibility of Godot is what allows a team of two full-time developers to make a big 25-hour RPG. It's just a very uncomplicated engine - you make stuff, you put it in, it's in the game. If there's anything that you need to fix, you don't have to submit a bug report to the back-end team and hope they fix it in the next two years; you just go in and fix it yourself."

Cassette Beasts 2002 is releasing in March 2027 for PC, Xbox Series X/S, PlayStation 5, and Nintendo Switch 2. You can wishlist it now on Steam.

#8912. Should I Exercise with a Phlegmy Cough? What You Need to Know

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

#8911. Sabine Marcelis takes a moment to reflect in first museum exhibition

Photography by Umberto Romito and Ivan Šuta

Sabine Marcelis has a knack for creating viral objects, from IKEA’s most-sold light to her mesmerising Candy Cube tables. Now, the designer is revealing the method behind her “magic” in an exhibition at Zürich‘s Museum für Gestaltung.

Light and Color is the first museum show dedicated entirely to Marcelis‘s work since she founded her studio 15 years ago.

In that time, the Rotterdam-based Kiwi has gone from being a student at the Design Academy Eindhoven to one of the most prolific and in-demand designers working today.

“This is the first time a museum has brought so much of my work together in one place,” Marcelis told Dezeen. “I’m always so preoccupied with what’s next that I don’t like to look back so much, but it’s amazing to have this moment to actually stop and look back for a minute.”

The show brings together 17 key pieces from the last decade and a half, going as far back as Tall Stripe – the first of many mirrors – and her signature resin Candy Cubes, which first catapulted the designer to international acclaim in 2014.

But Marcelis is adamant it should not be considered a retrospective.

“I didn’t want the show to feel like a retrospective in the sense of a chronological archive,” she said. “I wanted to select a variety of projects that each show a different way of working with light and colour.”

Rather than chronologically, the exhibits are arranged by colour, blending into each other like the soft gradients she favours in works like her curved glass chaise longues for the Barcelona Pavilion.

Her favourite materials – glass, resin and stone – recur throughout the exhibition, with carefully placed spotlights showing off the play of reflections and shadows the designer has learned to elicit through years of experimentation.

A prime example is her Lokum coffee table for Acerbis, stacked on top of each other on a curved wall to show the gradients of colour and water-like reflections created when the glass is seen at different angles and levels of illumination.

There are also two room-scale installations, reminiscent of Yayoi Kusama‘s Infinity Mirror Rooms, throwing back endless reflections of Marcelis’s viral IKEA “donut lamp” and the towering three-metre-tall Column lava lamp for Mathmos.

For the show’s curator Damian Fopp, these are less about Instagram bait and more about allowing visitors to experience the full visual effect of these objects in real life, rather than through a screen.

“Her work circulated widely as images, but no institution had looked at it as a whole,” he said. “This also made it interesting to shift the conversation back from online to physical.”

“And we wanted to show what lies behind those calm, effortless images: the testing, prototyping and production that I discovered when I visited her studio in Rotterdam.”

A mini-documentary and a book commissioned for the exhibition pull back the curtain on what it takes to create these perception-bending pieces with her team.

Over the years, these have become more ambitious in scale as well as sustainability, pivoting to 99 per cent biobased resin for her production and creating installations for the likes of Coachella and Apple HQ,

But no matter the size of the project, Marcelis says that materials remain her North Star.

“I wrote a one-sentence summary of what my studio does ten years ago,” she remembered. “‘A studio for material, installation and object design. Forever in search of magical moments within materiality and manufacturing processes to create unexpected experiences.'”

“I wouldn’t change that sentence today if I had to make the same summary again.”

#8909. Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

The same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

#8908. cantilevered pavilion by APAP extends 1970s woodland house in nicosia

defined by shifting woodland shadows by day, the glass and concrete pavilion transforms at night through a tailored lighting installation that recasts its architectural geometry.

APAP edited by christina vergopoulou November 4, 2026 3 min

Designed by architecture practice APAP, DIAGONAL is a residential extension to a 1970s dwelling situated on a wooded, elevated plot in Nicosia, Cyprus. Departing from the original home’s primary structural motif, defined by two parallel load-bearing walls, the project introduces an unprogrammed pavilion articulated by two horizontal planes that cantilever outward toward the central courtyard, establishing direct visual connections with the surrounding tree canopy.

Conceived by APAP Studio without a rigid functional brief, the open volume adapts to indeterminate domestic uses over time. Glazed perimeters capture the shifting patterns of foliage shadows and diurnal sunlight, turning the concrete and glass envelope into a receptive plane for natural light. After dusk, the volume functions as an illuminated vitrine via a custom four-part diagonal lighting armature suspended within the space. The bespoke fixture deploys three distinct color temperatures: very warm red light cast toward the sides, very cool white light directed up toward the ceiling, and warmer white light projected down onto the floor. This calibrated artificial lighting schema emphasizes the structural diagonal of the enclosure without requiring internal physical partitions.

#8907. Yinka Ilori reveals Tottenham Hotspur away shirt

Photography courtesy of Tottenham Hotspur Football Club

British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori has collaborated with Premier League football team Tottenham Hotspur to create a customised version of the club’s colourful away shirt.

Ilori reimagined the colourful away shirt, which was designed by Nike with a pattern of “never-before-seen visuals inspired by never-before-seen destinations”, by adding a graphic to the front and back.

On the front, in the position the sponsor logo is usually located, Ilori designed a circular motif combining the football club’s initials – THFC – with an abbreviation for London and the postcode for Tottenham, LDN17.

The lettering is bright orange with a white background.

On the rear of the shirt, Ilori created a graphic in his typical playful style around the letters COYS, which stands for Come On You Spurs.

Encircling the letters are the words “I know I am, I’m sure I am”, with the words “We are Tottenham wherever we go” around the whole graphic.

All of the lettering uses Ilori’s custom typeface, which was designed by type foundry British Standard Type for the designer in 2024.

According to the designer, who grew up in north London where the Populous-designed Tottenham Hotspur stadium is located, the collaboration aims to demonstrate the power of football to unite people.

“This project is a celebration of belonging and the power of football to bring people together,” said Ilori.

“For me, football is about the wider culture and the incredible sense of unity that comes from standing on the terraces, chanting alongside thousands of others,” he continued.

“I wanted the design to honour Tottenham Hotspur’s heritage while capturing that collective joy and spirit. The ‘Never Far From Home’ message really resonated with me, reflecting how football has the power to make you feel at home, wherever you are.”

The shirt is the latest design from the designer who has recently collaborated with brands including Brabantia and Veuve Clicquot.

Ilori also recently created a homeware and furniture collection for department store Dunelm.

#8906. 10 Signs You Might Not Really Be in Love: How to Tell the Difference

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

Wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:

Caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner plans suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future plans feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

If imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love plans a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

Shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

No respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

If your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024

Most estate planning advice assumes you will work until 60-65, accumulate wealth gradually, and have employer-provided benefits until Medicare kicks in. The FIRE path breaks every one of those assumptions. You may stop working at 35, 40, or 50 — meaning your estate plan must cover a potentially 40 to 50-year retirement, not the 20 to 25-year retirement conventional planning addresses.

This extended timeline creates unique vulnerabilities:

The SECURE Act fundamentally changed how inherited retirement accounts work, and this change matters enormously for FIRE households that have built large tax-advantaged portfolios.

Before the SECURE Act, non-spouse beneficiaries could "stretch" inherited IRA distributions over their own lifetime, allowing decades of tax-deferred growth. Now, most non-spouse beneficiaries must withdraw the entire inherited IRA balance within 10 years of the original owner's death. For a beneficiary in their peak earning years, this compressed timeline can push them into the 32% or 37% tax bracket on every distribution.

The FIRE advantage: Early retirees have years — sometimes decades — of lower taxable income between leaving work and taking Social Security or required minimum distributions. This creates a golden window for Roth conversions that no conventional retiree has.

A married couple who retires at 40 with $1.5 million in a traditional 401(k) and a $500,000 Roth IRA could systematically convert $80,000 to $100,000 per year from the traditional to the Roth, staying within the 22% bracket. Over 15 years, they convert $1.2 million to $1.5 million at a known, relatively low tax rate. Their heirs then inherit a Roth IRA that is completely tax-free — even under the SECURE Act's 10-year distribution rule.

Without conversions, those heirs would owe ordinary income tax on every dollar withdrawn from the inherited traditional IRA, potentially at 32% or higher if they are working professionals during their peak earning years. The tax savings for heirs can easily exceed $200,000 to $400,000 on a $1.5 million inherited traditional IRA.

Key Roth inheritance rule: Inherited Roth IRAs are still subject to the 10-year distribution rule, but the distributions are tax-free. The 10-year clock starts the year after the original owner's death.

A revocable living trust is the foundational estate planning tool for FIRE households. It provides three critical benefits that matter more for early retirees than conventional retirees:

Every early retiree needs three healthcare documents executed before leaving their employer:

Once you cross the $1 million net worth threshold — common in the FIRE community — asset protection becomes essential. You have decades of retirement ahead during which a lawsuit, car accident judgment, or liability claim could threaten the wealth you worked so hard to build.

For FIRE households pursuing charitable giving, a donor-advised fund (DAF) allows you to front-load charitable deductions in high-income years (or Roth conversion years), reduce your taxable estate, and distribute grants to charities over time. A DAF contribution is irrevocable and immediately reduces your estate while giving you advisory control over future grants.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Do not wait until traditional retirement age to complete your estate plan. The moment you leave employer benefits, you need a fully executed will or trust, healthcare directives, powers of attorney, updated beneficiary designations, and umbrella insurance. Many FIRE retirees leave their jobs with $1 million or more in assets and no estate plan in place. Every day without these documents is a day your family is exposed to probate, court-appointed guardianship, and preventable tax consequences.

Absolutely. If you have any assets, dependents, or strong preferences about medical care, you need at least a will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney. If you have reached FI with $500,000 or more in assets, a revocable living trust adds significant value through probate avoidance and incapacity protection.

Most non-spouse beneficiaries must now withdraw the entire inherited IRA or 401(k) within 10 years of the original owner's death. This compressed timeline can push heirs into high tax brackets. Roth conversions during your lifetime eliminate this tax burden because inherited Roth IRA distributions are tax-free.

For most early retirees, transferring your primary residence to a revocable living trust makes sense. It avoids probate on the home, enables seamless management if you become incapacitated, and does not affect your mortgage, property tax, or homestead exemption in most states. Consult your estate attorney about your state's specific rules.

Umbrella insurance provides liability coverage above the limits of your auto and homeowners policies. A $1 million umbrella policy typically costs $200 to $300 per year and protects against lawsuits, car accident judgments, and liability claims that exceed your underlying policy limits. For FIRE households with significant assets, it is one of the most cost-effective forms of protection available.

Yes, and early retirement is often the best time to do them. With no employment income, your taxable income is low, allowing you to convert traditional IRA or 401(k) balances to Roth at the 10%, 12%, or 22% bracket. This is significantly cheaper than the 32% or 37% rate your heirs might pay on inherited traditional IRA distributions.

Review your estate plan every three years at minimum and immediately after any major life event: marriage, divorce, birth of a child, death of a beneficiary, significant change in net worth, or a move to a new state. Early retirees have a longer planning horizon, making regular updates even more important than for conventional retirees.

Estate planning for early retirees is not a modified version of conventional retirement planning — it is a fundamentally different discipline. You face a longer incapacity window, a bigger healthcare gap, more exposure to tax law changes, and decades of asset protection needs. The FIRE community excels at building wealth through savings rate optimization and investment discipline. Apply that same rigor to your estate plan: execute foundational documents before leaving your job, optimize beneficiary designations for the SECURE Act, pursue Roth conversions during low-income years, and protect your assets with umbrella insurance and trust structures. The wealth you built deserves a plan that survives as long as your retirement.

#8904. Former workshop converted into contemporary Japanese home with "a sense of the passage of time"

Japanese studio Akio Isshiki Architects has transformed the home and workshop of a sheet-metal craftsperson in the castle town of Tatsuno into a modern house with a latticed wooden gate.

Architect Akio Isshiki, the founder of the eponymous studio, said he had to take a lot of different aspects into consideration when designing the project.

Among them was the location, as the two-storey home is located in a historic town known for being built around a medieval mountain castle.

“The project explores an architecture that responds naturally to the many contexts and conditions surrounding the house: the historic streetscape of the former castle town, traces of the former owner’s work as a sheet-metal craftsman, the client’s wishes, and practical constraints such as building regulations and structural requirements,” Isshiki told Dezeen.

For example, while the client had initially wanted a deck that would be connected to the dining room, the compact site made such a design difficult.

Instead, Isshiki removed part of the existing interior of the dining room to create a terrace space, which also includes a traditional-style engawa platform to connect the home with the garden.

Here, the studio added a sliding glass door that was designed so that its frame is hidden in the wall when it is closed, creating the impression of a fully open space.

Isshiki also wanted the 144-square-metre contemporary home to nod to more traditional Japanese houses.

“To sit comfortably within the townscape that retains the character of a former castle town, the spatial principles of traditional machiya – Japanese old townhouses – have been incorporated into this contemporary residence,” he explained.

“Examples include a long approach leading towards a bright garden at the back of the house, and an engawa, a narrow platform that connects the interior with the garden.”

The former workshop in front of the house was treated as a public-facing space. Where it looks onto the street, Isshiki added a large latticed, sliding gate, made from cedar, as well as a narrow entrance porch.

Inside, this multi-functional space becomes almost like an enclosed terrace. Here, Isshiki also added a small wooden toilet, inspired by those found in traditional machiya houses.

The studio kept a number of objects that were found in the old workshop, including a metal ring that now decorates a handrail next to the indoor staircase.

Isshiki relocated this staircase so that it sits at the front of the house, in the old workshop space – one of the biggest changes made to the layout of the house. A stone underneath the first step provides a space to remove footwear.

Isshiki’s studio used wood throughout the renovation, as the original building was made from timber and this material worked best with the existing neighbourhood, including a historic shrine that stands directly across from the house.

“The newly added wood, including the doors, is cedar, which is also the primary wood used in the original structure,” Isshiki said.

“Cedar is one of the most widely used types of wood in Japan and is readily available,” he continued.

“The contrast between the lighter new cedar and the existing cedar, which has darkened with age, brings a sense of the passage of time to the house.”

Akio Isshiki Architects also used earthen plasterwork in the home to create a tactile feel, while Tunisian tiles add decorative patterns in the kitchen. Here, the studio also created a built-in, combined wooden dining table and work surface.

On the top floor, which has a bedroom, living room and guest room, the studio mostly kept the original layout.

However, it added a sunken study space and a tokonoma, a recessed area used to display flowers and pieces of art.

“Through careful consideration of spatial dimensions, light, connections to the outdoors, materials, details, and relationships between spaces, the aim was to create a home that feels comfortable as a whole,” Isshiki concluded about the renovation.

His studio has previously designed a charred-cedar-clad house in Osaka and married old and new within a combined home and restaurant.

#8903. coperni closes: revisiting the fashion label’s strangest experiments in design and technology

from liquid textiles to garments embedded with microorganisms, coperni's experiments treated fashion as a platform for scientific research.

Coperni, the Paris fashion label that once sprayed a dress directly onto Bella Hadid in front of a live audience, has ceased operations. Founded by Sébastien Meyer and Arnaud Vaillant, the label spent the past few years turning some radical ideas into wearable objects.

Robot dogs walked alongside models, handbags were made from materials developed for space research, and a leather jacket became a functioning sound system. Much of this work involved collaborations with scientists and engineers, which brought onto the runway technologies rarely associated with fashion.

The news of Coperni’s closure, announced on November 4th, 2026, follows a dispute with its distributor and majority shareholder, Tomorrow. While the label’s future has come to an end, its experiments offer plenty worth revisiting. From liquid textiles that solidify on the body to clothing designed to interact with the skin’s microbiome, we look back at eight moments that made Coperni one of fashion’s most curious creative voices.

There can be no room for doubt: one of Coperni’s most recognizable moments came during its spring/summer 2023 show in Paris, when Bella Hadid stepped onto the runway to have a white dress sprayed directly onto her body. Developed with Fabrican, a material technology company founded by Spanish designer and scientist Manel Torres, the liquid contained fibers suspended in a solution that solidified into a flexible textile as it dried.

The process took place in front of the audience, with technicians gradually building the garment before a designer adjusted its neckline and cut a slit into the skirt. Within minutes, Hadid walked away wearing a fully formed dress.

Coperni Spring/Summer 23 Show | video via Coperni

For its fall/winter 2023 presentation, Coperni brought five Boston Dynamics Spot robots onto the runway to interact with models. Inspired by Jean de La Fontaine’s fable The Wolf and the Lamb, the performance imagined a possible relationship between humans and intelligent machines.

One robot gently removed a model’s jacket before returning it, while another briefly held onto Lila Moss’s handbag. The four-legged machines moved among the models and even approached the front row, turning the runway into an unusual encounter between fashion and robotics.

Coperni Fall/Winter 2023 Show | video via Coperni

For its fall/winter 2024 show, Coperni unveiled perhaps its most unusual material experiment: the Air Swipe Bag, developed with artist and researcher Ioannis Michaloudis. The translucent object was made from silica aerogel, an extremely lightweight solid consisting of approximately 99% air by volume and 1% glass-like material.

Associated with NASA’s research into capturing cosmic dust, aerogel gave the bag its pale, cloudlike appearance. Weighing around 33 grams, the sculptural accessory retained the recognizable Swipe silhouette despite its extraordinary material composition.

Air Swipe Bag by Coperni, made from 99% Air and 1% Glass | video via Coperni

The same collection introduced a different kind of wearable audio device: a 3D-printed handbag that doubled as a portable CD player. Based on Coperni’s curved Swipe silhouette, the metallic accessory accommodated a functioning disc player with wired headphones and a rechargeable battery.

Its appearance recalled the portable music devices of the 1990s, giving a familiar piece of consumer technology an unexpected second life as a fashion accessory.

For its spring/summer 2025 collection at Disneyland Paris, Coperni turned to an entirely different manufacturing process. Created with MIT spinout Rapid Liquid Print, the Ariel Swipe Bag was formed by extruding blue silicone into a bath of water-based gel.

The gel supported the material as a robotic nozzle drew the bag’s curved form, allowing the flexible object to take shape without conventional printed supports. Named after Disney’s mermaid character, the finished bag emerged from the gel with a soft, continuous surface.

Ariel Swipe Bag, Spring/Summer 2025 | video via Coperni

Coperni continued exploring the relationship between fashion and consumer technology in 2025 with its Tamagotchi Swipe Case, developed in collaboration with Japanese toy company Bandai. The miniature accessory adapted the brand’s recognizable handbag silhouette to accommodate a functioning digital pet, reviving the pocket-sized electronic toy that became popular in the late 1990s.

It arrived alongside Coperni’s fall/winter 2025 show, which took place inside a large-scale LAN party at Paris’s Adidas Arena, where hundreds of gamers played at computer stations while models moved between them.

Sound became a central theme of Coperni’s spring/summer 2024 collection, presented at IRCAM, the music and acoustics research institute in Paris. Working with Swedish audio company Transparent, the designers developed a leather jacket fitted with functioning speakers across its chest.

The engineering is surprisingly involved. Custom cavities were shaped to accommodate the audio components, with concealed wiring leading to an amplifier and battery pack stored in the jacket’s pockets. The finished garment allowed its wearer to carry a working sound system directly on the body.

One of the label’s final experiments moved into biotechnology. Released in October 2025, the C+ collection introduced close-fitting garments treated with probiotics and prebiotics, developed in collaboration with Swiss textile company HeiQ.

The fabric incorporates a bio-based matrix designed to release beneficial microorganisms through contact with the skin, activated by body heat and movement. The collection included leggings and bodysuits intended to support the skin’s microbiome during wear. It offered a different direction for Coperni’s interest in experimental design, imagining clothing as an active material that could interact with the body long after it left the runway.

#8902. Say What? 7 Tips to Unclog Your Blocked Ears

Earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears. There are many easy ways to get relief at home.

Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort. Thankfully, there are several effective methods to help unclog your ears and restore your hearing. Listen up!

Why are my ears clogged?

Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum. Here are the most common ways your ears can get blocked:

  • Earwax in the outer ear helps prevent particles and excess water from entering the middle ear. However, if earwax builds up too much outside the eardrum, it can cause a blockage.
  • If you’ve been swimming recently, some water might be stuck in your ear canal, pushing against your eardrum. When that water hangs around too long, it can lead to a swimmer’s ear, an outer ear infection.
  • Sinus infections, ear infections, and Eustachian tube dysfunction can pressure your eardrum’s inner side.
  • Allergies can cause uncomfortable inflammation and congestion in your ears. Your sinuses, throat, and ears are connected, so when you feel stuffed up and sniffly, your inner ear feels the pain too.
  • Changes in air pressure, like when you fly, can cause uncomfortable ear pressure.

Best clogged ear remedies

1. Pop and unclog

The easiest way to unclog your ears is by “popping” them. Just pinch your nose shut, seal your lips, and gently blow. This simple technique, known as the Valsalva maneuver, won’t clear earwax or fluid but is a common trick people use on planes.

2. Swallow, yawn, or chew

The Eustachian tubes connect your middle ear to the back of your throat. They briefly open when you swallow, yawn, or chew. Altitude changes can cause these tubes to close, but chewing gum or yawning can help reopen them. Alternatively, you can try the Toynbee maneuver, where you hold your nose and swallow.

3. Ear drops

Over-the-counter (OTC) ear drops can soften and dissolve excess earwax. If you prefer a DIY approach, warm a small amount of mineral oil and use an eye dropper to apply a few drops into your ear for a few minutes.

Pro tip: Baby oil or olive oil can also be used, but make sure it’s not too hot. Additionally, diluted hydrogen peroxide drops can be helpful.

4. Warmth and gravity

To loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily.

5. Hit the steam room

Steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths. 

6. Take allergy medication

Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears.

Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort.

7. Rinse away the gunk

Rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing.

When to see your doctor

Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention.

What not to do when you have clogged ears

  • Cotton swabs: Q-tips and other cotton swabs to remove earwax can push it further into your ear canal, so don’t do it. 
  • Candling: Ear candles might seem like a fun party trick, but there’s no science to prove they work, and they’ve been shown to cause injuries.
  • Sprays: Decongestant nasal sprays can be helpful, but using them too long can lead to rebound congestion.
  • Drying solutions: A few drops of rubbing alcohol or a mixture of one part vinegar and one part alcohol can help dry out the ears when you have a swimmer’s ear. However, doing this regularly can lead to irritation.

Takeaway

Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies.

PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

Apple's first-ever touchscreen MacBook is finally here! Find my hands-on impressions below, and scroll down for rolling coverage as reactions from critics and creators start to pour in across the web.

They said they wouldn't do it. A touchscreen MacBook has been rumoured since the dawn of time (well, the noughties), but, in a quote that's been infinitely dredged up across the internet over the last couple of weeks, Steve Jobs himself decried the concept as "ergonomically terrible". But Jobs also famously asked, "Who wants a stylus?" And the answer among millions of Apple Pencil users seems to be a resounding, "Us!"

And after a few days with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, I'm happy to report that this is very much a device—perhaps even the ultimate device—for creatives. But rather than the ability to touch the screen, it's all about the quality of that 'PROLED' display itself. Turns out there's a reason Apple decided to lead with that, and not touch, in the name of the device.

Simply put, it's the best laptop screen I've ever seen. With up to 2000 nits of peak brightness, 10,000,000:1 contrast, and P3 + Adobe RGB colour, this is a best-in-class display that puts every other OLED laptop screen I've used to shame. It gives creatives a portable reference-quality display, which means it recreates video, colour and contrast as faithfully as possible. Once you've used the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, everything else looks washed-out in comparison, and for that reason alone it's impossible not to recommend for creatives – so long as the small matter of the $2,899 starting price isn't a barrier.

When it comes to touch, as I've written before, in my testing I've found it to be a nice-to-have rather than a need-to-have. Now that we're all touchscreen natives (which wasn't so much the case when Jobs made those comments in 2010), certain navigational actions just feel right, even on a laptop. Scrolling through windows, pinching to zoom in on a photo or map, scrubbing through the timeline in Final Cut Pro; there are plenty of times when touching the screen feels more intuitive than reaching for the trackpad. And Apple's subtle UI tweaks, such as having navigational icons expand when touched, make the whole thing feel more natural.

But equally, there were plenty of times when I preferred to use the trackpad – particularly when a certain level of accuracy was required. And despite Apple claiming to have produced a newly designed hinge with greater stability, it still wobbles. There's just no getting around the fact that a touchscreen on a vertical display is less ergonomic than it is on a flat one.

From a design perspective, the new MacBook Pro isn't a game-changer – unless you really missed the illuminating Apple logo (another noughties mainstay). There are improvements here and there; the Dynamic Island takes up less space than the notch, and slightly smaller bezels result in slightly larger viewing areas. But perhaps the most meaningful design change is the reduction in weight. That OLED panel has allowed for a 14% weight loss – making the 14-inch model, somewhat ironically, lighter than the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air.

But everything pales next to the screen. The PROLED XDR looks incredible. If you're looking for the most impressive visual fidelity available on a laptop, here it is. You can touch it if you like.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display is released tomorrow, with preorders available now. Prices start at $2899 for the 14-inch model, and $3399 for the 16-inch model.

And the YouTubers' reviews are making their way online too. Here's renowned Apple fan/creator iJustine's take. Like many, she's a fan of the glowing Apple logo.

And here's our sister site Tech Radar with, again, a very similar take: "While all the talk is about the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display being the first MacBook with a touchscreen, the touchscreen is arguably not its most interesting feature; it works fine, but macOS is still an operating system built for traditional laptop inputs. Instead, it’s the gorgeous tandem OLED screen and industry-leading battery life that should get you excited here."

The Verge's review is up, and it seems they share our opinion: the screen is incredible, the thinner and lighter design is welcome, and touch is... there. "Even if you love the touchscreen, you’ll use it a lot for a day or so and go back to using your laptop almost exactly the way you did before."

Hello and welcome to Creative Bloq's coverage of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. We'll be keeping this page updated with opinions from across the web, but for now, what do we think? In short, touch is nice, but it's that PROLED display that's the killer here. It's the brightest (and darkest) laptop screen we've ever used – and for creatives, having a portable reference-quality display could be a game-changer.

#8900. Are Tangerines Good for You? 5 Health Benefits You Might Love

Tangerines are not just tasty — they’re a powerhouse of nutrients. Packed with tangy flavor and vibrant orange color, these citrus delights offer a host of health benefits. From boosting your immune system to rejuvenating your skin, tangerines are nutrient-rich allies for your well-being. Let’s delve into their nutritional profile and discover why they’re a smart addition to your diet.

Tangerines are nutritional powerhouses. Here’s what each of these little champs pack under their orange belts:

Tangerines are teeny cousins of the orange but with a thinner, easier-to-peel skin. They boast a sweet and juicy flavor and pack a ton of vitamins, particularly vitamin C, as well as minerals like potassium, antioxidants, and dietary fiber.

These tiny bursts of sunshine have many benefits that can significantly enhance your health. Here’s why you might want to make tangerines a regular part of your diet:

Tangerines are loaded with vitamin C, turning them into tiny, tasty guardians for your health. This crucial vitamin supercharges your immune system by enhancing the function and effectiveness of white blood cells, which are essential for fighting off pathogens and infections. By improving the activity and response of these cells, vitamin C helps your body combat a wide range of infections more effectively.

Therefore, regular consumption of these mini-oranges satisfies your taste buds and boosts your body’s defense mechanisms — a win-win!

Want that glow? Tangerines have got you covered. They’re high in potassium, a real game-changer for regulating hydration and balancing fluid levels in your skin cells. This essential mineral keeps your skin cells plump and hydrated, warding off pesky, dry, dull patches.

Plus, potassium supports the removal of toxins and wastes, which means clearer, more radiant skin.

Tangerines are also a fantastic source of vitamin A, which strengthens the outer layer of your skin, smoothing out wrinkles and reducing fine lines. Along with vitamin C, it’s a potent antioxidant, protecting your skin from the damaging and aging effects of free radicals.

Are you having tummy troubles? Tangerines can help with a fiber boost that keeps things moving smoothly along your digestive tract.

These zesty little superheroes are your gut’s new best friends. They’re loaded with fiber that bulks up and softens things down there, making your bathroom visits smooth and speedy. This fruity fix helps manage everything from irregular pit stops to those bloated bleurgh days.

Fiber also balances your gut flora, promoting a healthy microbial environment in your intestines. This balance is crucial for optimal digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.

So, grab a tangerine to remedy your belly blues next time your gut feels out of whack.

Tangerines are a dynamo when it comes to battling serious health baddies like cancer and heart disease. These little orange wonders are loaded with flavonoids, natural compounds that help with heart health and cancer prevention.

Flavonoids help relax the blood vessels, lowering blood pressure levels and reducing the strain on your heart. This helps keep your ticker ticking smoothly and reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases like heart attacks and strokes.

But wait, there’s more! When it comes to cancer, flavonoids mess with the bad guys — cancer cells — stopping them from multiplying and spreading their nonsense around your body.

Keep your peepers sharp with a dose of vitamin A from tangerines. This essential nutrient and compounds like beta-carotene shield your eyes from age-related issues and support healthy vision. It plays a key role in creating rhodopsin, a protein in your eyes that allows you to see in low-light conditions.

Munching on tangerines helps keep your night vision in superhero shape and supports overall eye function, keeping your peepers sharp and responsive.

Furthermore, tangerines contain other essential eye health nutrients, like lutein and zeaxanthin. These antioxidants are found in high concentrations in the retina, where they help filter blue light and prevent oxidative damage, further protecting the eyes from conditions like cataracts.

Sure, tangerines are delish and make your taste buds do a happy dance, but they’re also packed with nutrients that can seriously amp up your well-being.

From giving your immune system a high-five to keeping your heart beating like a healthy drum, tangerines are basically wellness wrapped in a bright orange peel. So, go grab one and make it your main squeeze!

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024

#8899. Holst completes Adjaye-designed mass-timber library in Oregon

Photography by Christian Columbres

US architecture studio Holst has created a mass-timber library in Oregon, with a series of tall columns at the entrance and a central atrium, after taking over the project from Adjaye Associates.

The East County Library in Gresham features a trapezoidal roof structure on top of a mostly square building envelope, creating multi-storey covered entry programmes on each side.

These entry programmes are lined with massive glued-laminated (glulam) mass-timber columns that Holst said speak to a primary effect of the design: “awe and accessibility”.

“One of our major main vision points of the project was this idea of awe and accessibility,” Holst principal and creative director Brittany Shreiner told Dezeen.

Shreiner said that the accessible component comes from the dual entry programmes that open up to a plaza on one side, with space taken from a converted street, and an elevated entryway on the other that features ramps.

A rail line is located on one side and a bus line on the other, connecting the building to the wider public realm.

For the team, the building needed to be a “big civic moment”, thus the massive columned entryway. However, Shreiner said that the awe the studio aspired to create was more akin to that of a forest, and the mass timber helped them to express that.

Structurally, the building has a mix of concrete and mass timber elements, with mostly wooden floorplates and some walls, and concrete-and-steel cores.

The facade is a mix of vertical timber elements interspaced with high-performance concrete bands with scalloped shapes and vertical bands of glass.

At one point, a grey-toned concrete panelling system marks the semi-circular protrusion where the structure’s amphitheatre is.

The appearance of the building is close to the original design submitted by Adjaye Associates – Holst was the architect of record at the start.

However, after misconduct allegations against Adjaye Associates founder David Adjaye were made public in a Financial Times investigation, the studio was released from this project, among others. Adjaye denies the allegations.

Shriener said that the biggest changes in the design were the removal of screens that were supposed to overhang from the covered entryways and a tower that extended past the roof plane.

“There was still a lot of design to be done [at that time], but the bones of the building were there. The community buy-in was there. The stakeholder buy-in was there,” said Shriener.

“So, the county was definitely clear in their intention that they did not want to proceed with Adjaye as part of our team, and that they basically trusted us to bring the project forward, but they didn’t want to see a total redesign by any means.”

Having recently solidified itself as a name in the US mass timber game with a tall building in Portland, the studio focused on optimising the timber usage as it took over the design. It worked closely with local mass-timber supplier TimberLab for the materials.

One detail that stands out is the notches in the timber columns and beams that give the structure a cabin-like or residential appearance, while remaining monumental in scale.

More than just a style conceit, the notches play a role in the ceiling plane, hiding the mechanical systems and lighting.

Inside, vestibules compress the entry to the library, which then opens up into a main core that runs between the entrances, with a double-height atrium space in the middle, complete with a wood-slatted spiral staircase.

For Shriener, this middle space represents a “clearing” in the forest.

The primary book-storage spaces surround the main central area, with smaller breakout rooms and classrooms lying mostly on the perimeter.

Mass-timber elements remain visible throughout the interior spaces, with green carpets at times continuing the forest metaphor.

On the roof, a series of sawtooth lightwells bring diffuse light into the main central space, while a rooftop patio allows guests to enjoy the views of the mountains beyond.

Elsewhere in Oregon, Holst created a Gaudí-informed apartment building wrapped in wood.

Other projects that were completed after the fallout from the Adjaye allegations include the Princeton Art Museum, where David Adjaye “stepped back” from the project in the late stages, according to Princeton.

Photography by Christian Columbres

#8898. What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

From those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

You know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024

#8897. Tatiana Bilbao creates rammed-earth installation at Art Omi

Mexico-based architecture practice Tatiana Bilbao Estudio has created a large-scale outdoor installation made of rammed earth derived from local soil that’s meant to break down over time for New York arts centre Art Omi.

Tatiana Bilbao Estudio‘s Borrowed Earth installation consists of four 7.5-foot-tall rammed-earth cruciform crosses, with a shorter cross form in the centre that serves as a bench. Each form was made with compacted soil harvested from the Hudson Valley area.

Tatiana Bilbao Estudio based the design around a “repeatable basic unit” that eventually became the bench and surrounding columns.

The Borrowed Earth piece was commissioned by arts centre Art Omi, which oversees a 120-acre sculpture park at its campus in Ghent, New York.

Art Omi curator Julia van den Hout said rammed earth can be a “challenging material”, and it shaped much of the project’s design.

“They were not always crosses in our initial conversations,” van den Hout told Dezeen.

“As we started getting into the reality of trying to figure out how to construct this – because rammed earth is a challenging material to work with – and thinking structurally about how this would be built up, during those conversations, [it] shifted to being a cruciform column.”

“It also really resonated [because] it has such a strong classic modernist shape.”

The Art Omi and Tatiana Bilbao Estudio teams constructed the columns on site with guidance from rammed-earth consultant Raíz Arquitectura studio based out of Mexico.

The team used soil from a construction site just down the road from Art Omi, according to van den Hout. They mixed it with sand and lime and then packed the mixture layer by layer into wooden formwork to create the sculptures.

Van den Hout says the installation is designed to decay over a period of about two years, although the team does not have “a strict answer” about how long it will last given external elements like weather.

“It’ll be an experiment,” she said. “We don’t quite know how fast it’s going to go. It is definitely soft. It crumbles. It’s lovely and tactile in that when you touch it, you really feel that sense that erosion can happen pretty easily. But simultaneously, they feel very stable.”

Recently, MOS Architects created a sculpture at Art Omi made of aluminium, while Young Projects installed a frayed, wooden pavilion at the park in 2024.

Tatiana Bilbao Estudio completed a sprawling aquarium in 2023 in Mexico, where the studio is primarily based and also spoke to Dezeen in 2019 about the country’s rising generation of prominent female architects.
